boxes.x: Definitions Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection: SOFA rise ≥ 2 Septic shock = vasopressor to keep MAP ≥ 65 + lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid (mortality > 40%) qSOFA (RR ≥ 22, altered mentation, SBP ≤ 100) = prognostic only; not a screening tool (SSC 2021) Exam opening ABCDE + "this is septic shock from an abdominal source: time-critical" Senior help, ICU, surgeon/IR early; parallel not serial actions State the definitions in one line each, then move straight to management.

Within 1 hour Lactate (repeat if > 2) Blood cultures before antibiotics (without delaying them) Broad-spectrum antibiotics 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 (SSC: "suggest", weak) Vasopressor if MAP  65 yr not worse) Lactate clearance or capillary refill time (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: CRT-guided ≥ lactate-guided) Urine > 0.5 mL/kg/h, mentation Resuscitate to perfusion targets, not to CVP.

How much After initial bolus: give only if fluid responsive (PLR, PPV/SVV if ventilated, VTI change) CLOVERS (2023) & CLASSIC (2022): restrictive = liberal for mortality Watch for overload: rising FiO2, B-lines, VExUS congestion Which Balanced crystalloids preferred (SMART 2018: ↓ MAKE30; BaSICS & PLUS: no mortality difference) Saline: hyperchloraemic acidosis, possible AKI Albumin when large volumes needed (ALBIOS: no overall benefit; subgroup in shock) Avoid starches (6S, CHEST: AKI, RRT, death); gelatins not recommended Balanced crystalloid first, assess responsiveness before every further bolus.

Principles Identify source early: CT abdomen, US, line review Intervene within 6–12 h once resuscitated enough Least invasive effective option: percutaneous drainage > surgery when possible Remove infected devices (lines) after new access Examples Perforated viscus → laparotomy / laparoscopic washout Obstructed infected kidney → nephrostomy or stent Cholangitis → ERCP; necrotising fasciitis → radical debridement Antibiotics cannot sterilise an undrained source: say "source control within 6–12 hours".

Timing and choice Septic shock: within 1 hour (Kumar 2006: each hour delay ↑ mortality) Cover likely organisms + local resistance + risk factors (recent antibiotics, hospital, ESBL, MRSA, Pseudomonas) Abdominal: piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem ± anti-fungal if high risk PK/PD Loading dose regardless of renal function; ↑ Vd in sepsis Prolonged / continuous β-lactam infusion (BLING III 2024: ↓ mortality signal in meta-analysis) TDM for vancomycin, aminoglycosides, β-lactams Duration Short course after source control: STOP-IT (4 days ≈ longer) Procalcitonin to stop (SAPS, ADAPT-Sepsis): stop when ↓ ≥ 80% or < 0.5 µg/L; never to withhold initial therapy Daily de-escalation review "Hit hard and early, then de-escalate and stop early."

Sequence Noradrenaline first line; peripheral start acceptable short-term Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min when NA 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min (VASST: NA-sparing; possible benefit in less severe shock) Adrenaline as second/third agent; angiotensin II (ATHOS-3) in refractory vasoplegia Cardiac dysfunction Echo: septic cardiomyopathy → dobutamine if low output despite MAP Levosimendan: no benefit (LeoPARDS) Steroids Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if ongoing vasopressor (ADRENAL: faster shock reversal; APROCCHSS: ↓ mortality with fludrocortisone) Noradrenaline → vasopressin → hydrocortisone → echo-guided inotrope.

Metabolic resuscitation Vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone: VITAMINS, VICTAS negative; LOVIT: harm with vitamin C Thiamine only if deficient (alcohol, malnutrition) Immunomodulation Sepsis endotypes (hyper- vs hypo-inflammatory), precision medicine IL-1 blockade in macrophage activation-like syndrome; GM-CSF / IFN-γ in immunoparalysis: research only Blood purification (CytoSorb, polymyxin B: EUPHRATES negative) Other Beta-blockade (landiolol STRESS-L: no benefit) Personalised MAP targets; early vasopressors (CLOVERS) Mention promising ideas but conclude "not recommended outside trials".

Structure (10 marks) Definition and severity → resuscitation targets → fluids (type/amount, evidence) → source control → antimicrobials (timing, PK, duration, PCT) → vasopressors/steroids → emerging → summary Numbers to quote MAP 65, lactate > 2, 30 mL/kg, 1 hour, 6–12 h source control, NA 0.25 µg/kg/min for vasopressin, hydrocortisone 200 mg/day Name a trial for every recommendation: examiners reward evidence.

Criteria Within 1 week of insult; bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion/collapse Not fully explained by cardiac failure/overload (echo if no risk factor) PaO2/FiO2 with PEEP ≥ 5: mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe ≤ 100 2023 global definition Includes HFNO ≥ 30 L/min, SpO2/FiO2 ≤ 315, lung ultrasound in resource-limited settings Severe ARDS = P/F ≤ 100: say it, then escalate in steps.

Core Vt 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (ARDSNet ARMA 2000: mortality 40 → 31%) PBW male = 50 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4); female 45.5 + … Plateau ≤ 30 cmH2O; driving pressure ≤ 15 (Amato 2015: strongest predictor) Permissive hypercapnia, pH ≥ 7.20–7.25 SpO2 88–95% / PaO2 7.3–10.7 kPa Mechanical power Energy per minute (Vt, ΔP, RR, flow): lower is safer; avoid high RR 6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤ 30, ΔP ≤ 15.

PEEP Higher PEEP in moderate-severe ARDS (ALVEOLI, LOVS, EXPRESS: meta-analysis benefit if P/F ART 2017: staircase RM + titrated PEEP ↑ mortality → avoid prolonged high-pressure RM Short RM only after disconnection/derecruitment Individualise PEEP; avoid routine aggressive recruitment (ART).

Evidence PROSEVA 2013: P/F < 150 (FiO2 ≥ 0.6, PEEP ≥ 5), early (< 36 h), ≥ 16 h/day → 28-day mortality 33 → 16% Practice Trained team, pressure areas, ETT/line safety, eyes, enteral feed Stop when P/F ≥ 150 with PEEP ≤ 10, FiO2 ≤ 0.6 for 4 h after supine Contraindications: unstable spine, open abdomen, raised ICP (relative), pregnancy (relative, feasible) Prone early and long: PROSEVA is the single most important ARDS trial to quote.

NMB ACURASYS 2010: cisatracurium 48 h ↓ mortality; ROSE 2019: no benefit with lighter sedation and higher PEEP Use for dyssynchrony, high Pplat despite sedation, during proning Inhaled NO / prostacyclin Improve oxygenation transiently; no survival benefit, ↑ AKI with NO Rescue bridge to prone/ECMO, or RV failure Steroids Dexamethasone (DEXA-ARDS) for moderate-severe ARDS; COVID-19 (RECOVERY); CAP (CAPE COD hydrocortisone) Oxygenation improvement does not mean survival benefit.

Referral criteria (EOLIA) P/F  3 h, or  6 h pH  6 h (RR 35, Pplat ≤ 32) Despite optimal care incl. prone and NMB Evidence CESAR 2009: referral to ECMO centre ↓ death/disability EOLIA 2018: 35% vs 46% (NS), but crossover 28%; Bayesian and meta-analysis favour ECMO Contraindications Ventilated > 7 days with high settings (relative), irreversible disease, severe immunosuppression, contraindication to anticoagulation Refer early to a high-volume centre; ECMO is a bridge, not a cure.

Mortality predictors Age, severity (P/F), driving pressure, dead space fraction, non-pulmonary organ failure, immunosuppression RESP score (ECMO survival), PRESERVE score Ethics Resource allocation, candidacy, bridge to nowhere, family communication, time-limited trial, withdrawal on ECMO Finish the answer with prognosis and an ethical sentence.

HFNO / NIV FLORALI: HFNO ↓ intubation in P/F ≤ 200 and ↓ mortality vs NIV/O2 Watch HACOR score / ROX index; avoid delayed intubation and P-SILI Cause-specific CAP: early antibiotics, steroids (CAPE COD) in severe CAP Influenza: oseltamivir; COVID-19: dexamethasone, IL-6 blockade Conservative fluid strategy once shock resolved (FACTT) Treat the cause while protecting the lung.

Readiness Cause improving, P/F > 150–200 on PEEP ≤ 8, FiO2 ≤ 0.4–0.5 Haemodynamically stable (little or no vasopressor), awake (RASS 0/−1), cough, manageable secretions SBT 30–120 min T-piece or PSV 5–8 / PEEP 0–5 Failure: RR > 35, SpO2  140 or ↑ 20%, SBP > 180 or  7 days) Daily screen + daily SBT + paired sedation hold (ABC trial).

Load vs capacity Airway/lung: secretions, bronchospasm, ↑ resistance, PEEPi (COPD), effusion, oedema Brain: delirium, sedation, anxiety/psychological dependence Cardiac: weaning-induced pulmonary oedema (ischaemia, LV dysfunction) Diaphragm: ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction, phrenic injury, ICU-AW, electrolytes (↓ PO4, K, Mg), hypothyroid Endocrine/metabolic: metabolic alkalosis, nutrition, anaemia Frame it as respiratory load versus neuromuscular capacity, plus cardiac and psychological.

Mechanism Negative pleural pressure ↑ venous return and LV afterload; catecholamine surge; ischaemia Diagnosis Rise in Hb/protein > 5–6% during SBT, BNP rise, echo E/e′ ↑, lung US B-lines, PAOP > 18 Treatment Diuretics, nitrates, ischaemia treatment; extubate to NIV Suspect it in COPD + heart disease who fails within minutes with hypertension.

ICU-AW Critical illness polyneuropathy/myopathy; MRC sum score < 48 Risks: sepsis, MOF, hyperglycaemia, steroids, NMB, immobility Nerve conduction/EMG if atypical; exclude GBS, myasthenia, cord lesion Diaphragm Ultrasound: thickening fraction < 20–30% or excursion < 1 cm = dysfunction Avoid over-assistance and over-sedation; inspiratory muscle training Management Early mobilisation, glucose control, minimise steroids/NMB, nutrition, physiotherapy Prevention beats treatment: light sedation and early mobilisation.

T-piece Closest to post-extubation work of breathing; unmasks cardiac failure Higher failure rate, may delay extubation PSV 5–8 Easier, compensates tube resistance (but upper airway oedema after extubation adds similar load) Subirà 2019 (JAMA): 30 min PSV 8 → more successful extubation than 2 h T-piece After extubation (high risk) NIV or HFNO+NIV (HIGH-WEAN) for > 65 yr, heart failure, COPD, obesity Cuff leak test in high-risk for stridor → steroids 12–24 h before Choose PSV for most; T-piece when cardiac failure is suspected.

Benefits Less sedation, comfort, oral hygiene, ↓ dead space and resistance, easier weaning and mobilisation, ward discharge Timing TracMan 2013: early (day 1–4) vs late (≥ day 10) → no mortality difference; 45% of late group never needed one Consider after ~10 days if weaning not imminent; earlier in neuro injury (SETPOINT2: no outcome benefit) Technique and risks Percutaneous dilatational (bronchoscopy, US) vs surgical Bleeding, loss of airway, stenosis; NTSP safety bundles Tracheostomy does not cut mortality; it facilitates weaning.

Steps Identify and treat each cause; daily SBT or progressive reduction of PSV Tracheostomy mask trials (↑ duration), night rest on ventilator Specialised weaning unit, home NIV for hypercapnic COPD Systematic: diagnose, correct, retest, rehabilitate.

Steps pH → primary process (HCO3 / PaCO2) Compensation: Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 (± 2) mmHg Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3), normal 8–12; correct for albumin: +2.5 per 10 g/L below 40 Delta ratio (ΔAG/ΔHCO3):  2 + metabolic alkalosis Osmolar gap = measured − (2Na + glucose + urea), > 10 abnormal Always correct the anion gap for albumin in ICU patients.

GOLDMARK Glycols (ethylene, propylene) Oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid) L-lactate D-lactate (short bowel) Methanol Aspirin Renal failure Ketoacidosis (diabetic, alcoholic, starvation) In pancreatitis + alcohol Lactate (shock, ischaemia), AKA, AKI, toxic alcohol co-ingestion, thiamine deficiency Use GOLDMARK and then point to the likely ones in the stem.

boxes.t: 3. Type A vs Type B lactic acidosis
boxes.x: Type A (hypoperfusion/hypoxia) Shock, regional ischaemia (mesenteric), severe hypoxaemia, anaemia, CO poisoning Type B (no hypoperfusion) B1 disease: liver failure, sepsis (aerobic glycolysis, β2 stimulation), malignancy, thiamine deficiency B2 drugs: metformin, adrenaline, salbutamol, propofol infusion syndrome, linezolid, NRTIs, cyanide (nitroprusside) B3 inborn errors How to separate Perfusion markers (CRT, ScvO2, CO2 gap > 6 mmHg), lactate/pyruvate, response to resuscitation, drug history A lactate that does not fall with resuscitation: think Type B or hidden ischaemia.

Steps Treat the cause: resuscitate, source control, stop offending drugs, thiamine Ventilation: match respiratory compensation if intubated (avoid ↓ minute volume) Vasopressors for shock (catecholamine response falls at pH BICAR-ICU 2018: no overall benefit; pH ≤ 7.20 + AKI (KDIGO 2–3) → ↓ mortality and RRT Indicated: NAGMA with bicarbonate loss, hyperkalaemia, TCA/salicylate toxicity RRT Refractory acidosis, AKI, toxins (dialysable) Quote BICAR-ICU: bicarbonate helps in pH ≤ 7.2 with AKI.

Pyroglutamic (5-oxoproline) Glutathione depletion: chronic paracetamol + sepsis, malnutrition, liver/renal disease, flucloxacillin, vigabatrin; women HAGMA without lactate/ketones/toxic alcohol; urine organic acids (5-oxoproline) Stop paracetamol and flucloxacillin, give N-acetylcysteine Propylene glycol Solvent in IV lorazepam, diazepam, phenobarbital, etomidate High doses → HAGMA, raised osmolar gap, lactate (metabolised to L-lactate), AKI Monitor osmolar gap (> 10–12) in prolonged high-dose lorazepam; stop drug, RRT if severe Unexplained HAGMA in ICU: check osmolar gap and drug chart.

Features Early ↑ osmolar gap → later ↑ anion gap Ethylene glycol: oxalate crystals, AKI, hypocalcaemia Methanol: visual loss, basal ganglia necrosis Treatment Fomepizole (or ethanol) to block alcohol dehydrogenase Haemodialysis (EXTRIP): severe acidosis, AKI, visual signs, high level Cofactors: thiamine + pyridoxine (EG), folinic acid (methanol); bicarbonate High AG + high osmolar gap = toxic alcohol until proven otherwise.

KDIGO Stage 1: Cr × 1.5–1.9 or ↑ 26.5 µmol/L; UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h 6–12 h Stage 2: × 2–2.9; stage 3: × 3, Cr ≥ 354, RRT, UO < 0.3 × 24 h or anuria 12 h RRT timing and dose STARRT-AKI, AKIKI: early start no benefit; start for life-threatening indications (AEIOU) Dose 20–25 mL/kg/h effluent (RENAL, ATN) Citrate anticoagulation preferred for CRRT No benefit from accelerated RRT: wait for a clear indication.

Limitations Static pressure ≠ volume; poor predictor of fluid responsiveness (Marik 2013: AUC ≈ 0.56) Affected by RV function, tricuspid disease, PEEP, intra-abdominal pressure, compliance, tamponade High CVP (e.g. 16) with oliguria → venous congestion lowers renal perfusion pressure (MAP − CVP) Where CVP helps Trend, RV failure, tamponade, safety ceiling for fluids, ScvO2 sampling, waveform (cannon a, large v) "CVP tells you about the right heart and congestion, not about fluid need."

Dynamic tests Passive leg raise: ↑ CO/VTI ≥ 10% (works in AF, spontaneous breathing) PPV/SVV > 12–13% only if ventilated Vt ≥ 8, sinus rhythm, closed chest, no spontaneous effort End-expiratory occlusion (↑ CO ≥ 5%), mini-fluid challenge 100 mL, tidal volume challenge IVC variability (limited; spontaneous breathing unreliable) Responsive ≠ needs fluid: give only if responsive AND hypoperfused.

Pulse contour (FloTrac, LiDCO, PiCCO) Continuous CO and SVV; uncalibrated less accurate in vasoplegia, arrhythmia, IABP, poor arterial trace Transpulmonary thermodilution (PiCCO, VolumeView) Calibrated CO, GEDV (preload), EVLW (oedema), PVPI; needs central line + femoral arterial; recalibrate Pulmonary artery catheter CO, PAOP, PAP, SvO2, PVR; RV failure, pulmonary hypertension, cardiac surgery PAC-Man 2005: no mortality benefit; complications Echocardiography Diagnosis: LV/RV function, tamponade, valves, LVOT obstruction (SAM), VTI Operator-dependent, intermittent; TOE after cardiac surgery Echo to diagnose, a continuous CO monitor to titrate.

Patterns LV failure: ↓ CO/CI  18, ↑ SVR, ↓ SvO2; echo poor LVEF RV failure: ↑ CVP > PAOP, dilated RV, D-shaped septum, TAPSE Tamponade: equalised pressures, collapsing RA/RV, low CO; localised clot after surgery Vasoplegia: normal/↑ CO, ↓ SVR Hypovolaemia: ↓ CO, small hyperdynamic LV, responsive to PLR Name the phenotype, then match the drug to the problem.

LV failure Optimise preload, inotrope (dobutamine/milrinone), noradrenaline for MAP, reduce afterload when MAP allows Mechanical support: IABP (IABP-SHOCK II: no benefit in MI), Impella, VA-ECMO (ECLS-SHOCK: no benefit routinely) RV failure Avoid overload; maintain MAP > PAP (noradrenaline, vasopressin) Milrinone/dobutamine, inhaled NO/epoprostenol, lower PEEP/plateau, correct hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis Tamponade Re-sternotomy (cardiac surgery) or pericardiocentesis; keep preload and HR, avoid high PEEP RV failure: "pressure up, pulmonary resistance down, avoid fluids".

Causes Bleeding/hypovolaemia, tamponade, LV/RV dysfunction (stunning, graft failure), valve dysfunction/SAM after MV repair, vasoplegia, arrhythmia, pacing problems Actions Check drains, ROTEM, echo (TOE), ECG, pacing wires (AV pacing 90) Methylene blue for refractory vasoplegia; CALS for arrest (resternotomy < 5 min) After cardiac surgery: think bleeding and tamponade first.

SCAI stages A at risk, B beginning, C classic, D deteriorating, E extremis Key steps Early revascularisation of culprit lesion (SHOCK trial); culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK) Lactate and end-organ monitoring; shock team; noradrenaline > dopamine (SOAP II) Revascularise early, support wisely, avoid routine mechanical devices.

Example: PT 35 s, aPTT 55 s, fibrinogen 0.8, platelets 45, D-dimer > 20,000 Consumption + dilution + liver synthetic failure Low fibrinogen + very high D-dimer + oozing from lines → DIC and/or hyperfibrinolysis on background of cirrhosis Rebalanced haemostasis in cirrhosis ↓ pro- and anticoagulant factors (protein C, AT); ↑ factor VIII and vWF INR does not predict bleeding; global tests (TEG/ROTEM) better Do not treat the INR; treat bleeding guided by global tests.

boxes.t: 2. Liver disease vs DIC vs hyperfibrinolysis
boxes.x: Liver disease Normal/↑ factor VIII, low factor V and VII, stable picture, splenomegaly-related thrombocytopenia DIC ISTH score ≥ 5 (platelets, D-dimer/FDP, PT, fibrinogen); trigger (sepsis, shock, trauma) ↓ factor VIII (consumed), falling platelets and fibrinogen over time, schistocytes Hyperfibrinolysis Very low fibrinogen, very high D-dimer, oozing; ROTEM: ML > 15% in EXTEM, corrected by APTEM; euglobulin lysis time short Factor VIII separates them: high in liver disease, low in DIC.

General Control the source (endoscopy, TIPS, surgery), warm, Ca2+ > 1.1, pH > 7.2 Restrictive transfusion Hb 70 g/L in variceal bleeding (Villanueva 2013 ↓ mortality) Targets Fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L (> 2 in obstetric): cryoprecipitate 10 units or concentrate 3–4 g Platelets > 50 ×10⁹/L if bleeding (> 100 for neurosurgery) FFP: only if ROTEM CT prolonged or active bleeding with ↑ PT; volume overload ↑ portal pressure Tranexamic acid for hyperfibrinolysis (HALT-IT: no benefit in GI bleed and ↑ VTE) Give the specific product for the specific defect.

Steps Terlipressin/octreotide, antibiotics (ceftriaxone), endoscopic band ligation < 12 h Airway protection; restrictive transfusion Pre-emptive TIPS (< 72 h) in Child C 10–13 or B with active bleed (Baveno VII) Balloon tamponade/esophageal stent as bridge Vasoactive drug + antibiotics + early banding + consider early TIPS.

Evidence Variceal bleeding (Bosch 2004, 2008): no benefit overall Trauma (CONTROL): ↓ transfusion, no mortality benefit Off-label use ↑ arterial thrombosis (Levi 2010 NEJM) If used Last resort after surgical control and correction of fibrinogen, platelets, Ca, pH, temperature Not recommended routinely: thrombosis risk without survival benefit.

Reading ROTEM CT (clotting time) ↑ → factors → FFP/PCC A5/A10 FIBTEM  15% → antifibrinolytic HEPTEM vs INTEM → heparin effect Evidence Cirrhosis procedures: TEG-guided ↓ products without more bleeding (De Pietri 2016) Cardiac surgery and trauma: ↓ transfusion Limitations Insensitive to antiplatelet drugs, vWF, hypothermia (run at 37 °C) Fast, global, guides products: but treat the patient, not the trace.

Key points RBC:FFP:platelets ≈ 1:1:1 until results (PROPPR) TXA 1 g within 3 h in trauma (CRASH-2) and PPH (WOMAN) Permissive hypotension in trauma (not TBI) Monitor Ca, K, temperature, lactate; avoid > 2 L crystalloid Activate early, balanced products, then switch to goal-directed.

ILAE 2015 t1 = 5 min (treat), t2 = 30 min (risk of damage) for convulsive SE Established SE: fails benzodiazepines Refractory: fails benzodiazepine + one second-line drug Super-refractory: continues ≥ 24 h after anaesthetic or recurs on weaning Time is brain: every step has a time target.

Doses Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (4 mg), repeat once Midazolam 10 mg IM/buccal (RAMPART: IM midazolam ≥ IV lorazepam pre-hospital) Diazepam 10 mg IV Pitfalls Under-dosing is common; ABC, glucose (thiamine first if malnourished), check airway Adequate benzodiazepine dose, then move on within 10 minutes.

ESETT 2019 Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4.5 g), fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3 g): equal efficacy ≈ 47% Choice Levetiracetam: few interactions; adjust in renal failure Phenytoin: arrhythmia, hypotension, purple glove; monitor ECG; level Valproate: avoid in liver disease, mitochondrial disease, pregnancy; hyperammonaemia; levels Lacosamide 200–400 mg: PR prolongation; phenobarbital 15–20 mg/kg No winner in ESETT: choose by comorbidity and side-effects.

Agents Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg then 0.05–2 mg/kg/h: tachyphylaxis Propofol 1–2 mg/kg then 2–10 mg/kg/h: PRIS (keep Ketamine (NMDA): useful later when GABA receptors internalised; haemodynamically stable Thiopental/pentobarbital: hypotension, immunosuppression, long half-life Goals Continuous EEG: seizure suppression or burst suppression for 24–48 h, then slow wean Intubation, vasopressors, temperature control Balance seizure control against deep sedation harms: aim for the least EEG suppression that works.

Options Ketamine, ketogenic diet, immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, rituximab), magnesium, pyridoxine in children Hypothermia (HYBERNATUS: no outcome benefit), surgery for focus, ECT NORSE / FIRES New-onset refractory SE without clear cause; autoimmune encephalitis (NMDA-R) common Early first-line immunotherapy within 72 h; anakinra/tocilizumab in FIRES Think autoimmune early in previously healthy young adults.

Tests Glucose, Na, Ca, Mg, urea, liver tests, ammonia, toxicology, antiseizure drug levels, pregnancy (eclampsia) CT then MRI; LP (infection, autoimmune panel, HSV PCR) EEG to confirm cessation and detect non-convulsive SE Common causes Low drug levels/withdrawal, alcohol, stroke, tumour, trauma, infection (HSV), autoimmune, metabolic, eclampsia Treat seizures and search for the cause at the same time.
Quick pearls SAH: nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly, secure aneurysm  −30, IVIG/PLEX Brain death: prerequisites, apnoea test, ancillary tests Learn one-line management of each neuro emergency.

BTF 4th ed / SIBICC Treat ICP > 22 mmHg; CPP 60–70 mmHg SBP ≥ 100 (50–69 yr) / ≥ 110 (15–49 or > 70) Avoid hypoxia (SpO2 > 94%, PaO2 10–13 kPa), PaCO2 4.5–5 kPa Na 140–145, glucose 6–10, normothermia, Hb > 70 (TRAIN: > 90 better in brain injury) Who needs ICP monitoring GCS 3–8 with abnormal CT, or normal CT + 2 of age > 40, posturing, SBP < 90 Prevent secondary injury: hypoxia, hypotension, hyper/hypocapnia, fever, hyponatraemia.

Tier 0 (all) Head-up 30°, neck neutral, loose ties, sedation/analgesia, normothermia, seizures prophylaxis 7 days (levetiracetam/phenytoin) Tier 1 CPP 60–70, ↑ sedation/analgesia, PaCO2 4.7–5.3 kPa Osmotherapy: mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline (Na up to 155, osm < 320) CSF drainage if EVD, EEG Tiers: escalate only when the lower tier fails; go back down when ICP settles.

Tier 2 Mild hypocapnia 4.0–4.5 kPa (with PbtO2/SjvO2 monitoring) Neuromuscular blockade trial MAP challenge to assess autoregulation Repeat CT, consult neurosurgery Tier 3 Barbiturate coma (titrate to burst suppression) Secondary decompressive craniectomy Mild hypothermia 35–36 °C Know what belongs to each tier: examiners ask exactly that.

Hyperventilation ↓ ICP by vasoconstriction but ↓ CBF → ischaemia; avoid PaCO2 DECRA 2011: early bifrontal → worse outcome RESCUEicp 2016: last tier ICP > 25 → ↓ mortality (27 vs 49%) but ↑ vegetative/severe disability Hypothermia Eurotherm3235: ICP-driven hypothermia ↑ unfavourable outcome POLAR: prophylactic hypothermia no benefit Lower ICP ≠ better outcome: the classic exam point.

PbtO2 Target > 20 mmHg; treat hypoxia via FiO2, CPP, PaCO2, Hb, sedation BOOST-II: ↓ time with hypoxia, trend to better outcome; BOOST-3 ongoing/results Microdialysis Lactate/pyruvate ratio > 25–40 = metabolic crisis; glucose, glutamate Others PRx (autoregulation) → CPPopt; SjvO2 55–75%; TCD; continuous EEG; pupillometry Multimodal monitoring personalises CPP and PaCO2 targets.

Points TXA within 3 h in mild-moderate TBI (CRASH-3) No steroids (CRASH: harm) Albumin harmful (SAFE-TBI) VTE prophylaxis after stable CT (24–72 h) Prognosis: IMPACT/CRASH calculators; avoid early withdrawal CRASH-3 for TXA, CRASH for steroids, SAFE-TBI for albumin.

boxes.t: 1. Systematic approach to the comatose overdose
boxes.x: Resuscitate ABC, intubate if GCS ≤ 8 or failing airway; glucose; thiamine ECG early (QRS, QTc, R in aVR, bradyarrhythmia), temperature, pupils Naloxone trial if opioid suspected Assess History (collateral, packets, pill bottles), examination for toxidrome Bloods: paracetamol and salicylate levels in all, ABG, lactate, osmolar gap, CK, U&E, glucose Contact poison centre (TOXBASE) Then Decontamination, enhanced elimination, antidotes, organ support, psychiatric review Resuscitate → ECG → levels → decontaminate → antidote → support.

Activated charcoal 50 g within 1 h of a toxic dose of an adsorbable drug; later for sustained-release or anticholinergic Only with protected airway; contraindicated: hydrocarbons, corrosives, ileus Not for metals, lithium, iron, alcohols Gastric lavage Not routine (AACT/EAPCCT 2013): aspiration, perforation, little benefit Rare: life-threatening amount < 1 h with no antidote (e.g. colchicine) Whole bowel irrigation Body packers, sustained-release, iron, lithium: PEG 1–2 L/h Charcoal yes if early and airway safe; lavage almost never.

Patterns Opioid: coma, miosis, ↓ RR Cholinergic (organophosphates): SLUDGE/DUMBELS, bradycardia, miosis, bronchorrhoea Anticholinergic (TCA, antihistamines): hot, dry, red, mydriasis, tachycardia, retention, delirium Sympathomimetic (cocaine, amphetamine): hyperthermia, sweating, tachycardia, mydriasis Sedative-hypnotic: coma, normal pupils, normal vitals Serotonin: clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia Brady + hypotension + hypothermia β-blocker, CCB, digoxin, clonidine, opioids, sedatives, organophosphate, hypothyroid Pupils, skin, temperature and heart rate sort most toxidromes.

Features Bradycardia, hypotension, AV block; CCB → hyperglycaemia (insulin release blocked); β-blocker → hypoglycaemia; propranolol → seizures, wide QRS Treatment Atropine, fluids, calcium (CaCl 10% 10–20 mL, repeat), glucagon 5–10 mg (β-blocker) High-dose insulin euglycaemia 1 U/kg bolus then 1–10 U/kg/h + dextrose, K monitoring Vasopressors/inotropes (adrenaline), pacing Lipid emulsion 20% 1.5 mL/kg if refractory (lipophilic drug) VA-ECMO for refractory shock; methylene blue for vasoplegia Calcium, high-dose insulin, catecholamines, then ECMO.

Features Nausea, visual (yellow) changes, any arrhythmia (bidirectional VT, AV block with atrial tachycardia), hyperkalaemia in acute toxicity Digoxin-specific Fab Indications: life-threatening arrhythmia, K > 5–6 (acute), level > 10–15 ng/mL (acute) or > 6 (chronic), end-organ damage Dose (vials) = level (ng/mL) × weight (kg) / 100; or 10 vials empirically in acute Avoid Calcium in hyperkalaemia (traditional caution), cardioversion if possible; correct Mg and K Hyperkalaemia in acute digoxin poisoning = give Fab.

Features Na channel block: QRS > 100 ms (seizures), > 160 ms (VT), R in aVR > 3 mm Anticholinergic, α-block hypotension, seizures, coma Treatment Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mmol/kg boluses to pH 7.45–7.55 and narrow QRS Hyperventilate if intubated; benzodiazepines for seizures (no phenytoin) Noradrenaline for hypotension; lidocaine for VT; lipid emulsion if arrest Avoid class Ia/Ic, flumazenil, physostigmine TCA: bicarbonate and benzodiazepines.

Haemodialysis (EXTRIP) Lithium, salicylate, toxic alcohols, metformin (MALA), valproate, theophylline, barbiturates Urinary alkalinisation Salicylate (urine pH 7.5–8.5); phenobarbital Specific antidotes Paracetamol → NAC; opioids → naloxone; benzodiazepines → flumazenil (rarely); organophosphates → atropine + pralidoxime; cyanide → hydroxocobalamin; CO → O2 / hyperbaric; methaemoglobin → methylene blue Know which poisons are dialysable: "I STUMBLE" / EXTRIP list.

boxes.x: Principles Beneficence: act in the patient's best interests (realistic benefit) Non-maleficence: avoid burdensome treatment without benefit (CPR, ECMO in MOF + dementia) Autonomy: patient's own values via advance directive or surrogate (substituted judgement); families cannot demand inappropriate treatment Justice: fair use of ICU resources In the "do everything" case Respect family role but decision is about the patient's values, not family wishes Explore what "everything" means: fear, guilt, religion, mistrust Apply each principle to the scenario, not as a list of definitions.

Before Quiet room, key family, nurse, senior doctor, interpreter, consistent team message, review facts During (VALUE / SPIKES) Value what family say Acknowledge emotions Listen Understand the patient as a person Elicit questions Ask what they know, give a warning shot, explain prognosis plainly, silence, recommendation After Document, follow-up meeting, support (chaplain, social worker) Evidence Lautrette 2007: VALUE + brochure ↓ PTSD, anxiety, depression in relatives Make a recommendation; do not hand the decision burden to the family.

Definitions (ATS 2015) Futile: cannot achieve its physiological goal (strict, rare; e.g. CPR in refractory MOF) Potentially inappropriate treatment: some chance of effect but competing ethical considerations (burden vs benefit) Time-limited trial: agreed period (e.g. 3–7 days) with defined goals, then reassess Resolving conflict Communication, second opinion, ethics committee, mediation, offer transfer, legal route last Use "potentially inappropriate", not "futile", unless strictly physiological.

Process Consensus and documentation; DNACPR Withdrawing and withholding are ethically equivalent Stop non-comfort measures (bloods, monitoring alarms, feeds as appropriate) Practical Symptom control: opioids and benzodiazepines titrated to distress (double effect; not to hasten death) Vasopressors stopped; terminal extubation or terminal wean; anticipate secretions (glycopyrronium) Family presence, privacy, spiritual support, organ donation referral (DCD) before withdrawal Comfort is the goal; document intent and doses.

Capacity Understand, retain, weigh, communicate; time and decision-specific Without capacity Advance directive, legal proxy, best interests; local legal and religious framework (in Egypt: family-centred decisions, consult hospital ethics/legal) Other topics Brain death diagnosis, organ donation, confidentiality, research consent (deferred), resource allocation, triage State that practice follows local law and institutional policy.

Integrate early Symptom assessment, goals-of-care conversation within 72 h of admission in high-risk patients Triggers: advanced dementia, MOF, prolonged ventilation, poor functional baseline After death Bereavement support, debrief staff, moral distress, Ethicus data on variation Palliative care is active treatment, not abandonment.

= VASST 2008: vasopressin = NA (possible benefit in less severe shock) ✔ ADRENAL 2018: faster shock reversal; ✔ APROCCHSS 2018: ↓ mortality = SEPSISPAM 2014: MAP 80–85 not better; 65 trial 2020 ✔ ATHOS-3: angiotensin II raises MAP ✖ LOVIT 2022: vitamin C harm; = VITAMINS, VICTAS = STRESS-L 2023: landiolol no benefit MAP 65, NA first, add vasopressin and hydrocortisone.

= STOP-IT 2015: 4 days after source control = longer ✔ SAPS 2016, ADAPT-Sepsis: PCT-guided stopping ↓ duration ✔ BLING III 2024: continuous β-lactam (meta-analysis ↓ mortality) ✖ MERINO 2018: pip-taz worse than meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia Shorter, guided, extended-infusion.

files.f: 12 How to Write a 10-Mark SEQ Answer.pdf
files.title: 12 How to Write a 10-Mark SEQ Answer

boxes.x: Split 2 min: read stem twice, underline every task word (discuss, compare, outline, evidence) 1 min: plan headings matching the parts and their marks 13 min: write 2 min: check every part answered, add a summary line Paper level Answer easiest first, never leave a question blank: the first marks of each question are the easiest Stop at 18 min; return if time remains Marks follow the parts: a blank part costs more than a short one.

Seven headings 1. Interpretation: what is going on, severity, numbers 2. Differential: most likely first, life-threatening not to miss 3. Immediate management: ABC, resuscitation, specific first actions 4. Definitive / ongoing care: targets, drugs with doses, monitoring 5. Evidence: trial name + year + one-line result 6. Controversy and emerging: what is debated, what is new 7. Ethics and communication: family, consent, limits of care Use the frame for every scenario: examiners recognise the structure.

Do Headings and short bullet points Numbers and doses (MAP 65, Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg) Name trials with year and result Prioritise: "first …, then …" Answer the exact question asked (if it says compare, use a table) Don't Long prose paragraphs, repeating the stem Lists without explanation for "discuss" Abbreviations without first spelling them out One idea per line; one mark per idea.

Meanings Outline: list main points briefly Describe: what, how, with detail Discuss: points for and against, evidence, conclusion Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, ideally a table Justify / rationale: why, with evidence Evaluate: strengths, weaknesses, verdict The command word tells you how to write the part.

boxes.t: 5. Evidence: how to quote a trial
boxes.x: Template Name (year), population, intervention vs control, main result, limitation e.g. "PROSEVA (2013): severe ARDS P/F < 150, prone ≥ 16 h/day → 28-day mortality 16% vs 33%; experienced centres." When unsure Say the direction of evidence: "large RCTs show no mortality benefit" Quote guidelines: SSC 2021, ESICM 2023, BTF 2016, ATS 2015 Two well-quoted trials beat five vague ones.

First lines "68-year-old diabetic with septic shock from faecal peritonitis: vasopressor-dependent, MAP  40%)." "Immediate priorities run in parallel: airway and oxygen, MAP 65 with noradrenaline, antibiotics within one hour, source control within 6–12 hours." Closing line "Daily review: de-escalate antibiotics, stop steroids when off vasopressors, discuss goals with family." A strong first and last line frame the whole answer.

Core ALS High-quality CPR: 100–120/min, 5–6 cm, full recoil, pauses < 10 s, rotate every 2 min Shockable: shock → 2 min CPR; adrenaline 1 mg + amiodarone 300 mg after 3rd shock (150 mg after 5th) Non-shockable: adrenaline 1 mg ASAP, then every 3–5 min Airway: stepwise; waveform capnography for all intubated patients Monitoring CPR quality ETCO2 > 10–20 mmHg; sudden rise = ROSC; < 10 after 20 min = poor prognosis Arterial diastolic pressure > 25–35 mmHg (coronary perfusion surrogate) Reversible causes and rescue 4 Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, K+/metabolic, hypothermia) and 4 Ts (tension, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis) Focused echo in pauses; ECPR for selected refractory VF; PCI/thrombolysis when cause is clear Minimise no-flow time; every answer starts with CPR quality and early defibrillation.

Immediate priorities Coronary angiography: emergent if STEMI; consider if shock/electrical instability SpO2 94–98%, PaCO2 normal, MAP ≥ 65 (avoid hypotension), glucose 7.8–10 mmol/L Lung-protective ventilation; treat seizures (EEG); avoid hyperthermia Temperature control Prevent fever (≤ 37.5 °C) for ≥ 72 h in comatose survivors TTM (2013) 33 vs 36 °C and TTM2 (2021) 33 °C vs normothermia: no difference HYPERION: possible benefit of 33 °C in non-shockable rhythms; treat shivering Neuroprognostication (≥ 72 h, confounders excluded) Absent pupillary + corneal reflexes; bilaterally absent N20 SSEP Highly malignant EEG, status myoclonus ≤ 72 h, NSE > 60 µg/L, diffuse injury on CT/MRI Need ≥ 2 concordant predictors; avoid premature withdrawal Post-arrest syndrome = brain injury + myocardial dysfunction + ischaemia–reperfusion + cause.

Staging Mild 32–35 °C (shivering); moderate 28–32 °C (no shivering, AF, J waves); severe < 28 °C (coma, VF risk) Cold diuresis, coagulopathy, left-shifted O2 curve, slowed drug metabolism Rewarming Passive external → active external (forced air) → active internal (warm fluids, lavage, ECLS) Arrest or unstable: ECLS (VA-ECMO/bypass) is the rewarming method of choice Cardiac arrest specifics < 30 °C: up to 3 shocks, withhold adrenaline; 30–35 °C: double drug interval Mechanical CPR for transfer; K+ > 12 mmol/L suggests non-survivable; HOPE score for ECLS Complications: afterdrop, rewarming shock, arrhythmias, electrolyte shifts "Not dead until warm and dead" – unless obvious lethal injury or very high K+.

Definition and staging SBP < 90 (or vasopressor) + hypoperfusion + CI < 2.2 with raised filling pressure SCAI A–E (at risk → extremis); causes: AMI 80%, mechanical complications, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy Management Early revascularisation (SHOCK); culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK) Noradrenaline first; dobutamine/milrinone for low output PA catheter: CPO = MAP × CO / 451 (< 0.6 W = poor prognosis); shock team Mechanical support IABP: no mortality benefit (IABP-SHOCK II); keep for mechanical complications Impella CP improved survival in STEMI-CS (DanGer-Shock); routine VA-ECMO no benefit (ECLS-SHOCK) Answer structure: define → stage → revascularise → drugs → monitor → MCS → escalate/ceiling.

Clinical profiles Warm–wet (commonest), cold–wet, warm–dry, cold–dry Phenotypes: decompensated HF, hypertensive pulmonary oedema, RV failure, cardiogenic shock Find precipitant: ACS, arrhythmia, hypertension, infection, PE, non-adherence (CHAMPIT) Acute treatment Oxygen to SpO2 > 90%; CPAP/NIV for pulmonary oedema (faster relief – 3CPO) IV nitrates for high BP; IV loop diuretic (DOSE: bolus = infusion); check natriuresis at 2–6 h Avoid routine morphine; inotropes only with hypoperfusion Before discharge Quadruple GDMT: ARNI/ACEi, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor Rapid up-titration (STRONG-HF); devices (ICD/CRT) when indicated Decongest by natriuresis targets, not by weight alone.

STEMI Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor; primary PCI within 120 min, else lysis within 10 min Inferior MI: right-sided leads (V4R) – RV infarct: avoid nitrates, cautious fluids Bradycardia/AV block: atropine, pacing; O2 only if SpO2 < 90% NSTE-ACS hs-troponin 0/1 h algorithm; GRACE score Immediate angiography (< 2 h) if shock, refractory pain, arrhythmia; early (< 24 h) if high risk Mechanical complications VSR (new murmur, O2 step-up), papillary muscle rupture (acute MR), free wall rupture (tamponade) Others: LV thrombus/aneurysm, pericarditis, arrhythmias New murmur + shock after MI = echo now for a mechanical complication.

Physiology Pericardial pressure > chamber filling pressure; speed of accumulation matters most Pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg from ventricular interdependence Diagnosis Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds); low voltage, electrical alternans Echo: RA systolic and RV diastolic collapse, plethoric IVC, inflow variation (MV > 25%) Management Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis; surgery for haemopericardium, dissection, loculated effusion Fluid bolus to temporise; avoid positive pressure ventilation where possible Send fluid for cytology/culture; window or drain for malignant recurrence Intubating a tamponade patient can precipitate arrest – drain first if possible.

Definitions Emergency = severe BP + acute target-organ damage; urgency = no acute damage Organs: encephalopathy, stroke/ICH, ACS, pulmonary oedema, dissection, AKI, TMA, retinopathy General treatment IV titratable agents (labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine), arterial line MAP ↓ ≤ 25% in first hour, 160/100 by 2–6 h, normal over 24–48 h; avoid sublingual nifedipine Special targets Aortic dissection: SBP < 120, HR < 60 within 20 min (beta blocker first) Ischaemic stroke: < 185/110 for lysis; otherwise treat only if > 220/120 Pre-eclampsia: labetalol/hydralazine/nifedipine + magnesium; phaeochromocytoma: alpha before beta Too fast a fall causes watershed ischaemia – except in dissection.

New AF in ICU Triggers: sepsis, leak/surgery, low K/Mg, catecholamines, hypovolaemia, hypoxia Unstable due to AF → synchronised DC cardioversion Correct K 4–5, Mg > 1; rate control: amiodarone if hypotensive, beta blocker (esmolol/landiolol) if BP allows Anticoagulation by CHA2DS2-VASc vs bleeding risk; > 48 h needs anticoagulation/TOE before cardioversion Other SVTs AVNRT/AVRT: vagal manoeuvres, adenosine 6–12–18 mg Flutter: sawtooth, 2:1 at 150/min – rate control, cardioversion, ablation MAT: treat lung disease, Mg; pre-excited AF: avoid AV-nodal blockers, use procainamide/DC Treat the precipitant first – many ICU AF episodes revert spontaneously.

Electrical storm ≥ 3 sustained VT/VF episodes (or ICD therapies) in 24 h Causes: scar re-entry, ischaemia, electrolytes, drugs, sympathetic drive, thyrotoxicosis Management Unstable VT: cardioversion; VF: defibrillation; correct K+ and Mg2+ Amiodarone ± lidocaine; propranolol for sympathetic blockade; deep sedation/intubation Interrogate ICD; exclude ischaemia; refractory: ablation, stellate ganglion block, MCS Torsades de pointes Magnesium 2 g IV; stop QT-prolonging drugs; K+ > 4.5 Increase rate: isoprenaline or overdrive pacing Monomorphic VT with scar = re-entry; polymorphic VT = think ischaemia or long QT.

Classification Stanford A (ascending, surgical) vs B (distal to left subclavian); DeBakey I–III Includes dissection, intramural haematoma, penetrating ulcer Management Esmolol/labetalol to HR < 60, then vasodilator to SBP 100–120; analgesia Type A: emergency surgery (mortality 1–2%/h untreated) Type B uncomplicated: medical; complicated (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain/BP): TEVAR Complications AR, tamponade, coronary occlusion, stroke, paraplegia Mesenteric, renal and limb malperfusion; rupture Arm BP difference + tearing back pain + AR murmur = CT angiography now.

Duke criteria Major: typical organism in 2 cultures/persistent bacteraemia; vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation Minor: predisposition, fever, vascular and immunological phenomena, atypical micro Definite: 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor Treatment MSSA: flucloxacillin/cefazolin; MRSA: vancomycin/daptomycin; 4–6 weeks POET: partial oral therapy safe in stable left-sided IE Surgery indications Heart failure from valve dysfunction; uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia, fungi) Embolic prevention: vegetation > 10 mm with embolism or > 30 mm; Endocarditis Team S. aureus bacteraemia always needs echo (TOE) and repeat cultures.

Pathophysiology Thin, afterload-sensitive RV; ↑ PVR → dilatation, TR, septal shift → low LV filling Hypotension → RV ischaemia → spiral of failure Management Treat trigger; avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis (raise PVR) Preload: usually diurese/ultrafiltrate; fluid only if clearly underfilled Keep systemic BP: noradrenaline, vasopressin; inotropes: dobutamine, milrinone Pulmonary vasodilators: inhaled NO/epoprostenol, IV prostacyclin; VA-ECMO as bridge Intubation danger Induction vasodilation + positive pressure + apnoeic hypercapnia → arrest Pressors running, haemodynamically stable induction, low PEEP, ECMO standby In RV failure, protect coronary perfusion: MAP above pulmonary pressure.

Rutherford classification I viable; IIa marginally threatened (minimal sensory loss); IIb immediately threatened (sensory + motor) III irreversible: paralysis, anaesthesia, rigor 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishing cold Management IV heparin immediately; analgesia IIb: urgent embolectomy or endovascular thrombectomy; IIa: catheter thrombolysis or surgery III: amputation or palliation After revascularisation Compartment syndrome – fasciotomy; reperfusion hyperkalaemia, acidosis, myoglobinuria/AKI Find source (AF, LV thrombus) – echo and long-term anticoagulation Sensory loss with weakness = hours matter.

Four types Hypovolaemic and cardiogenic: low CO, high SVR (cardiogenic has high filling pressures) Obstructive (tamponade, PE, tension): low CO, raised CVP; distributive: high CO, low SVR Bedside assessment (RUSH) Pump: LV/RV function, effusion; Tank: IVC, FAST, B-lines, pleura; Pipes: aorta, DVT Lactate, ScvO2, CO2 gap, capillary refill, mottling, urine output Resuscitation Fluid responsiveness: PLR with real-time CO (≥ 10%), PPV if ventilated in sinus rhythm 250–500 mL boluses with reassessment; early noradrenaline to MAP ≥ 65 Treat cause in parallel: antibiotics/source, drainage, reperfusion, thrombolysis Ultrasound first, fluids second – shock type decides treatment.

Severity CURB-65 ≥ 3 severe; IDSA/ATS major: vasopressors or ventilation; ≥ 3 minor criteria Antimicrobials Beta-lactam + macrolide (or respiratory quinolone); within 1 h if shock Post-influenza/necrotising: cover S. aureus incl. MRSA (linezolid); oseltamivir for influenza Tests: cultures, urinary pneumococcal/Legionella antigens, viral PCR; 5–7 days if improving Corticosteroids CAPE COD (2023): hydrocortisone 200 mg/day ↓ 28-day mortality in severe CAP Not for influenza pneumonia; watch glucose, infection Severe CAP answer: severity → antibiotics → steroids → oxygen/ventilation strategy.

Differential by host HIV CD4 < 200: Pneumocystis; neutropenia: Gram-negatives, Aspergillus; transplant: CMV, fungi, Nocardia Non-infective: drug toxicity, lymphoma, Kaposi, DAH, IRIS Pneumocystis (PJP) Induced sputum/BAL PCR; beta-D-glucan supportive; LDH raised Co-trimoxazole high dose 21 days; prednisolone if PaO2 < 9.3 kPa Alternatives: primaquine + clindamycin, IV pentamidine ART timing Start within 2 weeks of PJP treatment; watch for IRIS Delay ART in cryptococcal/TB meningitis Early BAL changes management in most immunocompromised patients.

Diagnosis Pneumonia > 48 h after intubation: new infiltrate + fever/WBC/purulence/worse oxygenation Lower airway sample before antibiotics (ETA semi-quantitative or BAL ≥ 10⁴ CFU/mL) Empirical treatment Anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam; add MRSA cover if local MRSA > 10–20% Second Gram-negative agent if shock or high resistance; de-escalate; 7 days Prevention bundle Head up 30–45°, sedation holds + SBT, subglottic drainage, cuff 20–30 cmH2O Avoid circuit changes, early extubation; SDD in low-resistance units (SuDDICU) Shorter courses (7 days) are as effective and reduce resistance.

Types Primary: autoimmune, TB, haemorrhage, metastases – low aldosterone (high K+) Secondary: pituitary disease, steroid withdrawal (commonest in ICU) Adrenal crisis Hypotension refractory to fluids, vomiting, confusion, low Na, high K, hypoglycaemia Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV now, then 200 mg/24 h; saline 1 L in first hour; glucose Take cortisol/ACTH first only if it does not delay treatment Prevention Sick-day rules, emergency injection kit, steroid card; peri-operative cover Never wait for a cortisol result before giving hydrocortisone in suspected crisis.

boxes.t: Ch 55 · CIRCI and steroids in septic shock
boxes.x: Concept Inadequate corticosteroid activity for illness severity: HPA dysfunction, reduced cortisol clearance, tissue resistance Random cortisol/ACTH test unreliable in septic shock Evidence ADRENAL: no mortality benefit, faster shock reversal APROCCHSS: hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone ↓ 90-day mortality; CORTICUS: no benefit SSC 2021: hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if noradrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h Adverse effects Hyperglycaemia, hypernatraemia, weakness, infection, GI bleeding, delirium Steroids in septic shock reverse shock faster; mortality benefit is inconsistent.

Approach Cultures then antibiotics within 1 h; ESBL risk → carbapenem ± amikacin Ultrasound/CT for obstruction, abscess, emphysematous pyelonephritis Source control Obstructed infected kidney = emergency decompression Nephrostomy (no anaesthesia) or retrograde stent – equivalent; stone treatment later Resistance risk Recent antibiotics/hospitalisation, long-term catheter, instrumentation Nursing-home residence, prior ESBL/CRE, travel to high-prevalence areas Pus under pressure needs drainage – antibiotics alone fail.

Sepsis-3 Sepsis: infection + organ dysfunction (SOFA ≥ 2); shock: vasopressor for MAP 65 + lactate > 2 after fluids qSOFA is prognostic, not a screening tool Hour-1 bundle Lactate, cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid if hypoperfused, noradrenaline Vasopressin when noradrenaline 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min; source control within 6–12 h Evidence EGDT trials (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe): no benefit; balanced crystalloids (SMART), avoid starch CLASSIC/CLOVERS: restrictive = liberal; ANDROMEDA-SHOCK: capillary refill targeting Time to antibiotics and source control drives outcome.

Risk factors Prolonged neutropenia, haematological malignancy, HSCT, GVHD, high-dose steroids ICU: COPD on steroids, cirrhosis, severe influenza/COVID-19 Diagnosis CT: halo sign (early), air crescent (late), cavitation Galactomannan (serum/BAL), Aspergillus PCR, BAL culture (septate hyphae at 45°) Treatment Voriconazole or isavuconazole first-line; liposomal amphotericin if mucormycosis possible TDM for voriconazole; reduce immunosuppression; ≥ 6–12 weeks Influenza-associated aspergillosis: send BAL galactomannan in ventilated patients.

Mechanism Autoinfection persists for decades; steroids/HTLV-1 → massive larval migration Larvae carry gut bacteria → Gram-negative bacteraemia/meningitis; eosinophilia often absent Diagnosis Larvae in sputum/BAL/stool (agar plate culture); serology (false negatives) Management Ivermectin daily until negative for 2 weeks (subcutaneous if ileus) Reduce steroids; antibiotics for enteric organisms Screen/treat people from endemic areas before immunosuppression Unexplained Gram-negative sepsis on steroids in someone from the tropics – think Strongyloides.

Viruses Ebola/Marburg (body fluids), Lassa (rodents), CCHF (ticks), dengue, yellow fever Incubation ≤ 21 days; exclude malaria first Infection control High-level isolation, notify public health, full PPE with trained donning/doffing buddy Limit procedures/samples, dedicated equipment, waste protocols Treatment Aggressive fluids and electrolytes; organ support improves survival Ebola Zaire: monoclonal antibodies (PALM); Lassa: ribavirin Staff safety first – no exposure-prone procedure without full PPE.

Severe falciparum criteria Impaired consciousness, seizures, prostration, parasitaemia > 10% (> 2–5% non-immune) Hypoglycaemia, lactate > 5, Hb < 7, AKI, jaundice, ARDS, shock, DIC Treatment IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h then daily (AQUAMAT, SEAQUAMAT) Then full oral ACT; watch delayed haemolysis Glucose, cautious fluids, RRT, seizure control, cover bacteraemia; no exchange transfusion Artesunate beats quinine – give it without delay.

Phases Febrile → critical (defervescence, 24–48 h plasma leak) → recovery (fluid reabsorption) Warning signs / severe dengue Abdominal pain, vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, rising haematocrit with falling platelets Severe: shock (pulse pressure ≤ 20), respiratory distress from leak, severe bleeding, organ failure Management Crystalloid 5–10 mL/kg/h titrated to haematocrit, vitals, urine; colloid if refractory Reduce fluid as leak ends; falling haematocrit + instability = bleeding → transfuse No NSAIDs/IM injections; no prophylactic platelets Danger is the afebrile critical phase – fever settling is not recovery.

Features Rodent-urine water exposure; fever, calf myalgia, conjunctival suffusion Weil's disease: jaundice + AKI + bleeding; pulmonary haemorrhage = highest mortality Diagnosis PCR blood (week 1) and urine (later); IgM ELISA, MAT Hypokalaemic non-oliguric AKI, high CK, low platelets, conjugated bilirubin Treatment Penicillin, ceftriaxone or doxycycline; Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction possible Early daily dialysis, lung-protective ventilation, ECMO for haemorrhage Jaundice with high CK and hypokalaemic AKI after flooding = leptospirosis.

Severity Non-severe: WBC < 15, creatinine < 133; severe: WBC ≥ 15 or creatinine > 133 Fulminant: shock, ileus, megacolon Treatment Non-severe/severe: fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin 10 days Fulminant: oral/NG vancomycin 500 mg qds + IV metronidazole ± rectal vancomycin Early surgery: subtotal colectomy or loop ileostomy + lavage Control and recurrence Contact precautions, soap and water, sporicidal cleaning; stop PPIs/unneeded antibiotics Bezlotoxumab, faecal microbiota transplant for recurrences Rising lactate or WBC > 25 in fulminant CDI = surgical review now.

Classification Uncomplicated vs complicated; community vs healthcare-associated (resistant) Primary (SBP), secondary (perforation, leak), tertiary (persistent) Management Source control within 6–12 h (relaparotomy, stoma, percutaneous drainage) Healthcare-associated: pip-taz or carbapenem ± antifungal ± enterococcal cover Peritoneal cultures, de-escalate Duration STOP-IT: 4 days after adequate source control Source control is the treatment; antibiotics are adjuncts.

boxes.t: Ch 89 · Abdominal and extremity compartment syndrome
boxes.x: Definitions IAH ≥ 12 mmHg (grades I–IV); ACS = IAP > 20 with new organ failure APP = MAP − IAP, aim > 60 Effects Oliguria, high airway pressures, low venous return/CO, raised ICP, gut ischaemia Management Sedation, paralysis, NG/rectal decompression, drain ascites, negative fluid balance Decompressive laparotomy if refractory Limb compartment syndrome: measure pressures, fasciotomy Measure bladder pressure in every high-risk patient – clinical exam is unreliable.

Airway and inhalation Early intubation if stridor, hoarseness, facial burns, soot 100% O2 for CO; hydroxocobalamin for suspected cyanide Fluids Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA; half in first 8 h from burn Titrate to urine 0.5 mL/kg/h; avoid fluid creep; albumin rescue Ongoing care Escharotomy for circumferential burns; early excision and grafting Hypermetabolism: early enteral feeding, high protein, propranolol, oxandrolone; infection control Formula is a starting point – urine output decides the rate.

Recognition Pain out of proportion, spreading erythema, bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia, shock Types: I polymicrobial, II group A strep, III clostridial/Vibrio; LRINEC supportive only Management Immediate surgical debridement, re-look within 24 h Pip-taz/carbapenem + vancomycin/linezolid + clindamycin (toxin suppression) Resuscitation; IVIG for streptococcal toxic shock Imaging Do not delay surgery for CT when suspicion is high Every hour of delayed debridement raises mortality.

boxes.t: Ch 5 · NIV and high-flow nasal oxygen
boxes.x: HFNO physiology Flow up to 60 L/min, FiO2 to 1.0, dead-space washout, low PEEP, humidification Evidence FLORALI: HFNO ↓ 90-day mortality vs NIV/standard O2 in de novo hypoxaemia NIV first-line in COPD hypercapnia and cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; helmet NIV promising HFNO for pre-oxygenation and after extubation in low-risk patients Failure ROX index (SpO2/FiO2 ÷ RR) < 3.85 at 12 h predicts failure; HACOR for NIV Tachypnoea, paradox, rising FiO2, shock, falling GCS → intubate; avoid delay Delayed intubation after HFNO/NIV failure increases mortality.

Definition (Berlin) Within 1 week, bilateral opacities, not cardiac; PaO2/FiO2 on PEEP ≥ 5: 200–300 / 100–200 / ≤ 100 2023 global definition adds HFNO, SpO2/FiO2 and ultrasound Ventilation Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, plateau ≤ 30, driving pressure < 15; higher PEEP if moderate–severe Permissive hypercapnia (pH > 7.2), SpO2 88–95%; avoid aggressive recruitment (ART) Adjuncts Prone ≥ 16 h if P/F < 150 (PROSEVA); conservative fluids (FACTT) NMB for dyssynchrony (ROSE: no routine benefit); VV-ECMO for refractory cases (EOLIA) Small tidal volumes and prone positioning are the two mortality-reducing interventions.

Initial treatment Controlled O2 to 88–92%; bronchodilators; prednisolone 40 mg 5 days; antibiotics if purulent NIV pH < 7.35 and PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa: NIV ↓ intubation and mortality IPAP 15→20–25, EPAP 4–5; ABG at 1–2 h Contraindications: arrest, cannot protect airway, vomiting, facial trauma, undrained pneumothorax Invasive ventilation Low RR, long expiratory time, measure PEEPi, external PEEP ≤ 80% PEEPi Target pre-morbid PaCO2/HCO3; early extubation to NIV Over-oxygenation worsens hypercapnia – titrate to 88–92%.

Severity Life-threatening: PEF < 33%, SpO2 < 92%, normal PaCO2, silent chest, exhaustion, arrhythmia Near-fatal: raised PaCO2 or needing ventilation Medical therapy Continuous salbutamol, ipratropium, steroids, IV magnesium 2 g Consider IV salbutamol/aminophylline/adrenaline, ketamine; heliox limited Ventilation Ketamine induction, large ETT, fluid preload RR 8–10, Vt 6–8 mL/kg, I:E ≥ 1:4, plateau < 30; permissive hypercapnia Arrest/hypotension: disconnect and compress chest; exclude pneumothorax; ECMO rescue Normal PaCO2 in a breathless asthmatic is a danger sign.

PE risk classes High risk: persistent hypotension or arrest; intermediate-high: RV dysfunction + troponin Low risk: sPESI 0, no RV strain High-risk PE UFH + systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg/2 h) unless contraindicated Contraindicated: catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy; VA-ECMO RV support: noradrenaline, dobutamine, avoid big fluid loads and intubation where possible Prophylaxis LMWH > UFH (PROTECT); IPC if bleeding risk; adding IPC gives no extra benefit (PREVENT) Thrombolysis is for haemodynamic instability – not for RV strain alone.

Key facts Any volume threatening airway or gas exchange; > 90% from bronchial arteries Causes: bronchiectasis, TB/aspergilloma, cancer, CF, AVM, vasculitis, coagulopathy Airway first Bleeding side down; large ETT (≥ 8.0); lung isolation (selective intubation, DLT, blocker) TXA, correct coagulopathy; bronchoscopy for localisation and local measures Definitive CT angiography → bronchial artery embolisation (first-line) Surgery for localised disease after failed embolisation Patients die of asphyxia, not blood loss – protect the good lung.

Sedation principles Analgesia first; RASS 0 to −2; daily awakening + breathing trial Propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines; ABCDEF bundle Delirium CAM-ICU or ICDSC; hypoactive commonest, worst prognosis Risk: age, dementia, alcohol, benzodiazepines, sepsis, restraints, sleep loss Management Treat causes; reorientation, sleep, mobilisation, family, glasses/hearing aids Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium (MIND-USA, AID-ICU); dexmedetomidine for agitation Delirium duration predicts long-term cognitive impairment.

Definition and causes ≥ 21 days for ≥ 6 h/day ICU-acquired weakness, diaphragm dysfunction, overload, cardiac, malnutrition, delirium Weaning Daily trach-collar trials of increasing length beat PSV wean (Jubran 2013) Inspiratory muscle training, mobilisation, nutrition, fluid removal, speaking valve Tracheostomy and outcome TracMan: early vs late – no mortality difference About half liberated; 1-year mortality ≈ 50% – discuss goals Prolonged ventilation is a multidisciplinary rehabilitation problem.

Definition Worsening < 1 month with new bilateral ground-glass not due to cardiac failure/fluid Exclude infection, PE, pneumothorax, drug toxicity, aspiration Management Oxygen/HFNO, antibiotics until infection excluded, steroids (weak evidence) Cyclophosphamide harmful (EXAFIP); continue antifibrotic; palliate dyspnoea Ventilation Invasive ventilation mortality > 80–90% Reserve for transplant bridge or reversible cause; early goals-of-care talk Decide the ceiling of care before the patient needs intubation.

Readiness Cause improving, P/F > 150–200 on PEEP ≤ 8, FiO2 ≤ 0.4–0.5, stable, awake, cough SBT 30–120 min low PSV/T-piece; PSV 8 for 30 min helps success RSBI < 105; failure: RR > 35, SpO2 < 90%, HR/BP change, distress Pair with awakening trial (ABC) After extubation High risk (age > 65, cardiac/lung disease, weak cough): prophylactic NIV ± HFNO (HIGH-WEAN) Low risk: HFNO; cuff leak test + steroids if stridor risk Most patients pass their first SBT – test daily.

Causes Capillaritis: ANCA vasculitis, anti-GBM, SLE; bland: coagulopathy, mitral stenosis; DAD: HSCT Diagnosis Falling Hb, infiltrates, progressively bloody BAL, haemosiderin-laden macrophages > 20% ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA/dsDNA, urinalysis (red cell casts), renal biopsy Treatment Methylprednisolone 0.5–1 g/day × 3; cyclophosphamide or rituximab Plasma exchange for anti-GBM (PEXIVAS: no benefit in ANCA overall) Supportive ventilation, RRT, ECMO Haemoptysis may be absent – suspect DAH when Hb falls with new infiltrates.

Exudate vs transudate Light's criteria: protein ratio > 0.5, LDH ratio > 0.6, LDH > 2/3 ULN Pleural infection pH < 7.2, low glucose, high LDH, septations = complicated; drain + antibiotics Small-bore drain adequate; tPA + DNase (MIST-2); VATS if failing Pneumothorax on ventilator Rising pressures, hypoxia, hypotension, absent sliding on ultrasound Tension: immediate decompression then drain; persistent leak = bronchopleural fistula Any pneumothorax on positive pressure needs a drain.

Life threats Airway obstruction, tension/open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest, tamponade Flail and contusion Regional analgesia (epidural, serratus/erector spinae block), HFNO/NIV, avoid overload Rib fixation ↓ ventilator days and pneumonia Haemothorax Thoracotomy if > 1500 mL initially or > 200 mL/h for 2–4 h, or instability Retained haemothorax: VATS within 3–7 days Analgesia is the main treatment that prevents respiratory failure after rib fractures.

Indications (VV-ECMO) EOLIA: P/F < 50 for > 3 h, < 80 for > 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO2 ≥ 8 kPa for > 6 h Reversible disease, ventilation < 7 days VV vs VA VV: lung support only; VA: heart + lung support VA problems: limb ischaemia, LV distension, differential hypoxia Management and evidence Ultraprotective ventilation; blood flow → O2, sweep → CO2; anticoagulation, haemolysis watch CESAR and EOLIA support referral; ECCO2R (REST) no benefit ECMO buys time for lungs to recover – it is not a treatment of the disease.

KDIGO Creatinine ↑ ≥ 26.5 µmol/L in 48 h or ≥ 1.5× in 7 days, or UO < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h Stage 1: 1.5–1.9×; stage 2: 2–2.9× / oliguria ≥ 12 h; stage 3: ≥ 3×, ≥ 354 µmol/L, RRT, anuria Limits of creatinine Late rise, muscle mass, dilution, reduced production in sepsis Newer tools NGAL, KIM-1, TIMP-2 × IGFBP7 (> 0.3); biomarker-guided bundle (PrevAKI) Furosemide stress test: < 200 mL in 2 h predicts progression Work-up: urine microscopy, ultrasound, review nephrotoxins Urine output is the earliest KDIGO signal – measure it hourly.

General Restore perfusion, avoid overload, balanced crystalloids, stop nephrotoxins, dose drugs Diuretics for volume only RRT indications Refractory K+, acidosis (pH < 7.15), overload with hypoxaemia, uraemic complications, toxins Timing: AKIKI, IDEAL-ICU, STARRT-AKI – no benefit from early start; AKIKI2 – excessive delay harmful Modality CRRT if unstable or raised ICP; dose 20–25 mL/kg/h delivered (RENAL, ATN) Regional citrate preferred over heparin Start RRT for indications, not for a creatinine number.

Mechanism of AKI Myoglobin casts, direct tubular toxicity, vasoconstriction, hypovolaemia Causes Crush, immobilisation, exertion, seizures, hyperthermia, drugs (statins, cocaine), infection, low K/PO4 Management Treat hyperkalaemia first; aggressive crystalloid aiming UO 200–300 mL/h Bicarbonate/mannitol unproven; don't treat asymptomatic low Ca Check compartments (fasciotomy); RRT for refractory K+, acidosis, overload Dipstick blood with no red cells = myoglobin.

Diagnosis Confirm hypotonic; urine osm < 100 = water excess; > 100 = ADH Urine Na > 30 + euvolaemia: SIADH, thiazide, hypothyroid, adrenal; < 30: hypovolaemia/oedema Severe symptoms 3% saline 150 mL over 20 min, repeat ×2–3; aim +4–6 mmol/L SALSA: bolus as safe as infusion; check Na 2–4 hourly Osmotic demyelination Limit ≤ 10 mmol/L/24 h (≤ 8 if alcohol, malnutrition, low K, liver disease) Overcorrection: D5W ± desmopressin to re-lower Treat symptoms fast, then slow down – the first 5 mmol/L matters most.

Causes Water loss (intake, insensible, GI, osmotic diuresis), diabetes insipidus, sodium gain Correction Free water deficit = TBW × (Na/140 − 1) Restore volume first if shocked; then water enterally or D5W plus ongoing losses Chronic: ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/day Diabetes insipidus Polyuria with dilute urine and high Na; desmopressin response = central Central: desmopressin; nephrogenic: treat cause, thiazide ICU hypernatraemia is often iatrogenic – watch saline and bicarbonate.

ECG Peaked T → long PR, flat P → wide QRS → sine wave, VF/asystole Emergency treatment Calcium chloride/gluconate until ECG improves Insulin 10 U + glucose; salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised; bicarbonate if acidotic Remove K: stop ACEi/MRA, loop diuretic, binders (SZC, patiromer), dialysis Causes Reduced excretion (AKI, drugs), shift (acidosis, insulin lack), cell breakdown, pseudohyperkalaemia Calcium protects the heart but does not lower potassium.

Criteria Hypotonic hyponatraemia, urine osm > 100, urine Na > 30, euvolaemia Normal thyroid and adrenal function, no diuretics Causes Small cell lung cancer, CNS disease, pneumonia/ventilation, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine), pain, nausea Treatment Symptoms: 3% saline boluses Chronic: fluid restriction, oral urea, loop + salt; tolvaptan (overcorrection, liver risk) Isotonic saline can worsen SIADH hyponatraemia.

Diagnosis Ketones ≥ 3, glucose > 11 (or known diabetes), pH < 7.3 or HCO3 < 15 Severe: ketones > 6, HCO3 < 5, pH < 7.0, K < 3.5, GCS < 12 Treatment Fluids 1 L/h then tailored; FRIII 0.1 U/kg/h; continue basal insulin Add 10% dextrose when glucose < 14; K+ 40 mmol/L if 3.5–5.5; hold insulin if K < 3.5 Targets: ketones ↓ 0.5/h, HCO3 ↑ 3/h, glucose ↓ 3/h Complications Hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema, hyperchloraemia, aspiration, VTE Euglycaemic DKA occurs with SGLT2 inhibitors – check ketones.

Diagnosis Clinical; Burch–Wartofsky ≥ 45; fever, AF, heart failure, CNS and GI-hepatic dysfunction Triggers: surgery, infection, contrast, stopping drugs, childbirth Treatment order Beta blocker (propranolol/esmolol) PTU (or carbimazole) to block synthesis; iodine ≥ 1 h later Hydrocortisone; cooling, paracetamol (not aspirin); treat trigger Refractory: plasmapheresis, thyroidectomy Thionamide before iodine – otherwise iodine fuels hormone synthesis.

Diagnosis Osmolality ≥ 320, glucose ≥ 30, severe dehydration, ketones < 3, pH > 7.3 Treatment 0.9% saline first; osmolality ↓ 3–8 mOsm/kg/h Insulin 0.05 U/kg/h only when glucose stops falling with fluids (or ketotic) Glucose ↓ ≤ 5 mmol/L/h; replace K; VTE prophylaxis; treat trigger Complications Cerebral oedema, osmotic demyelination, thrombosis, AKI, foot ulcers; mortality > DKA In HHS fluids do most of the work – insulin comes later and lower.

Features Reduced consciousness, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation Hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, effusions; triggers: infection, cold, sedatives Treatment Hydrocortisone before levothyroxine IV levothyroxine 200–400 µg load then 50–100 µg/day (lower in cardiac disease) Ventilate for hypercapnia, passive rewarming, glucose, careful Na correction Thyroid hormone without steroid can precipitate adrenal crisis.

Reperfusion IV alteplase/tenecteplase within 4.5 h; BP < 185/110 before, < 180/105 after Thrombectomy for LVO within 6 h; to 24 h with mismatch (DAWN, DEFUSE-3); large core also benefits ICU care No antithrombotics 24 h post-lysis; normoglycaemia, normothermia; swallow screen Haemorrhagic transformation: stop lysis, cryoprecipitate/TXA Malignant MCA infarction Oedema peaks day 2–5; hemicraniectomy within 48 h ≤ 60 years ↓ mortality DESTINY II (> 60): survival with more disability – discuss values Time is brain: door-to-needle and door-to-groin targets.

Immediate actions Ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly ± amoxicillin (> 60/immunocompromised) ± vancomycin Dexamethasone 10 mg 6-hourly × 4 days with first dose CT before LP only if focal signs, seizures, papilloedema, GCS < 10, immunocompromise CSF Bacterial: neutrophils, protein > 1 g/L, glucose < 40% serum Viral: lymphocytes, normal glucose; TB/fungal: lymphocytes, very low glucose Public health Droplet precautions 24 h; notify; ciprofloxacin prophylaxis for close contacts Never delay antibiotics for imaging or LP.

Causes HSV-1, VZV, enterovirus, arboviruses; autoimmune (NMDAR, LGI1); Listeria, TB Investigation CSF HSV PCR (repeat if early negative), autoimmune antibodies, MRI, EEG Treatment IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8-hourly immediately, 14–21 days if HSV Autoimmune: steroids, IVIG/PLEX, tumour removal, rituximab ICU complications Seizures/NCSE, raised ICP, autonomic instability, SIADH, aciclovir nephrotoxicity Start aciclovir on suspicion – do not wait for PCR.

Acute care Reverse anticoagulation: andexanet (ANNEXA-I) or 4F-PCC; vitamin K for warfarin SBP to 140 (not < 110) smoothly; care bundle (INTERACT3) Airway if GCS ≤ 8; treat seizures, no prophylaxis ICH score GCS, volume ≥ 30 mL, IVH, infratentorial, age ≥ 80; avoid early DNAR Surgery EVD for hydrocephalus; cerebellar > 3 cm: evacuate Minimally invasive evacuation of lobar ICH (ENRICH) may help Haematoma expansion is the modifiable target – BP and reversal fast.

Grading WFNS (GCS + motor deficit), Hunt–Hess; modified Fisher predicts vasospasm Early management Secure aneurysm early; coiling if feasible (ISAT) SBP < 160 before securing; nimodipine 60 mg 4-hourly × 21 days EVD for hydrocephalus; euvolaemia, normonatraemia Delayed cerebral ischaemia Day 4–14; new deficit; TCD/CT perfusion Euvolaemia, induced hypertension; endovascular rescue; exclude other causes No prophylactic triple-H – only induced hypertension for established DCI.

Definitions ≥ 5 min seizure or no recovery; established = after benzodiazepines; refractory; super-refractory Management Benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam/IM midazolam) ×2 Second-line: levetiracetam, valproate or fosphenytoin – equal (ESETT) Refractory: intubate, midazolam/propofol/thiopental, continuous EEG Find cause: glucose, electrolytes, drugs, infection, structural; thiamine Complications Hypoxia, aspiration, acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, neuronal injury Under-dosed benzodiazepines are the commonest error.

Features D2 blockade; hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental state, autonomic lability; high CK Differentials Serotonin syndrome (clonus, rapid onset), malignant hyperthermia (anaesthesia), anticholinergic Management Stop drug; cooling, fluids, treat rhabdomyolysis Benzodiazepines, bromocriptine, dantrolene; paralyse if extreme; ECT if refractory NMS evolves over days; serotonin syndrome over hours.

Prevent secondary injury SBP ≥ 100–110, PaO2 > 10 kPa, PaCO2 4.5–5, head up 30°, Na 140–150, normothermia Seizure prophylaxis 7 days; VTE prophylaxis once stable Tiered ICP therapy (ICP < 22, CPP 60–70) Tier 1: sedation, CSF drainage, mannitol/hypertonic saline Tier 2: mild hypocapnia, paralysis, MAP challenge Tier 3: barbiturates, decompressive craniectomy (RESCUEicp), hypothermia not early (Eurotherm) Drugs Steroids harmful (CRASH); TXA within 3 h for mild–moderate TBI (CRASH-3) One episode of hypotension doubles mortality in severe TBI.

Mechanism Energy failure, excitotoxicity, reperfusion injury; vulnerable hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum Prognostication (≥ 72 h) Absent pupillary/corneal reflexes, absent N20, malignant EEG, NSE > 60, imaging injury Status myoclonus; ≥ 2 concordant predictors Next steps Honest family discussion; withdrawal with palliative care Assess brainstem death; organ donation referral Sedation and hypothermia must be excluded before predicting poor outcome.

Causes GBS, myasthenic crisis, botulism, organophosphates, electrolytes, ICU-acquired weakness, cord lesion Intubation (20/30/40) VC < 20 mL/kg, MIP weaker than −30, MEP < 40; bulbar failure; avoid suxamethonium GBS treatment IVIG 2 g/kg or plasma exchange (no steroids) Dysautonomia, VTE prophylaxis, neuropathic pain, early tracheostomy, rehabilitation Measure VC serially – SpO2 and PaCO2 deteriorate late.

boxes.t: Ch 58 · Zika virus and Guillain–Barré syndrome
boxes.x: Zika Aedes-borne flavivirus; also sexual/vertical; rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia; microcephaly Diagnosis RT-PCR blood/urine; serology cross-reacts with dengue (PRNT) GBS: CSF albuminocytological dissociation, nerve conduction studies Management Respiratory monitoring, IVIG or PLEX, dysautonomia care Public health: mosquito avoidance, pregnancy advice Post-infectious GBS follows the infection by 1–3 weeks.

Risk scores Glasgow–Blatchford (pre-endoscopy; 0–1 outpatient); Rockall (post-endoscopy) Before endoscopy Restrictive transfusion Hb 7 (8 if cardiac disease); IV PPI; erythromycin pre-scope Correct coagulopathy; stop NSAIDs; TXA not recommended (HALT-IT); protect airway Endoscopy and after Within 24 h (12 h if unstable); Forrest Ia–IIa: dual therapy (adrenaline + clips/thermal) High-dose PPI 72 h; H. pylori eradication Rebleed: repeat endoscopy → embolisation → surgery Over-transfusion increases rebleeding.

Initial care Airway protection; Hb target 7–8 Terlipressin or octreotide 2–5 days; ceftriaxone up to 7 days Endoscopy Within 12 h: band ligation (oesophageal); cyanoacrylate (gastric) Uncontrolled: balloon tamponade or oesophageal stent → rescue TIPS Pre-emptive TIPS and prophylaxis Child C 10–13 or B > 7 with active bleeding: TIPS within 72 h ↑ survival NSBB (carvedilol) + repeat banding; lactulose; transplant assessment Antibiotics in variceal bleeding reduce mortality – never omit them.

Severity (revised Atlanta) Mild: no organ failure; moderately severe: transient (< 48 h) or local complications; severe: persistent Management Moderate fluids with Ringer's lactate (WATERFALL: aggressive harmful) Early enteral feeding; analgesia; no prophylactic antibiotics ERCP only for cholangitis; same-admission cholecystectomy in mild biliary disease Infected necrosis Gas on CT or deterioration after 1–2 weeks; antibiotics penetrating necrosis Step-up: delay ≥ 4 weeks, drain then necrosectomy (endoscopic/percutaneous) Organ failure duration, not enzymes, defines severity.

Definition and causes INR ≥ 1.5 + encephalopathy without cirrhosis; hyperacute/acute/subacute Paracetamol, viral hepatitis, DILI, autoimmune, Wilson's, ischaemic, Budd–Chiari, pregnancy King's criteria (paracetamol) pH < 7.3 (or lactate > 3 after fluids), or INR > 6.5 + creatinine > 300 + grade 3–4 HE ICU care NAC for all; refer early to transplant centre Intubate grade 3–4; Na 145–155, head-up, normocapnia; ammonia > 150 → CRRT Noradrenaline, glucose checks, infection screening; plasma exchange improves transplant-free survival Cerebral oedema is the main cause of death in hyperacute failure.

Assessment Diverticula, angiodysplasia, ischaemic colitis, malignancy, post-polypectomy Exclude upper source; shock index > 1 = unstable; Oakland score for discharge Management Restrictive transfusion; reverse anticoagulants if life-threatening Unstable: CT angiography → embolisation; stable: colonoscopy within 24 h Surgery Ongoing instability with failed IR/endoscopy; segmental resection after localisation In unstable bleeding, CT angiography comes before colonoscopy.

Assessment NUTRIC or NRS-2002; indirect calorimetry; 20–25 kcal/kg built up; protein 1.2–2.0 g/kg Route and timing Enteral within 24–48 h once stable; trophic first week (EDEN, PermiT, TARGET) PN delayed to day 3–7 if well nourished (EPaNIC); earlier if malnourished Gastric first; prokinetics, then post-pyloric Refeeding Low PO4, K, Mg; thiamine first; start 10–15 kcal/kg/day and replace daily Early full feeding gives no benefit – build up slowly.

Diagnosis Ascitic neutrophils ≥ 250/mm³; culture in blood bottles Secondary peritonitis: polymicrobial, protein > 10 g/L, glucose < 2.8, high LDH → CT Treatment Third-generation cephalosporin; albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 + 1 g/kg day 3 Stop nephrotoxins/diuretics; repeat tap at 48 h; long-term quinolone prophylaxis Hepatorenal syndrome-AKI No response to albumin, no shock/nephrotoxins; terlipressin + albumin; transplant Albumin in SBP prevents renal failure and saves lives.

boxes.t: Ch 75 · Alcohol-related liver disease in ICU
boxes.x: Severe alcoholic hepatitis Jaundice < 8 weeks, AST > ALT; Maddrey ≥ 32 or MELD > 20 Treatment Prednisolone 40 mg × 28 days (STOPAH: short-term benefit); Lille ≥ 0.45 at day 7 → stop Nutrition 35–40 kcal/kg; thiamine; infection screening; NAC may help Associated problems Alcohol withdrawal (lorazepam/oxazepam), Wernicke's, HE (lactulose, rifaximin) Abstinence support; early transplant discussion in selected patients Exclude infection before starting steroids.

Causes SBO: adhesions, hernia, cancer, Crohn's; LBO: cancer, volvulus, stricture; Ogilvie's Management Fluids, correct K, NG decompression; water-soluble contrast for adhesive SBO Frailty and goals of care Surgery Strangulation signs, rising lactate, closed loop, failure after 48–72 h Caecum > 12 cm; stent as bridge for obstructing cancer; endoscopic decompression of sigmoid volvulus Closed-loop obstruction is a surgical emergency.

Cholangitis (Tokyo 2018) Inflammation + cholestasis + imaging; grade III = organ dysfunction Treatment Cultures, pip-taz (± vancomycin if healthcare-associated) Biliary drainage: ERCP within 24 h (ASAP in grade III); PTC if ERCP fails Antibiotics 4–7 days after source control Acalculous cholecystitis Critically ill, TPN, burns; wall > 3.5 mm, fluid, sludge Antibiotics + percutaneous cholecystostomy Severe cholangitis needs drainage, not just antibiotics.

Indications Damage control, abdominal compartment syndrome, re-look for peritonitis/ischaemia ICU care NPWT with fascial traction; aim fascial closure within 7 days Replace protein-rich losses; early enteral nutrition; analgesia; monitor IAP Complications Enteroatmospheric fistula, loss of domain, hernia, infection, hypothermia Early fascial closure reduces fistulas and mortality.

boxes.t: Ch 4 · Hypovolaemic shock and massive transfusion
boxes.x: Damage-control resuscitation Activate MTP; RBC:FFP:platelets ≈ 1:1:1 (PROPPR) Permissive hypotension (SBP 80–90) except TBI; minimise crystalloid TXA within 3 h (CRASH-2); pelvic binder, surgery/IR, REBOA in selected centres Lethal triad (+ calcium) Warm fluids and patient; restore perfusion; fibrinogen > 1.5–2 g/L; ionised Ca > 1.1 Monitoring and complications TEG/ROTEM goal-directed therapy Hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, TACO, TRALI Early plasma and haemorrhage control beat large crystalloid volumes.

Thrombotic microangiopathy differentials TTP (ADAMTS13 < 10%), STEC-HUS, atypical HUS, DIC, HELLP, malignant hypertension, drugs Treatment Urgent plasma exchange (PLASMIC score; don't wait for ADAMTS13) Steroids + rituximab; caplacizumab (HERCULES) Avoid platelet transfusion unless life-threatening bleeding Monitoring Platelets and LDH daily; troponin and neurological status; ADAMTS13 for relapse Normal clotting with schistocytes and low platelets = TMA, not DIC.

boxes.t: Ch 77 · Acute promyelocytic leukaemia and DIC
boxes.x: Emergency t(15;17) PML-RARA; DIC with hyperfibrinolysis → early haemorrhagic death Treatment ATRA immediately on suspicion + arsenic trioxide or chemotherapy Keep platelets > 30–50, fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L; avoid invasive procedures Differentiation syndrome Fever, dyspnoea, infiltrates, effusions, weight gain, AKI Dexamethasone 10 mg 12-hourly; prophylaxis if WBC > 10 Give ATRA before genetic confirmation.
