boxes.x: Definition and causes Colonic dilatation > 6 cm + systemic toxicity Causes: UC, Crohn's, C. difficile, CMV, ischaemia Medical management IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly; stop opioids/anticholinergics Fluids, K, VTE prophylaxis, rule out C. difficile/CMV Rescue: infliximab or ciclosporin at day 3–5 if no response Surgery Perforation, haemorrhage, worsening, no response to rescue → colectomy Day 3 review: no response → rescue therapy or surgery.

Definitions (WSACS) IAH ≥ 12 mmHg (grades I–IV); ACS > 20 + new organ dysfunction APP = MAP − IAP (target ≥ 60) Organ effects ↓ Venous return/CO, ↑ airway pressures, AKI (renal compression), gut ischaemia, ↑ ICP Management Evacuate gut (NGT, rectal tube), drain ascites, sedation/NMB Negative balance, avoid tight dressings; decompressive laparotomy if ACS Measure bladder pressure in at-risk patients.

Types Arterial embolism (AF), arterial thrombosis, venous thrombosis, non-occlusive (NOMI) Diagnosis Pain out of proportion; lactate late; CT angiography Management Fluids, anticoagulation, antibiotics Revascularisation (endovascular/surgical) + resection of dead bowel; second look NOMI: treat low flow, vasodilators (papaverine) Pain out of proportion in AF → CT angiography.

Cerebral oedema Ammonia → glutamine → astrocyte swelling, ↑ ICP; herniation Emergency management Head up, Na 145–155, hyperventilation briefly, mannitol/HTS RRT to lower ammonia; temperature 35–36 Liver support and transplant Plasma exchange (high-volume: Larsen 2016 benefit) MARS not proven; emergency transplantation (King's criteria) Ammonia > 150 → protect the brain.

Diagnosis MAHA (schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin) + thrombocytopenia ± neuro, renal, fever ADAMTS13 < 10%; PLASMIC score ≥ 6 high probability Emergency management Plasma exchange daily (start before ADAMTS13 result) Steroids, caplacizumab, rituximab; avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding TMA differential HUS (STEC/atypical), DIC, HELLP, malignant hypertension, drug-induced, scleroderma crisis Suspected TTP is an emergency: PLEX without delay.

Classification STEC-HUS (E. coli O157), atypical (complement-mediated), secondary (pregnancy, drugs, transplant) Atypical HUS Eculizumab (anti-C5) after excluding TTP; meningococcal vaccination Plasma exchange as bridge STEC-HUS Supportive, RRT; avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs Complement blockade transforms aHUS outcome.

4T score Thrombocytopenia (> 50% fall), timing (5–10 days), thrombosis, no other cause ≥ 4 intermediate/high → stop heparin, test Pathophysiology IgG against PF4–heparin complexes → platelet activation and thrombosis Management Stop all heparin; argatroban or bivalirudin (or fondaparinux) Anti-PF4 ELISA, functional assay (SRA); no platelet transfusion Warfarin only when platelets recover (> 150) HIT causes thrombosis, not bleeding: anticoagulate with a non-heparin agent.

ISTH overt DIC score Platelets, fibrin markers (D-dimer), PT prolongation, fibrinogen; ≥ 5 = overt DIC Pathophysiology Tissue factor-driven thrombin generation, consumption of factors, fibrinolysis inhibition (PAI-1) in sepsis Management Treat the cause (source control, antibiotics) Platelets < 50 if bleeding (< 10–20 if not), FFP, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen < 1.5 Prophylactic heparin if not bleeding DIC is a sign of disease: treat the cause, replace if bleeding.

Causes Sepsis, DIC, dilution, drugs (heparin, linezolid, beta-lactams), HIT, TMA, ECMO, liver disease Diagnostic approach Blood film (schistocytes, pseudothrombocytopenia), coagulation, 4T, ADAMTS13 Prophylactic thresholds < 10 ×10^9/L no bleeding; < 20 CVC (ultrasound guided: PACER — avoid transfusion) < 50 surgery/LP; < 100 neurosurgery Check the film before platelets: exclude HIT and TTP.

Massive transfusion ≥ 10 units RBC in 24 h or ≥ 4 in 1 h Damage control: permissive hypotension (not in TBI), 1:1:1 (PROPPR), TXA within 3 h (CRASH-2) ROTEM-guided therapy A5 FIBTEM < 10 mm: fibrinogen/cryo EXTEM CT > 80 s: FFP/PCC; EXTEM A5 < 35 + FIBTEM normal: platelets ML > 15%: TXA Complications Hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, acidosis, TRALI, TACO Viscoelastic testing guides targeted correction.

Differentiate TRALI: within 6 h, non-cardiogenic oedema, fever, hypotension, normal BNP TACO: hypertension, high BNP, positive balance, response to diuretics Management TRALI: stop, supportive, ventilation, no diuretics TACO: stop, diuretics, NIV Other reactions Febrile, allergic, anaphylaxis (IgA), haemolytic (ABO), septic TRALI is low pressure; TACO is high pressure.

By phase Pre-engraftment (< 30 days): neutropenic sepsis, mucositis, VOD/SOS, engraftment syndrome Early (30–100): acute GVHD, CMV, fungal infection Late (> 100): chronic GVHD, encapsulated bacteria Differential Acute GVHD (skin, gut, liver), engraftment syndrome, infection, drug reactions, VOD Management High-dose methylprednisolone for GVHD; ruxolitinib if refractory Defibrotide for VOD; antimicrobials Rash + diarrhoea + jaundice after HSCT → acute GVHD.

Definition and triggers Hyperinflammation from uncontrolled macrophage activation Triggers: viral (EBV), malignancy (lymphoma), autoimmune (MAS) Diagnosis HLH-2004 (5 of 8: fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, high TG/low fibrinogen, ferritin > 500, sCD25, NK activity, haemophagocytosis) HScore; ferritin often > 10,000 Management Dexamethasone, etoposide, anakinra, IVIG; treat trigger (rituximab for EBV) Very high ferritin + cytopenias + fever → think HLH.

Causes Blood sampling, bleeding, inflammation (hepcidin), renal failure, haemolysis, nutrition Thresholds Hb 7 g/dL (TRICC, TRISS); 8 if cardiac (MINT 2023 suggests ≥ 10 in MI) Reducing anaemia Less sampling (small tubes), cell salvage, IV iron, EPO (selected) Restrictive transfusion is safe in most ICU patients.

Warfarin reversal 4-factor PCC 25–50 IU/kg + vitamin K 5–10 mg IV FFP if PCC unavailable DOAC reversal Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g Xa inhibitors: andexanet alfa or PCC 50 IU/kg Restarting Mechanical valve: restart heparin after 48–72 h in ICH (balance risk) AF: 7–14 days depending on bleed severity PCC is faster and better than FFP for warfarin reversal.

boxes.t: Sickle cell crisis and acute chest syndrome
boxes.x: Acute chest syndrome New infiltrate + chest pain, fever, hypoxia; causes: infection, fat embolism, infarction Management O2, analgesia, incentive spirometry, antibiotics (macrolide + cephalosporin) Transfusion: simple or exchange (HbS < 30%) Other complications Vaso-occlusive crisis, stroke, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis, priapism Exchange transfusion for severe ACS.

Definition BP ≥ 140/90 after 20 weeks + proteinuria or organ dysfunction Severe: BP ≥ 160/110, platelets < 100, liver/renal impairment, pulmonary oedema, neuro/visual Eclampsia management Magnesium sulphate 4 g IV over 5–15 min, then 1 g/h for 24 h (Magpie) Recurrent seizures: further 2 g; monitor reflexes, RR, UO, levels (toxicity: calcium gluconate) Delivery after stabilisation BP control Target < 150/100 (or 135/85); labetalol, nifedipine, hydralazine Magnesium for seizures and urgent BP control for stroke prevention.

boxes.t: HELLP versus acute fatty liver of pregnancy
boxes.x: Comparison HELLP: haemolysis, high liver enzymes, low platelets; with pre-eclampsia AFLP: liver failure, hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, AKI; Swansea criteria Management Delivery after stabilisation; correct coagulopathy, glucose Magnesium if pre-eclampsia; transplant rarely HELLP complications DIC, abruption, AKI, hepatic haematoma/rupture, pulmonary oedema Delivery is the definitive treatment for both.

Diagnosis Sudden hypoxia, hypotension/arrest, coagulopathy during labour/delivery Pathophysiology: anaphylactoid response → pulmonary hypertension, RV failure, DIC Resuscitation ALS, left uterine displacement, perimortem CS within 5 min RV support (inotropes, iNO), ECMO Coagulopathy Massive transfusion, fibrinogen > 2 g/L, TXA AFE: rapid collapse + DIC: treat RV failure and coagulopathy.

Definition and causes ≥ 500 mL vaginal, ≥ 1000 mL CS (major > 1500) 4 Ts: tone (70%), trauma, tissue, thrombin Atonic PPH Uterine massage, oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol TXA 1 g within 3 h (WOMAN); balloon tamponade, B-Lynch, embolisation, hysterectomy Fibrinogen < 2 g/L predicts severe PPH; replace with cryo/fibrinogen concentrate Early TXA and fibrinogen replacement save lives.

Definition LVEF < 45% in late pregnancy to months postpartum, no other cause Risks: multiparity, age, pre-eclampsia, twins, African ancestry ICU management Standard heart failure therapy (avoid ACEI antepartum) Bromocriptine (blocks prolactin), anticoagulation if EF < 35% MCS/ECMO, transplant Prognosis 50% recover; recurrence risk in future pregnancies Bromocriptine is specific therapy for PPCM.

Physiological changes ↑ CO, ↑ blood volume, ↓ FRC, ↑ O2 consumption, aortocaval compression after 20 weeks ALS modifications Manual left uterine displacement, early airway (smaller ETT), IV access above diaphragm Perimortem caesarean within 5 min if > 20 weeks and no ROSC Reversible causes Bleeding, AFE, eclampsia, Mg toxicity, cardiac disease, sepsis, anaesthetic complications Perimortem CS helps the mother first.

Causes Endometritis, wound infection, UTI, pneumonia, mastitis, septic abortion Group A strep most deadly Recognition challenges Physiological changes (tachycardia, low BP, high WBC) mask sepsis; use obstetric scores (MEOWS, omqSOFA) Management Hour-1 bundle; broad antibiotics (pip-taz/carbapenem + clindamycin for toxin) Source control, fetal monitoring Pregnancy hides sepsis: use obstetric early warning scores.

Changes ↑ Minute ventilation (respiratory alkalosis), ↓ FRC, PaCO2 4 kPa normal Ventilation targets SpO2 ≥ 95%, PaO2 > 9.3 kPa, PaCO2 4–4.7 kPa (fetal) Prone possible with care; ECMO if refractory Delivery timing May improve maternal respiratory mechanics; decided with obstetrics Influenza: oseltamivir Avoid maternal hypoxia: fetal oxygenation depends on it.

Pathophysiology VEGF-driven capillary leak after hCG (IVF) Severe: ascites, haemoconcentration, oliguria, thrombosis ICU management Fluids (albumin), paracentesis, thromboprophylaxis Avoid diuretics unless overloaded Complications Thrombosis, AKI, ARDS, pleural effusion, ovarian torsion Capillary leak syndrome: careful fluids and thromboprophylaxis.

Definition Severe vomiting, weight loss > 5%, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance Complications: Wernicke's, hypoK, hypoNa, Mallory–Weiss Management IV fluids (avoid dextrose before thiamine), thiamine, antiemetics K, Mg replacement; VTE prophylaxis Exclude Thyrotoxicosis, molar pregnancy, pancreatitis, hepatitis, DKA Thiamine before glucose in hyperemesis.

Toxidromes Anticholinergic: hot, dry, mydriasis, delirium, retention Cholinergic: SLUDGE, miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea Sympathomimetic: hypertension, tachycardia, mydriasis, sweating Opioid: coma, miosis, respiratory depression; sedative-hypnotic: coma, normal pupils General management ABC, glucose, ECG, temperature; history and pill counts Decontamination: activated charcoal within 1 h if airway safe Enhanced elimination: dialysis (lithium, salicylate, methanol), urinary alkalinisation Antidotes: naloxone, flumazenil (rare), NAC, fomepizole Specific treatment Depends on toxin; consult poison centre Recognise the toxidrome, then give the antidote.

Mechanism Inhibits acetylcholinesterase → muscarinic + nicotinic + CNS effects Muscarinic: SLUDGE, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia; nicotinic: fasciculation, weakness Management Decontaminate, atropine (double dose every 5 min until chest dry, HR > 80, SBP > 80) Pralidoxime (controversial), benzodiazepines for seizures; intubate (avoid suxamethonium) Intermediate syndrome 24–96 h: proximal weakness, cranial nerves, respiratory failure Delayed polyneuropathy (2–3 weeks) Titrate atropine to a dry chest, not to pupils.

Toxicity Phosphine gas: inhibits cytochrome oxidase → cellular hypoxia Refractory shock, myocardial toxicity, metabolic acidosis, ARDS Management No antidote; supportive; avoid water lavage (releases gas) Magnesium, calcium, bicarbonate, vasopressors, IABP/ECMO Poor prognostic factors Shock, pH < 7.2, ECG changes, large dose, delay Supportive care only: early ECMO may help.

Mechanism Na-channel block (wide QRS), alpha-block (hypotension), anticholinergic, GABA block (seizures) Management Sodium bicarbonate 1–2 mEq/kg if QRS > 100 ms or arrhythmia; target pH 7.45–7.55 Benzodiazepines for seizures; intralipid; avoid physostigmine and flumazenil Monitoring ECG for ≥ 6 h; QRS normal and asymptomatic → discharge Wide QRS in TCA overdose: give bicarbonate.

Acid–base Early respiratory alkalosis (respiratory centre stimulation), then HAGMA (uncoupling) Management Urinary alkalinisation (bicarbonate, urine pH 7.5–8.5); correct K Avoid intubation (worsens acidosis); if needed, maintain hyperventilation Haemodialysis indications Level > 7.2 mmol/L (100 mg/dL), CNS symptoms, AKI, pulmonary oedema, refractory acidosis Don't let intubation stop the hyperventilation.

boxes.t: Calcium channel blocker and beta-blocker overdose
boxes.x: Comparison CCB: hyperglycaemia, vasodilation (amlodipine) Beta-blocker: hypoglycaemia, bradycardia, bronchospasm Stepwise management Fluids, calcium, atropine, vasopressors High-dose insulin euglycaemia (1 U/kg bolus, 1–10 U/kg/h) Glucagon (beta-blocker), lipid emulsion, pacing, ECMO Monitoring HDI Glucose every 30 min, K, echo High-dose insulin is the key therapy.

CO pathophysiology Binds Hb (240× O2) → left shift; mitochondrial toxicity Management 100% O2 (half-life 4–6 h → 74–90 min) Hyperbaric O2: COHb > 25%, LOC, neuro signs, pregnancy, ischaemia Cyanide Fire smoke, lactate > 8 mmol/L, high venous O2 Hydroxocobalamin 5 g Smoke victim with high lactate → give hydroxocobalamin.

boxes.t: Serotonin syndrome, NMS and malignant hyperthermia
boxes.x: Comparison Serotonin: rapid onset, clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhoea NMS: slow onset, rigidity, bradyreflexia; MH: anaesthetic triggers, hypercarbia Serotonin management Stop drugs, benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine NMS and MH NMS: stop drug, dantrolene, bromocriptine MH: stop volatiles, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, cooling Clonus = serotonin; rigidity = NMS.

boxes.t: Ethical principles and withdrawal of treatment
boxes.x: Four principles Beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy, justice Withdrawal of treatment Equivalent to withholding ethically; decision by consensus Family meeting, document, palliative care Practical aspects Symptom control (opioids, sedatives), stop non-comfort treatments, family presence Withdrawal is a change of goals, not of care.

boxes.t: Mental capacity and refusal of treatment
boxes.x: Capacity Understand, retain, weigh information, communicate decision Decision-specific; presume capacity Management Respect competent refusal (Jehovah's Witness): cell salvage, EPO, iron, TXA Unconscious patient Advance directive valid → respect it; otherwise best interests A capable adult may refuse life-saving treatment.

Admission factors Reversibility, patient wishes, comorbidity, frailty, likely benefit DNACPR Decision not to attempt CPR; discussed with patient/family, reviewed Futility Treatment with no reasonable chance of benefit; value-laden concept DNACPR does not mean do not treat.

boxes.t: Breaking bad news and family conflict
boxes.x: Structured approach (SPIKES) Setting, perception, invitation, knowledge, emotions, strategy/summary Supporting families Regular meetings, consistent message, diaries, psychology Conflict Listen, second opinion, mediation, ethics committee Communication prevents most ICU conflicts.

Ethical principles Dead donor rule, consent, separation of donation and treatment teams DBD vs DCD DBD: brain death; DCD: circulatory death after withdrawal (5 min stand-off) Family conflict Specialist nurse, respect wishes, time Separate end-of-life decisions from donation.

Frameworks Utilitarian (most lives saved), egalitarian, fairness, transparency Criteria SOFA, frailty, likely benefit; not age or disability alone Patients not allocated Palliative care, reassessment, communication Triage must be transparent and consistent.

Disclosure Duty of candour: apologise, explain, support Investigation Root cause analysis, no blame, learning System measures Smart pumps, double checks, standard concentrations, electronic prescribing Errors are system failures: fix the system.

Valid consent Informed, voluntary, capacity Incapacitated patients Deferred consent, proxy consent, ethics committee approval Issues Vulnerability, equipoise, data protection Research needs equipoise and protection of the vulnerable.

Define electrical storm ≥ 3 separate episodes of sustained VT/VF (or appropriate ICD therapies) within 24 hours Episodes separated by ≥ 5 minutes of sinus rhythm; incessant VT is a variant Associated with high short-term mortality; a medical emergency Outline your immediate management in the first hour Defibrillate/cardiovert unstable VT; check ICD interrogation (appropriate vs inappropriate shocks) Treat triggers: replace K+ to 4.5–5 and Mg2+ (2 g IV), stop proarrhythmic drugs, look for ischaemia (ECG, troponin, urgent angiography if ACS) Sedation and analgesia (e.g., midazolam/propofol, fentanyl) to blunt sympathetic drive; intubate if needed Non-selective β-blocker (propranolol 40 mg 6-hourly orally or esmolol infusion) – the single most effective drug to blunt sympathetic drive Amiodarone 150–300 mg IV load then infusion; lidocaine as add-on, especially if ischaemic VT Reprogram ICD to avoid repeated painful shocks (ATP first); avoid unnecessary shocks Explain why sympathetic blockade is central to its treatment and how propranolol differs from metoprolol in this setting Each shock causes pain/catecholamine surge → more VT (vicious circle) Catecholamines shorten refractoriness, increase automaticity and triggered activity Propranolol is non-selective (β1 + β2) and lipophilic → central sympatholytic effect Propranolol + amiodarone superior to metoprolol + amiodarone in storm (SHIELD/Chatzidou data) List the options if the storm persists despite drugs Deep sedation with intubation and ventilation Left stellate ganglion block (LSGB) or thoracic epidural anaesthesia for cardiac sympathetic denervation Urgent catheter ablation of the VT substrate (reduces recurrence) Mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO) as bridge if haemodynamically unstable Overdrive pacing; surgical cardiac sympathetic denervation; transplant/LVAD evaluation

Describe the role of the autonomic nervous system in ventricular arrhythmia and the rationale for neuromodulation Cardiac sympathetic fibres pass through the stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglia, mainly left-sided to the ventricles Sympathetic activation increases dispersion of repolarisation, triggered activity and re-entry Blocking the stellate ganglion removes this input without negative inotropy of large β-blocker doses Useful as a rescue or bridge to ablation in refractory storm Describe how a stellate ganglion block is done and its complications Ultrasound-guided injection of local anaesthetic (e.g., bupivacaine/lidocaine) near the stellate ganglion at C6–C7, left side first Can be a single shot or catheter infusion; bilateral if left alone fails Expected Horner syndrome confirms block Complications: vascular injection (vertebral artery → seizures), recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy, pneumothorax, haematoma, phrenic palsy What further therapies would you consider, and what are your goals for this patient over the next 24 hours Thoracic epidural (T1–T4) as alternative neuromodulation Urgent electrophysiology for mapping and ablation (with MCS support if needed) VA-ECMO or Impella if haemodynamic collapse with recurrent VT Correct electrolytes; exclude myocarditis (MRI/biopsy) and drug toxicity Polymorphic VT with normal QT → look for ischaemia; consider quinidine in selected cases Early discussion of advanced heart failure options (LVAD/transplant)

Name the echo sign described and list four other echo findings of acute RV pressure overload McConnell sign: RV free-wall akinesia/hypokinesia with apical sparing (normal or hyperkinetic apex) RV dilatation: RV/LV basal diameter ratio > 1.0 Septal flattening / D-shaped LV (paradoxical septal motion) Reduced TAPSE (< 16 mm) 60/60 sign: RV outflow acceleration time < 60 ms with TR gradient < 60 mmHg Dilated non-collapsing IVC; mobile right heart thrombus Classify the severity of her PE according to the ESC 2019 risk stratification High risk = haemodynamic instability (cardiac arrest, SBP < 90 mmHg or vasopressor need, persistent hypotension) Intermediate-high = no shock + PESI III–V/sPESI ≥ 1 + RV dysfunction on imaging AND raised troponin Intermediate-low = one or none of RV dysfunction/troponin She is normotensive with RV dysfunction and raised troponin → intermediate-high risk Outline her management Anticoagulation with LMWH or UFH (UFH if reperfusion may be needed) Do not give routine full-dose systemic thrombolysis (PEITHO: less decompensation but more major/intracranial bleeding) Monitor closely; rescue thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h) if she deteriorates Catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy if decompensating with high bleeding risk Careful oxygen; avoid large fluid boluses and intubation if possible (RV collapse) PE response team; consider IVC filter only if anticoagulation contraindicated

Explain the pathophysiology of RV failure in massive PE Sudden rise in pulmonary vascular resistance (clot + vasoconstriction from serotonin/thromboxane) Thin-walled RV dilates, wall tension rises, RV O2 demand increases Septum shifts left (ventricular interdependence) → LV under-filling, low cardiac output Hypotension lowers RV coronary perfusion → RV ischaemia → spiral of failure Describe the management of this high-risk PE, including thrombolysis dosing and contraindications UFH bolus 80 U/kg then infusion Systemic thrombolysis: alteplase 100 mg over 2 h (or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min, max 50 mg, in peri-arrest) Absolute contraindications: prior haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic stroke < 6 months, CNS tumour, major trauma/surgery/head injury < 3 weeks, active bleeding Noradrenaline for hypotension; avoid fluid overload (≤ 500 mL); dobutamine if low output Surgical embolectomy or catheter therapy if thrombolysis contraindicated or fails VA-ECMO for refractory shock or cardiac arrest What are the risks of intubating this patient and how would you reduce them Induction agents cause vasodilatation and myocardial depression → arrest Positive pressure raises RV afterload and reduces venous return Prefer awake/HFNC strategy if possible; if needed, ketamine/etomidate, vasopressor running Low tidal volume, low PEEP, avoid hypercapnia and hypoxaemia (increase PVR)

boxes.t: Cardiac tamponade and pulsus paradoxus — Q5
boxes.x: Define pulsus paradoxus and explain its mechanism Fall in systolic BP > 10 mmHg during inspiration Inspiration increases venous return to the RV; in tamponade the fixed pericardial volume makes the septum bulge into the LV LV filling and stroke volume fall (exaggerated ventricular interdependence) Pulmonary venous pooling on inspiration further reduces LV preload Other causes: severe asthma/COPD, massive PE, hypovolaemia, RV infarction Describe the echocardiographic signs of tamponade Pericardial effusion (often circumferential) RA systolic collapse (early, sensitive) and RV diastolic collapse (more specific) Dilated plethoric IVC (> 2.1 cm, < 50% collapse) Respiratory variation of mitral inflow E velocity > 25% (tricuspid > 40%) Swinging heart (corresponds to electrical alternans) Outline her management Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid or apical), leave drain Supportive: fluid bolus to keep preload, avoid positive-pressure ventilation and sedation if possible Vasopressor/inotrope as a temporising bridge only Send fluid for cytology, culture, protein, LDH Malignant effusion: consider pericardial window or intrapericardial therapy to prevent reaccumulation Avoid diuretics and vasodilators

boxes.t: Cardiac tamponade and pulsus paradoxus — Q6
boxes.x: What is the best management of the tamponade in this patient, and why Immediate transfer to theatre for emergency surgical repair Avoid routine full pericardiocentesis: restoring BP can re-open the tear, extend the dissection and cause fatal rebleeding Controlled drainage of small volumes (just enough to keep MAP ~60 mmHg) only if surgery cannot happen at once and patient is peri-arrest List the classification systems for aortic dissection and the complications of type A Stanford A = ascending aorta involved (surgical); B = not involving ascending aorta DeBakey I (ascending + beyond), II (ascending only), III (descending only) Type A complications: tamponade, acute aortic regurgitation, coronary occlusion (MI, usually RCA), stroke Malperfusion of gut, kidneys or limbs; rupture Describe the medical management of a haemodynamically stable acute dissection Analgesia (opioids) to reduce sympathetic drive IV β-blocker first (esmolol or labetalol) to HR < 60/min – reduces dP/dt (shear stress) Then vasodilator if needed (nitroprusside, nicardipine, GTN) to SBP 100–120 mmHg Do not give vasodilator before β-blocker (reflex tachycardia) Arterial line (right radial usually), urine output, serial lactate for malperfusion Type B: TEVAR if complicated (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain/hypertension)

Define recirculation and explain why it occurs here Oxygenated return blood is drawn back into the drainage cannula without passing through the systemic circulation Effective ECMO support falls even though circuit flow is high Risk factors: drainage and return cannula tips too close, high pump flow, low cardiac output, raised intrathoracic/abdominal pressure High pre-oxygenator saturation (86%) with falling SaO2 strongly suggests recirculation How would you confirm and quantify it Recirculation fraction R = (SpreO2 − SvO2) / (SpostO2 − SvO2) × 100 SvO2 measured from a true mixed/central venous sample (e.g., PA catheter) – often estimated Echo (or X-ray) to check cannula tip positions and distance (ideally > 10 cm apart) Ultrasound dilution (Transonic) gives direct measurement Clue: rising SpreO2 when flow is increased, with no SaO2 improvement How would you manage it, and what are the other causes of hypoxaemia on VV ECMO Reposition cannulas to increase tip separation (under echo/fluoro) Reduce pump flow to find the optimal flow (less recirculation) Change configuration (e.g., bicaval dual-lumen cannula with return jet aimed at the tricuspid valve) Optimise cardiac output and reduce intrathoracic pressure Other causes: ECMO flow too low relative to cardiac output (high native CO), oxygenator failure (check post-oxygenator PO2), low Hb, high VO2 (fever, shivering) Treat high native output: cool, sedate, β-blocker in selected cases; add a second drainage cannula

State the EOLIA entry criteria for VV ECMO and whether she meets them PaO2/FiO2 < 50 mmHg for > 3 h PaO2/FiO2 < 80 mmHg for > 6 h pH < 7.25 with PaCO2 ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h (RR ↑ to 35, Pplat ≤ 32) She meets criteria (P/F 52, pH 7.18/PaCO2 82) after optimal conventional therapy Describe the ventilator strategy once ECMO is running Ultra-protective ventilation ('lung rest'): Pplat ≤ 24–25 cmH2O, driving pressure ≤ 14–15 Low RR (~10/min), PEEP ≥ 10 cmH2O to prevent atelectasis FiO2 reduced to lowest tolerated (e.g., 0.3–0.5) Control PaCO2 with sweep gas; avoid rapid PaCO2 fall (> 50% in 24 h, risk of brain injury) List the main complications of VV ECMO and how anticoagulation is managed Bleeding (ICH, cannula site, GI) – most common Thrombosis: oxygenator, circuit, cannula-associated DVT Haemolysis (plasma free Hb), HIT, acquired von Willebrand syndrome Infection, limb ischaemia (femoral), air embolism, cannula dislodgement UFH titrated to anti-Xa 0.2–0.3 IU/mL or aPTT 1.5×; lower or stop if bleeding (circuits tolerate brief heparin-free periods) Bivalirudin if HIT

boxes.t: North–south syndrome on VA ECMO — Q9
boxes.x: Explain what is happening North–south (Harlequin) syndrome = differential hypoxaemia Recovering LV ejects deoxygenated blood (poorly oxygenated by oedematous lungs) into the aortic root Retrograde ECMO flow from the femoral artery meets native flow at a 'mixing point' in the aorta Coronary and cerebral (upper body) circulation get hypoxic blood while lower body gets ECMO blood How would you monitor for it ABG from the right radial artery (closest to coronary/cerebral flow); right-hand SpO2 Bilateral cerebral NIRS Echo to assess aortic valve opening and LV ejection Compare right radial PaO2 with post-oxygenator PO2 Outline the management options Optimise lung function: increase PEEP and FiO2, treat pulmonary oedema (diuresis/ultrafiltration), bronchoscopy Increase ECMO flow to push the mixing point proximally (may increase LV afterload) Convert to V-AV ECMO (add return cannula into the internal jugular) or V-V if heart recovered Move arterial return to axillary/subclavian or central aorta Consider weaning trial if LV has recovered sufficiently

boxes.t: North–south syndrome on VA ECMO — Q10
boxes.x: What is the problem, and why does it occur LV distension (LV stasis) on VA-ECMO Retrograde arterial flow increases LV afterload Poorly contracting LV cannot open the aortic valve; bronchial and Thebesian venous return keep filling it Results: raised LVEDP → pulmonary oedema, LV/aortic root thrombus, impaired recovery Describe the strategies for LV unloading (venting) Reduce ECMO flow to the minimum that keeps perfusion; add inotrope (dobutamine/milrinone) to help ejection IABP (reduces afterload and promotes aortic valve opening) Impella ('ECPELLA') – active LV unloading Atrial septostomy (balloon) or surgical LV/LA vent Monitor with echo, pulse pressure and pulmonary artery pressure How would you assess readiness to wean from VA-ECMO Underlying cause recovering; MAP > 65 with low-dose inotrope; pulsatile arterial trace Flow reduction trial to 1–1.5 L/min with echo: LVEF > 20–25%, LVOT VTI ≥ 10 cm, TDSa ≥ 6 cm/s Stable lactate and oxygenation during trial; adequate lung function If no recovery: bridge to durable LVAD/transplant or palliation (bridge-to-decision)

Describe the normal timing of inflation and deflation and their haemodynamic effects Inflation at the dicrotic notch (aortic valve closure, start of diastole) Inflation raises diastolic pressure → increases coronary perfusion (diastolic augmentation) Deflation just before systole (before the upstroke) Deflation lowers end-diastolic aortic pressure → reduced afterload and myocardial O2 demand Describe the four timing errors, how each appears, and its consequence Early inflation: before the dicrotic notch → premature aortic valve closure, raised LVEDP, reduced stroke volume, increased O2 demand Late inflation: after the dicrotic notch → sub-optimal diastolic augmentation and coronary perfusion Early deflation: augmented pressure falls sharply then a U-shape before systole → poor afterload reduction, possible retrograde coronary/carotid flow Late deflation: assisted end-diastolic pressure ≥ unassisted; balloon still inflated at systole → increased afterload and O2 demand (most dangerous) What are the triggering options ECG (R wave) trigger – most common Arterial pressure trigger (if ECG poor) Pacing spike trigger Internal/asynchronous mode only during cardiac arrest/no output

List the indications and contraindications for IABP Indications: mechanical MI complications (VSD, acute MR) as bridge, refractory ischaemia, high-risk PCI/CABG support Cardiogenic shock is no longer a routine indication (IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit) Absolute contraindications: moderate–severe aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection Relative: aortic aneurysm, severe peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled sepsis/bleeding Describe the complications of IABP Limb ischaemia (check distal pulses); vascular injury, dissection Bleeding, thrombocytopenia, haemolysis Balloon rupture (blood in the helium line) → gas embolism Malposition: renal artery occlusion (too low) or left subclavian/cerebral (too high); tip 2–3 cm below the left subclavian (2nd–3rd rib space on CXR) Explain why the IABP helps a patient with VSD or acute MR, and what is its effect on cardiac output Afterload reduction lowers systemic resistance → more forward flow and less left-to-right shunt/regurgitant volume Diastolic augmentation improves coronary perfusion of ischaemic myocardium Cardiac output increases modestly (~0.5–1 L/min) Needs some native cardiac function and a stable rhythm Impella or VA-ECMO if more support needed

Why is his anaphylaxis resistant to treatment β-blockade blunts the β1 (inotropic/chronotropic) and β2 (bronchodilator, mediator-release inhibition) effects of adrenaline Unopposed α effects and reflex vagal tone may cause bradycardia β-blocked patients have more severe and refractory reactions ACE inhibitors also worsen severity (bradykinin) Which drug would you give next? Explain its mechanism and dose Glucagon Activates adenylate cyclase via glucagon receptors, raising cAMP independently of β-receptors → inotropy and chronotropy Dose 1–5 mg IV over 5 minutes, then infusion 5–15 µg/min titrated Side effects: nausea and vomiting (protect airway), hyperglycaemia Outline the management of refractory anaphylaxis Adrenaline infusion titrated (start 0.05–0.1 µg/kg/min), via dedicated line Rapid fluids 500–1000 mL boluses (large volumes may be needed – capillary leak) Second vasopressor: noradrenaline or vasopressin; consider methylene blue for vasoplegia Airway: early intubation by the most experienced person if stridor/oedema; nebulised adrenaline Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only – they do not treat shock Send mast cell tryptase (soon after, 1–2 h, and > 24 h); observe for biphasic reaction ECMO in refractory shock/arrest; atropine for bradycardia

List the most common causes of perioperative anaphylaxis and grade the severity Common triggers: antibiotics (now the leading cause in UK, e.g., teicoplanin, cefazolin), NMBAs (rocuronium, suxamethonium), chlorhexidine, patent blue dye Latex less common now Grade I skin only; II moderate multi-organ; III life-threatening (shock, severe bronchospasm); IV cardiac/respiratory arrest This is grade III Describe the immediate management Call for help, stop all trigger agents, 100% O2, secure airway Adrenaline IV 50 µg boluses (titrated) in anaesthetised patient (IM 0.5 mg if no IV access/monitoring) Rapid crystalloid 20 mL/kg; elevate legs Start adrenaline infusion if more than 2–3 boluses needed CPR with standard arrest doses if SBP < 50 mmHg or arrest What investigations and follow-up are needed Mast cell tryptase: as soon as possible after resuscitation, at 1–2 h, and baseline at > 24 h Raised tryptase supports IgE/mast cell mechanism (normal does not exclude) Document all drugs and timings; report to national system Refer to allergy clinic for skin testing (4–6 weeks later) Inform patient and GP; alert bracelet

boxes.t: Post-ROSC care and temperature control — Q15
boxes.x: Describe the ERC–ESICM 2021 recommendations for temperature management and the evidence behind them Actively prevent fever (> 37.7 °C) for at least 72 h in patients who remain comatose TTM2 (2021): 33 °C vs normothermia with early fever treatment – no difference in 6-month mortality or function TTM1 (2013): 33 vs 36 °C – no difference Do not actively rewarm hypothermic patients quickly; avoid shivering (sedation, magnesium) Outline your physiological targets in the first 24 hours MAP > 65 mmHg (and adequate urine output, falling lactate) SpO2 94–98%; avoid hypoxaemia and hyperoxia Normocapnia (PaCO2 35–45 mmHg) Glucose 7.8–10 mmol/L; avoid hypoglycaemia Treat seizures; continuous or intermittent EEG Lung-protective ventilation 6–8 mL/kg PBW When is urgent coronary angiography indicated STEMI on ECG → emergency angiography/PCI No ST elevation: angiography only if high suspicion of ongoing coronary occlusion or haemodynamic/electrical instability COACT and TOMAHAWK: no benefit from immediate routine angiography in non-STEMI post-arrest

boxes.t: Post-ROSC care and temperature control — Q16
boxes.x: Describe the ERC–ESICM multimodal neuroprognostication algorithm Assess at ≥ 72 h after ROSC, after excluding confounders (sedation, hypothermia, metabolic) Prerequisite: comatose with motor response ≤ extension (M ≤ 3) Poor outcome likely if ≥ 2 of: absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at ≥ 72 h; bilaterally absent N20 SSEP waves at ≥ 24 h Highly malignant EEG (suppressed background ± periodic discharges, burst suppression) at > 24 h NSE > 60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h; status myoclonus ≤ 72 h Diffuse anoxic injury on CT (loss of grey–white differentiation) or MRI (DWI changes) What confounders must be excluded Residual sedatives/analgesics/neuromuscular blockers (renal/hepatic failure prolongs) Hypothermia Severe metabolic derangement (Na, glucose, urea, hepatic encephalopathy) Non-convulsive status epilepticus How would you communicate uncertainty to the family Private setting, senior clinician with nurse; use plain language Explain that prognosis is based on several tests over time, not one Avoid premature withdrawal decisions (self-fulfilling prophecy) Document, offer follow-up meetings; consider organ donation pathway if appropriate

List the 'reversible causes' of cardiac arrest and identify the likely one here 4 Hs: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia and metabolic, hypothermia 4 Ts: thrombosis (coronary/pulmonary), tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins Likely hyperkalaemia (missed dialysis, peaked T waves, K+ 8.1) Outline the specific treatment during CPR, with doses Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV rapid bolus (repeat if needed) – membrane stabilisation Insulin 10 units soluble + 25 g glucose IV rapid injection Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 50 mL IV if severe acidosis or renal failure Consider haemodialysis during CPR for refractory arrest; ECPR in selected centres Continue standard ALS; avoid treating with magnesium or amiodarone instead What should be done after ROSC Monitor glucose (hypoglycaemia after insulin) hourly for 6 h; glucose infusion Check K+ frequently (rebound rise as insulin effect wanes) Urgent dialysis Potassium binder (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer); salbutamol nebs as adjunct

Describe the ECG changes of hyperkalaemia in order of severity Peaked (tented) T waves PR prolongation, P-wave flattening/loss QRS widening, bradycardia, junctional rhythm Sine wave pattern → VF/asystole/PEA Explain how calcium works and describe the emergency treatment Calcium raises the threshold potential, restoring the gap with the resting membrane potential → stabilises the myocardium (does not lower K+) Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL (or chloride 10 mL) over 5–10 min; repeat if ECG unchanged; works within minutes, lasts 30–60 min Shift: insulin 10 U + glucose 25 g; salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised Bicarbonate only if acidotic Remove: stop ACEI/spironolactone, binders, loop diuretic if passing urine, dialysis if refractory/anuric Transcutaneous pacing / isoprenaline for bradycardia if unresponsive List the causes of pseudohyperkalaemia and of true hyperkalaemia Pseudo: haemolysed sample, prolonged tourniquet/fist clenching, very high WCC or platelets, delayed processing, EDTA contamination True – reduced excretion: AKI/CKD, drugs (ACEI/ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim), Addison, type 4 RTA True – shift/release: acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, suxamethonium, insulin deficiency, digoxin toxicity

Calculate the anion gap and explain the acid–base disorder AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3) = 141 − (118 + 16) = 7 mmol/L (corrected for albumin ≈ 9.5) → normal Hyperchloraemic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from large-volume saline Saline has Na = Cl = 154 mmol/L, SID = 0 → dilutes plasma SID → acidosis Respiratory compensation appropriate (expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × 16 + 8 ± 2 = 30–34; actual 36 → mild additional respiratory acidosis) Which fluid would you choose and why? Summarise the evidence Balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) preferred in sepsis (SSC 2021) SMART (2018): balanced fluids reduced major adverse kidney events vs saline BaSICS and PLUS (2021–22): no significant mortality difference overall; possible harm of saline in TBI excluded – use saline in brain injury Avoid starches (6S, CHEST: AKI, RRT, mortality) and gelatins Albumin may be added after large crystalloid volumes (ALBIOS: no overall benefit, possible benefit in septic shock) What are the harms of fluid overload in sepsis Pulmonary oedema, worse oxygenation, longer ventilation AKI (renal venous congestion), raised intra-abdominal pressure Gut oedema, ileus, poor wound healing Positive fluid balance independently associated with mortality; consider de-resuscitation once stable (ROSE model)

Define fluid responsiveness and describe how you would assess it in this patient Increase in stroke volume or cardiac output ≥ 10–15% after fluid challenge Passive leg raise with real-time CO measurement (VTI, pulse contour) – increase ≥ 10% predicts response Pulse pressure variation > 12–13% (only if fully ventilated, VT ≥ 8 mL/kg, sinus rhythm, closed chest) Mini-fluid challenge (100–250 mL) with VTI change; end-expiratory occlusion test IVC variation and CVP are poor predictors What are the limitations of using pulse pressure variation Spontaneous breathing efforts Arrhythmias (AF) Low tidal volume (< 8 mL/kg) or low lung compliance → false negatives Open chest, RV failure, raised intra-abdominal pressure → false positives/negatives Describe the phases of fluid therapy (ROSE model) Resuscitation: rapid boluses to restore perfusion (minutes) Optimisation: titrated fluid guided by responsiveness (hours) Stabilisation: maintenance only, aim neutral balance (days) Evacuation (de-resuscitation): active fluid removal with diuretics/ultrafiltration

Define reverse triggering and explain its mechanism Patient–ventilator dyssynchrony in which a passive, machine-initiated breath triggers an involuntary diaphragm contraction Mechanism: respiratory entrainment – a reflex coupling (stretch-reflex/vagal) between lung inflation and brainstem respiratory output, with a fixed phase relation (e.g., 1:1, 1:2) Typically seen in deeply sedated patients (e.g., ARDS) with no own triggering How do you recognise it on the ventilator waveforms Volume control: concave dip in the pressure trace during or after inspiration of a mandatory breath If the effort persists into expiration → double triggering/breath stacking (VT up to double) Pressure control: increase in flow and volume during the breath Oesophageal pressure or diaphragm EMG confirms (effort follows the machine breath) What are its consequences and how is it managed Breath stacking → high tidal volumes and transpulmonary pressures (VILI) Eccentric (lengthening) diaphragm contractions → diaphragm injury; pendelluft Management: adjust sedation (lighter or deeper), change RR or inspiratory time to break entrainment, switch to a patient-triggered mode Neuromuscular blockade if severe ARDS and unsafe volumes Can also be beneficial (prevents diaphragm atrophy) if VT controlled

Classify patient–ventilator dyssynchrony with examples Trigger: ineffective efforts (missed triggers), auto-triggering, reverse triggering, double triggering Flow: flow starvation (too little flow for demand) or excessive flow Cycling: premature cycling (machine ends breath early) or delayed cycling (breath continues into patient expiration) This patient has ineffective triggering Explain the causes of ineffective triggering in COPD Intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP): patient must first generate pressure equal to PEEPi before the trigger is sensed Excess pressure support → large VT, long Ti → more air trapping and weaker drive Insensitive trigger setting Weak respiratory muscles, over-sedation, metabolic alkalosis How would you correct it Apply external PEEP to ~80% of PEEPi to reduce trigger work Reduce pressure support to lower VT and allow full expiration Increase expiratory trigger (cycle-off) % (e.g., from 25% to 40–50%) to shorten Ti Use a more sensitive flow trigger; treat bronchospasm; consider NAVA/PAV

Define transpulmonary pressure and give the formula Transpulmonary pressure (PL) = airway pressure − pleural pressure (estimated by oesophageal pressure, Pes) End-inspiratory PL = Pplat − Pes(insp) End-expiratory PL = PEEP(total) − Pes(exp) Calculate her end-inspiratory and end-expiratory transpulmonary pressures and interpret them End-inspiratory PL = 34 − 20 = 14 cmH2O → safe (< 20–25 cmH2O); high Pplat is due to a stiff chest wall End-expiratory PL = 10 − 16 = −6 cmH2O → alveoli collapse at end-expiration (atelectrauma) She needs more PEEP (to make end-expiratory PL ≥ 0, i.e., PEEP ~16–18) Plateau pressure overestimates lung stress in obesity/abdominal hypertension Explain the difference between lung stress and strain, and the role of the chest wall Stress = transpulmonary pressure (force per area on the lung) Strain = VT / FRC (change in volume relative to resting volume); harmful above ~1.5–2 Airway pressure is shared between lung and chest wall according to their elastances: PL = Paw × EL / (EL + ECW) Stiff chest wall (obesity, abdominal hypertension, oedema) takes more of the pressure → lung stress lower than Pplat suggests

Describe how an oesophageal balloon catheter is placed and its position checked Insert balloon catheter (nasal/oral) into the lower third of the oesophagus (~35–40 cm), inflate with the recommended small volume Positive pressure deflection when advanced into the stomach, then withdraw until cardiac oscillations appear Occlusion test (Baydur): during end-expiratory occlusion, ratio of ΔPes/ΔPaw with efforts (or chest compression if passive) should be 0.8–1.2 Check the trace for cardiac artefact and correct balloon volume Compare the two methods of using Pes to set PEEP and summarise EPVent-2 Absolute (direct) method: set PEEP so that end-expiratory PL is 0 to +5 cmH2O Elastance-derived method: end-inspiratory PL = Pplat × (EL/ERS), keep < 20–25 cmH2O EPVent-2 (2019): Pes-guided PEEP vs high PEEP/FiO2 table – no difference in mortality or ventilator-free days (post-hoc benefit if PEEP near 0 PL) What is driving pressure and why does it matter Driving pressure (ΔP) = Pplat − PEEP = VT / respiratory system compliance Reflects the tidal volume relative to the 'baby lung' size ΔP > 15 cmH2O strongly associated with mortality (Amato 2015); keep ≤ 14–15

Calculate his ROX index and interpret it ROX = (SpO2 / FiO2) / RR = (92 / 0.6) / 34 = 153 / 34 ≈ 4.5 ROX ≥ 4.88 at 2, 6 or 12 h predicts HFNC success (low risk of intubation) ROX < 2.85 at 2 h, < 3.47 at 6 h, < 3.85 at 12 h predicts failure 4.5 is between the cut-offs → reassess closely (repeat in 1–2 h); do not delay intubation if worsening List the other signs of HFNC failure Rising RR, accessory muscle use, thoraco-abdominal paradox Falling ROX over time; rising FiO2 requirement Altered mental state, haemodynamic instability HACOR score > 5 at 1 h on NIV; rising lactate Why is delayed intubation harmful in this patient Delayed intubation after HFNC failure is associated with higher mortality (Kang 2015) Strong inspiratory efforts cause patient self-inflicted lung injury (P-SILI) – large transpulmonary swings Intubation in extremis carries higher risk of hypoxaemia and arrest

Explain the physiological effects of HFNC Flow up to 60 L/min matches patient inspiratory flow → stable, accurate FiO2 (up to 1.0) Washes out anatomical dead space → improved CO2 clearance and lower minute ventilation need Small flow-dependent PEEP (~0.5–1 cmH2O per 10 L/min with mouth closed) → alveolar recruitment Heated, humidified gas improves secretion clearance and comfort; reduces work of breathing Summarise the evidence for HFNC FLORALI (2015): HFNC vs NIV vs standard O2 – no difference in intubation overall; lower 90-day mortality with HFNC; benefit in P/F ≤ 200 Post-extubation: HFNC non-inferior to NIV in high-risk patients (Hernández 2016); combining NIV + HFNC lowers reintubation (HIGH-WEAN) Preoxygenation/apnoeic oxygenation during intubation When would you choose NIV rather than HFNC Hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (pH < 7.35, PaCO2 > 45) Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema Immunocompromised – either HFNC or NIV acceptable Obesity hypoventilation; post-extubation in hypercapnic patients

boxes.t: RSBI and spontaneous breathing trial — Q27
boxes.x: Calculate his rapid shallow breathing index and interpret it RSBI = RR / VT (litres) = 32 / 0.25 = 128 breaths/min/L RSBI > 105 predicts weaning failure; < 105 predicts success (Yang & Tobin 1991) It is one tool alongside clinical assessment; SBT failure is likely here List the criteria for readiness to wean and how an SBT is performed Cause of respiratory failure improving; PaO2/FiO2 > 150–200 on PEEP ≤ 8 and FiO2 ≤ 0.4–0.5 Haemodynamically stable (no or low-dose vasopressor), awake/cooperative (RASS 0 to −1), adequate cough SBT: PS 5–8 cmH2O with PEEP ≤ 5, or T-piece, for 30–120 min Failure criteria: RR > 35, SpO2 < 90%, HR > 140, SBP change > 20%, agitation, sweating, accessory muscle use Give four causes of weaning failure Respiratory load > capacity (bronchospasm, secretions, auto-PEEP) Cardiac: weaning-induced pulmonary oedema (raised BNP, echo) Neuromuscular: ICU-acquired weakness, diaphragm dysfunction, electrolytes (K, PO4, Mg) Neuropsychological: delirium, anxiety; metabolic alkalosis; over-feeding

boxes.t: RSBI and spontaneous breathing trial — Q28
boxes.x: List the risk factors for extubation failure Age > 65, chronic heart or lung disease Ventilation > 7 days, failed previous SBT Weak cough, copious secretions, poor neurological state Hypercapnia at end of SBT, BMI > 30, upper airway problems How would you assess and manage the risk of post-extubation stridor Cuff leak test: leak < 110 mL (or < 12–24% of VT) suggests laryngeal oedema If no leak and high risk: methylprednisolone 20–40 mg IV 4-hourly (or similar), starting ≥ 4 h before extubation Post-extubation stridor: nebulised adrenaline, heliox, steroids; reintubate if needed What support would you use after extubation and why High-risk patients (this patient): prophylactic NIV immediately after extubation, ideally alternating with HFNC Reduces reintubation rate (HIGH-WEAN 2019; ERS/ATS guideline) Low-risk patients: HFNC reduces reintubation vs conventional O2 Do not use NIV as rescue for established post-extubation respiratory failure (delays reintubation, increased mortality)

What is auto-PEEP and how do you detect it Positive alveolar pressure at end-expiration due to incomplete emptying (dynamic hyperinflation) Flow–time curve: expiratory flow does not return to zero before next breath Measure with an end-expiratory hold (pause): total PEEP − set PEEP = intrinsic PEEP (requires passive patient) In spontaneously breathing patients: oesophageal pressure drop before flow starts Explain why her blood pressure has fallen High intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return to the right heart Raised pulmonary vascular resistance increases RV afterload Can cause PEA arrest; risk of barotrauma (tension pneumothorax) Outline your immediate actions and ventilator strategy Disconnect from the ventilator briefly and allow full exhalation (± gentle chest compression); fluid bolus Reduce minute ventilation: RR 10–12, VT 6–8 mL/kg; accept permissive hypercapnia (pH > 7.2) Increase expiratory time: high inspiratory flow (60–100 L/min), short Ti, I:E ≥ 1:4 Keep Pplat < 30, intrinsic PEEP < 10–15 cmH2O Treat bronchospasm: salbutamol, ipratropium, steroids, IV magnesium, ketamine; exclude pneumothorax

Explain the 'waterfall' concept and how external PEEP helps him In COPD, expiratory flow limitation occurs because small airways collapse (critical closing pressure) Applying external PEEP below that pressure does not raise alveolar pressure (like water over a waterfall) External PEEP reduces the pressure gradient the patient must overcome to trigger → less work of breathing Set external PEEP ~80% of intrinsic PEEP (here ~8 cmH2O); check that plateau pressure does not rise List the factors that increase dynamic hyperinflation High minute ventilation (high RR or VT) Short expiratory time (long Ti, low inspiratory flow) High airway resistance (bronchospasm, secretions, small ETT, kinked tube) Increased lung compliance (emphysema) How does auto-PEEP affect measurements on the ventilator and at the bedside Overestimates CVP and PAOP (transmitted pressure) Underestimates respiratory compliance if PEEPi ignored (Crs = VT / (Pplat − total PEEP)) Increases trigger work and causes ineffective triggering

Define the stress index and explain how it is obtained Coefficient b of the power equation fitted to the airway pressure–time curve during constant-flow inspiration: Paw = a·t^b + c Requires volume control with constant flow, passive patient (no efforts) Reflects the change in compliance during tidal inflation Interpret the three stress index values and state what you would do in each case b < 0.9 (upward concavity): compliance improves during inflation → tidal recruitment → increase PEEP b ≈ 0.9–1.1 (straight line): constant compliance → optimal b > 1.1 (downward concavity, curve bends upward): compliance falls → overdistension → reduce PEEP or VT Grothues/Ranieri: targeting SI 0.9–1.1 reduces inflammatory mediators What are the limitations of the stress index Needs passive patient and square-wave flow Affected by chest wall stiffness (obesity, abdominal hypertension) – may reflect chest wall, not lung Global measure – does not detect regional heterogeneity Visual estimation is imprecise without software; endotracheal tube resistance affects proximal pressure

Describe the Berlin definition of ARDS Onset within 1 week of a known insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms Bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion, collapse or nodules Not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload Severity on PEEP ≥ 5: mild P/F 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe ≤ 100 Outline your lung-protective ventilation strategy VT 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (range 4–8) Plateau pressure ≤ 30 cmH2O; driving pressure ≤ 15 cmH2O PEEP set by ARDSNet higher PEEP/FiO2 table, or by stress index/compliance/Pes Permissive hypercapnia (pH > 7.2); target SpO2 88–95% Describe the adjuncts for severe ARDS and the evidence for each Prone positioning ≥ 16 h/day when P/F < 150 (PROSEVA: mortality 16% vs 33%) Neuromuscular blockade for 48 h in early severe ARDS if dyssynchrony (ACURASYS benefit; ROSE no benefit) Conservative fluid strategy (FACTT) Avoid routine recruitment manoeuvres (ART trial: harm) VV ECMO for refractory hypoxaemia (EOLIA); steroids may be considered (dexamethasone in COVID; DEXA-ARDS)

Explain how raised intra-abdominal pressure affects respiratory mechanics Diaphragm pushed cephalad → reduced FRC, basal atelectasis Chest wall elastance rises → higher Pplat for the same VT A large part of Pplat is used to distend the chest wall, so lung stress may be lower than Pplat suggests About 20–80% of IAP is transmitted to the thorax How would you set PEEP and VT in this patient Measure Pes to calculate transpulmonary pressure (end-inspiratory < 20–25, end-expiratory ≥ 0) Higher PEEP may be needed to counter basal collapse Tolerate Pplat > 30 if transpulmonary pressure is safe What measures would reduce intra-abdominal pressure Nasogastric and rectal decompression; prokinetics Sedation/analgesia ± neuromuscular blockade to relax abdominal wall Avoid fluid overload; diuresis or ultrafiltration Drain ascites/collections; surgical decompression if ACS

Explain how prone positioning improves oxygenation and reduces lung injury More homogeneous distribution of transpulmonary pressure and ventilation (less dorsal collapse) Better V/Q matching: perfusion stays dorsal while ventilation moves dorsal Heart and abdomen no longer compress the dorsal lung Reduces overdistension and cyclic collapse (VILI); better secretion drainage State the indications and contraindications Indication: moderate–severe ARDS, P/F < 150 on FiO2 ≥ 0.6 and PEEP ≥ 5, early (< 36 h), ≥ 16 h/day Absolute contraindication: unstable spinal fracture; open abdomen/chest relative; raised ICP Relative: haemodynamic instability, recent sternotomy, pregnancy, facial trauma, massive haemoptysis List the complications of prone positioning Pressure sores (face, chest, knees), facial oedema ETT displacement/obstruction, line or drain dislodgement Haemodynamic instability on turning Brachial plexus injury, corneal abrasion, feed intolerance

Describe how you would screen him for delirium using the CAM-ICU Step 1: assess arousal with RASS; CAM-ICU can be done if RASS −3 to +4 (if −4/−5, reassess later) Feature 1: acute change or fluctuating course of mental status Feature 2: inattention (letters test 'SAVEAHAART' – > 2 errors) Feature 3: altered level of consciousness (RASS ≠ 0) Feature 4: disorganised thinking (yes/no questions, commands) Positive = 1 + 2 + (3 or 4); ICDSC ≥ 4 is an alternative tool List the subtypes of delirium and the predisposing and precipitating factors Hyperactive, hypoactive (most common, worst prognosis, often missed), mixed Predisposing: age, dementia, alcohol, hearing/visual impairment, frailty Precipitating: benzodiazepines, sepsis, hypoxia, metabolic derangement, pain, sleep deprivation, restraints Anticholinergic drugs, urinary retention, constipation, withdrawal What are the consequences of ICU delirium Increased mortality (each day of delirium raises risk) Longer ventilation and ICU/hospital stay Long-term cognitive impairment (BRAIN-ICU) Self-extubation, line removal, falls; higher costs

What is the first step in managing her delirium Identify and treat the cause: check hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, pain, urinary retention, constipation, infection, electrolytes, drugs (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines), alcohol withdrawal Ensure safety; do not restrain if avoidable Non-pharmacological measures first (reorientation, family, glasses/hearing aids, sleep hygiene) Describe the ABCDEF bundle A: assess, prevent and manage pain B: both spontaneous awakening and breathing trials C: choice of analgesia and sedation (light sedation, avoid benzodiazepines) D: delirium – assess, prevent, manage E: early mobility and exercise F: family engagement and empowerment What is the role of drugs No drug prevents or treats delirium routinely (PADIS 2018) MIND-USA and AID-ICU: haloperidol does not reduce delirium duration or mortality Short-term low-dose antipsychotic for severe agitation endangering safety Dexmedetomidine for agitated delirium preventing extubation (DahLIA)

Compare hypertonic saline and mannitol for raised ICP Both create an osmotic gradient drawing water from brain to plasma; mannitol also lowers viscosity Mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg over 15–20 min: osmotic diuresis → hypovolaemia, hypotension, AKI Hypertonic saline (e.g., 3% 250 mL, or 23.4% 30 mL via central line): volume expander, maintains BP/CPP HTS may be more effective and longer-lasting; no clear mortality difference (COBI trial: continuous HTS no benefit) What sodium and osmolality targets would you use during osmotherapy Target serum Na+ 145–155 mmol/L Stop or hold mannitol if serum osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg Osmolar gap > 20 mOsm/kg indicates mannitol accumulation (risk of AKI) List the complications of osmotherapy Rebound intracranial hypertension on stopping (leakage across a disrupted BBB) Hypernatraemia, hyperchloraemic acidosis (HTS), fluid overload, pulmonary oedema Mannitol: AKI, hypovolaemia, hyperkalaemia Osmotic demyelination if chronic hyponatraemia corrected rapidly

Calculate her osmolar gap if Na 150 mmol/L, glucose 6 mmol/L and urea 10 mmol/L, and interpret it Calculated osmolality = 2 Na + glucose + urea = 300 + 6 + 10 = 316 mOsm/kg Osmolar gap = measured − calculated = 335 − 316 = 19 mOsm/kg Gap near 20 suggests mannitol accumulation (not cleared) Risk of mannitol-induced AKI → stop mannitol, switch to hypertonic saline if needed Explain how mannitol causes AKI Osmotic nephrosis: vacuolisation of proximal tubular cells Renal vasoconstriction at high concentrations Hypovolaemia from osmotic diuresis How would you manage her fluids now Replace urine losses with isotonic fluid to avoid hypovolaemia Keep Na 145–155 with hypertonic saline if ICP control still needed Monitor electrolytes (K, Mg, PO4) and urine output closely Haemodialysis if severe AKI with high osmolar gap (removes mannitol) – use slow/CRRT to avoid ICP rise

boxes.t: Tiered management of raised ICP — Q39
boxes.x: Describe the Tier 0 and Tier 1 measures of the SIBICC algorithm Tier 0 (baseline): head up 30°, neutral neck, ETT ties loose; sedation/analgesia; normothermia; Na > 135; SpO2 ≥ 94%, PaCO2 35–45; Hb > 7; MAP for CPP ≥ 60 Tier 1: CPP 60–70 mmHg, deepen analgesia/sedation Tier 1: intermittent mannitol or hypertonic saline boluses Tier 1: CSF drainage via EVD if present; EEG for seizures; consider anticonvulsants Describe the Tier 2 and Tier 3 measures Tier 2: mild hypocapnia (PaCO2 32–35 mmHg), neuromuscular blockade trial, MAP challenge to assess autoregulation, raise CPP if autoregulation intact Tier 3: secondary decompressive craniectomy Tier 3: barbiturate (thiopental/pentobarbital) coma titrated to burst suppression Tier 3: mild hypothermia (35–36 °C) – Eurotherm showed harm from early routine use Which measures should NOT be used routinely Steroids (CRASH: increased mortality in TBI) Prophylactic hypothermia; profound hyperventilation (PaCO2 < 30) Routine CSF lumbar drainage Routine CPP > 90 mmHg

boxes.t: Tiered management of raised ICP — Q40
boxes.x: Explain the Monro–Kellie doctrine and intracranial compliance Skull is a fixed box: brain + blood + CSF volume is constant A rise in one must be compensated by a fall in another (CSF shift to spinal canal, venous blood displaced) When compensation is exhausted, small volume changes cause large ICP rises (steep part of the pressure–volume curve) Summarise the evidence for decompressive craniectomy in TBI DECRA (2011): early bifrontal DC for moderate ICP rise – lower ICP, but worse functional outcome RESCUEicp (2016): DC for refractory ICP > 25 – lower mortality (27% vs 49%), more survivors in vegetative state/severe disability At 24 months more favourable outcomes with DC in RESCUEicp Decision must include discussion of likely disability with family Describe the ICP waveform and what a P2 > P1 means P1 percussion wave (arterial pulse), P2 tidal wave (brain compliance), P3 dicrotic wave (aortic valve closure) Normally P1 > P2 > P3 P2 > P1 indicates reduced intracranial compliance

Define malignant MCA infarction and its features Large MCA infarct (> 50% of MCA territory, or DWI volume > 145 mL) with space-occupying oedema Progressive decline in consciousness within 24–72 h; herniation Mortality up to 80% with medical treatment alone Summarise the evidence for decompressive hemicraniectomy (DESTINY, DECIMAL, HAMLET) Pooled analysis (≤ 60 years, surgery within 48 h): mortality reduced from ~71% to ~22% More patients with mRS ≤ 3 (moderate disability) at 1 year HAMLET: benefit if surgery within 48 h; no benefit if delayed up to 96 h DESTINY II (> 60 years): improves survival, but most survivors severely disabled (mRS 4) Outline the medical management while awaiting surgery Head up 30°, normothermia, normoglycaemia, treat seizures Osmotherapy (mannitol or HTS) as a bridge Airway protection if GCS ≤ 8 BP management: avoid hypotension; ≤ 185/110 if thrombolysis given

What factors would influence the decision for hemicraniectomy Age (strongest evidence ≤ 60 years), time from onset (≤ 48 h) Pre-stroke function and comorbidities Patient's previously stated values about survival with disability Dominant hemisphere (aphasia) – historically a concern, but outcomes similar; surgery should not be denied on side alone How would you counsel the family Surgery greatly improves the chance of survival Most survivors, especially > 60 years, will remain dependent (mRS 4: unable to walk without help) Ask what she would have wanted; shared decision-making; time-limited trial if uncertain What are the complications of decompressive craniectomy Infection, haematoma, CSF leak Hydrocephalus, subdural hygroma 'Syndrome of the trephined' (sinking skin flap) Need for later cranioplasty and its complications

Define status epilepticus using the ILAE time points t1 = 5 min for convulsive SE: time after which seizure is unlikely to stop on its own → start treatment t2 = 30 min: time after which long-term neuronal injury is likely Outline the stepwise treatment with drugs and doses 0–5 min: ABC, O2, glucose check, IV access, thiamine if alcohol/malnutrition 5–20 min: benzodiazepine – lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg, repeat once) or IM midazolam 10 mg 20–40 min (established SE): levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4.5 g) or fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg or valproate 40 mg/kg – all equally effective (ESETT) 40+ min (refractory SE): intubate; anaesthetic infusion – midazolam, propofol or thiopental Look for the cause: CT, electrolytes, toxicology, LP if infection suspected What are the systemic complications of prolonged convulsive status epilepticus Hypoxia, aspiration, airway obstruction Lactic acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis → AKI Arrhythmias, neurogenic pulmonary oedema Hyperglycaemia then hypoglycaemia; cerebral oedema and neuronal injury

What is your next step and how would you titrate therapy Refractory SE → continuous anaesthetic infusion Midazolam (0.2 mg/kg bolus, 0.05–2 mg/kg/h) or propofol (1–2 mg/kg, 2–5 mg/kg/h – watch PRIS) or thiopental/pentobarbital Titrate to seizure suppression or burst suppression on continuous EEG for 24–48 h, then wean slowly Add another second-line drug (e.g., valproate or lacosamide); vasopressors often needed Define super-refractory status epilepticus and list the treatment options SE continuing ≥ 24 h after starting anaesthesia, or recurring on weaning Options: ketamine (NMDA antagonist), barbiturates, additional AEDs (perampanel, topiramate) Immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) for autoimmune causes; ketogenic diet; hypothermia What is non-convulsive status epilepticus and how is it diagnosed Ongoing electrographic seizures without obvious motor activity Suspect in coma, fluctuating consciousness, subtle twitching, after convulsive SE Diagnosis needs EEG (Salzburg criteria)

boxes.t: Apnoea test for brain death — Q45
boxes.x: List the prerequisites before brain death testing Known, irreversible cause of catastrophic brain injury (neuroimaging consistent) Exclusion of confounders: sedatives (wait ≥ 5 half-lives or levels), neuromuscular blockade (train-of-four) Core temperature ≥ 36 °C; SBP ≥ 100 mmHg or MAP ≥ 60 mmHg No severe electrolyte, acid–base or endocrine disturbance Describe how the apnoea test is performed and the criteria for a positive test Pre-oxygenate with FiO2 1.0 for ≥ 10 min; baseline ABG with PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, normal pH Disconnect (or CPAP), give O2 via catheter to the carina (6 L/min) or CPAP 10 cmH2O Observe for any respiratory movement for 8–10 min Positive (consistent with brain death): no breathing with PaCO2 ≥ 60 mmHg AND ≥ 20 mmHg above baseline (pH < 7.30) Abort if SBP < 90 mmHg, SpO2 < 85% or arrhythmia → ancillary test When are ancillary tests needed Apnoea test cannot be completed safely Confounders cannot be excluded; facial/eye injury prevents examination High cervical cord injury Tests: CT angiography, cerebral perfusion scintigraphy, four-vessel angiography, EEG

boxes.t: Apnoea test for brain death — Q46
boxes.x: Explain the physiological changes after brainstem death Catecholamine storm (Cushing reflex) → hypertension, tachycardia, myocardial injury, neurogenic pulmonary oedema Then loss of sympathetic tone → vasodilatation and hypotension Diabetes insipidus (posterior pituitary failure) → polyuria, hypernatraemia Hypothermia, coagulopathy (tissue factor release), hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency Outline the donor management targets MAP ≥ 60–70 mmHg; vasopressin first-line (also treats DI), then noradrenaline Desmopressin for DI; Na 135–150 mmol/L; replace urine losses Lung-protective ventilation (VT 6–8 mL/kg, PEEP 5–10), recruitment, SpO2 > 92% Methylprednisolone 15 mg/kg; consider T3/T4; glucose 4–10 mmol/L; temperature > 36 °C What are the ethical principles of organ donation after brain death Dead donor rule Separation of the death-confirming team from the transplant team Consent/authorisation from the patient's prior wishes or family Optimise organs without causing harm to the dignity of the patient

What drug improves neurological outcome after aneurysmal SAH? Give the regimen Nimodipine 60 mg orally (or NG) every 4 hours for 21 days If hypotension: 30 mg every 2 hours Improves outcome by reducing delayed cerebral ischaemia, not angiographic vasospasm Describe your assessment of her new deficit Likely delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) – peaks day 4–14 Exclude other causes: hydrocephalus, rebleeding, seizures, hyponatraemia, hypoxia, infection, hypoglycaemia Urgent CT and CT angiography/perfusion; transcranial Doppler (mean velocity > 120 cm/s, Lindegaard ratio > 3) Check sodium, glucose, ABG and EEG if NCSE suspected Outline the management of DCI and treatments that are NOT recommended Euvolaemia; induced hypertension (raise SBP in steps with vasopressor) while monitoring response Endovascular rescue: intra-arterial vasodilators (verapamil, milrinone, nimodipine) or angioplasty if refractory Not recommended: prophylactic triple-H therapy (hypervolaemia harmful) Not recommended: routine magnesium (MASH-2), statins (STASH), clazosentan for outcome

Grade his SAH using WFNS and modified Fisher scales WFNS grade II (GCS 13–14 without motor deficit) Modified Fisher grade 4 (thick SAH with IVH) Modified Fisher 3–4 indicates highest risk of vasospasm/DCI Describe the early management until the aneurysm is secured Secure aneurysm as early as possible (within 24 h); endovascular coiling preferred if suitable (ISAT) SBP < 160 mmHg (reduce rebleeding risk) Nimodipine; analgesia; antiemetics; treat seizures if present (no routine prophylaxis) EVD if hydrocephalus/IVH with reduced consciousness Short course tranexamic acid not recommended routinely (ULTRA) Compare SIADH and cerebral salt wasting after SAH Both: hyponatraemia with concentrated urine (high urine Na) SIADH: euvolaemic/hypervolaemic → fluid restriction is NOT advised in SAH (risk of DCI) CSW: hypovolaemic (natriuresis + polyuria) → isotonic/hypertonic saline, fludrocortisone

Explain the 'saturation gap' and why pulse oximetry reads around 85% Saturation gap = difference between SaO2 calculated from PaO2 (normal) and measured SpO2/co-oximetry SaO2 MetHb (Fe3+) cannot carry O2 and absorbs light equally at 660 and 940 nm → ratio ~1 → SpO2 reads ~85% regardless of true value PaO2 is normal because dissolved O2 is unaffected; co-oximetry needed for diagnosis Describe the pathophysiology of methaemoglobinaemia and list common causes Haem iron oxidised from ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+) form Remaining haem shows increased O2 affinity (left shift) → impaired tissue O2 delivery Normally reduced by NADH–cytochrome b5 reductase (main) and NADPH–MetHb reductase (needs methylene blue) Causes: dapsone, local anaesthetics (benzocaine, prilocaine), nitrites/nitrates, nitric oxide, primaquine, rasburicase; congenital Outline the treatment Stop the offending drug; high-flow O2 Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min if symptomatic or MetHb > 20–30% (repeat after 30–60 min if needed) Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (ineffective, causes haemolysis) → exchange transfusion or hyperbaric O2 Dapsone has a long half-life (metabolites) → rebound; repeat doses; activated charcoal (multiple doses) Ascorbic acid as an alternative where methylene blue unavailable/contraindicated

Explain the mechanism of methylene blue in methaemoglobinaemia Methylene blue is reduced by NADPH–MetHb reductase to leukomethylene blue Leukomethylene blue reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+ (non-enzymatically) NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway (needs G6PD) – hence ineffective in G6PD deficiency List the adverse effects and contraindications of methylene blue Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs (MB is a potent MAO-A inhibitor) Haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; paradoxical MetHb at high doses (> 7 mg/kg) Falsely low SpO2 (blue dye) for a short time; blue-green urine and skin Pulmonary hypertension worsening; hypertension; avoid in pregnancy (teratogenic) When does methaemoglobinaemia fail to respond to methylene blue G6PD deficiency NADPH–MetHb reductase deficiency Sulfhaemoglobinaemia (irreversible; may be confused) Ongoing exposure/absorption (e.g., dapsone) or wrong diagnosis; consider exchange transfusion/HBO

Why do you suspect cyanide poisoning and how does cyanide cause toxicity Burning plastics, wool, silk release hydrogen cyanide; lactate > 8–10 mmol/L in a smoke victim strongly suggests cyanide Cyanide binds ferric iron in cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) → blocks oxidative phosphorylation Cells switch to anaerobic metabolism → lactic acidosis; venous blood bright red (high SvO2, cells cannot extract O2) Explain how hydroxocobalamin reverses cyanide toxicity and give the dose Hydroxocobalamin (vitamin B12a) has a cobalt ion that binds cyanide with high affinity Forms cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12), which is non-toxic and excreted in the urine Dose: 5 g IV over 15 min (70 mg/kg in children); repeat 5 g if needed Safe with CO poisoning (does not reduce O2 carrying), unlike nitrites List the side effects of hydroxocobalamin and the rest of the management Red skin and urine; interference with colorimetric lab tests and haemodialysis machines (blood leak alarm) Hypertension (also scavenges NO); allergy 100% O2 / consider HBO for CO poisoning; early airway assessment for inhalational injury Supportive care, vasopressors, treat acidosis

Describe the alternative antidotes and their mechanisms Sodium nitrite (300 mg IV) / amyl nitrite → induces methaemoglobinaemia; MetHb binds cyanide (cyanomethaemoglobin) away from cytochrome oxidase Sodium thiosulfate (12.5 g IV) → sulfur donor for rhodanese, converting cyanide to thiocyanate (renally excreted) Dicobalt edetate → cobalt chelates cyanide; toxic if no cyanide present (oedema, arrhythmias) Thiosulfate is slow alone; best combined Why are nitrites dangerous in smoke inhalation Smoke victims often have CO poisoning already reducing O2 carrying capacity Nitrites add MetHb → further loss of O2 carrying → worse tissue hypoxia Nitrites also cause vasodilatation and hypotension Outline the supportive treatment Airway, 100% O2, ventilation Fluids and vasopressors for shock Benzodiazepines for seizures Correct acidosis; avoid mouth-to-mouth resuscitation; decontaminate if skin exposure

Define vasoplegia after cardiopulmonary bypass and its risk factors Low SVR shock with normal or high cardiac output despite adequate volume, after CPB Due to inflammatory response, excess NO, vasopressin deficiency, KATP channel activation Risk factors: long bypass time, preoperative ACEI/ARB, β-blockers, heparin, low EF, LVAD/transplant surgery Which rescue therapy acts by inhibiting the nitric oxide/guanylate cyclase pathway? Explain its use Methylene blue Inhibits soluble guanylate cyclase (and NO synthase) → less cGMP → less vascular smooth muscle relaxation → raises SVR and MAP Dose 1–2 mg/kg IV over 20–60 min, then infusion if needed Avoid with serotonergic drugs, G6PD deficiency, pulmonary hypertension; interferes with SpO2 readings List the other options for refractory vasoplegia Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV (scavenges NO, inhibits NOS) Angiotensin II (ATHOS-3) Hydrocortisone Vasopressin if not already started; correct acidosis and hypocalcaemia

Calculate the anion gap and osmolar gap and interpret them AG = 140 − (100 + 6) = 34 mmol/L → high anion gap metabolic acidosis Calculated osmolality = 2 × 140 + 5 + 5 = 290; osmolar gap = 330 − 290 = 40 mOsm/kg (normal < 10) High AG + high osmolar gap + low lactate → toxic alcohol Calcium oxalate crystals → ethylene glycol Explain the metabolism of ethylene glycol and why it is toxic Ethylene glycol → (alcohol dehydrogenase) glycoaldehyde → glycolic acid (causes acidosis) → glyoxylic → oxalic acid Oxalate binds calcium → calcium oxalate crystals in kidneys (AKI), hypocalcaemia Parent compound causes osmolar gap; metabolites cause anion gap (gap shifts over time) Outline the treatment, including the antidote Antidote: fomepizole (15 mg/kg then 10 mg/kg 12-hourly) or ethanol – blocks alcohol dehydrogenase Haemodialysis: severe acidosis (pH < 7.25), AKI, high levels, visual signs (methanol), deteriorating Bicarbonate to correct acidosis; calcium only if symptomatic hypocalcaemia Cofactors: thiamine and pyridoxine (ethylene glycol)

Compare methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning Methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid; ethylene glycol → glycolic and oxalic acids Methanol: visual disturbance, optic disc oedema, blindness, basal ganglia (putamen) necrosis Ethylene glycol: CNS depression, cardiopulmonary failure, AKI with oxalate crystals, hypocalcaemia Both: early osmolar gap, later high AG acidosis Explain why the osmolar gap may be normal in a late presentation Parent alcohol (osmotically active) has been metabolised Toxic acid metabolites raise the anion gap but not the osmolar gap much So a normal osmolar gap does not exclude toxic alcohol poisoning List the indications for haemodialysis and cofactors used in methanol poisoning Severe acidosis, visual impairment, coma or seizures, AKI High methanol level (> 50 mg/dL; EXTRIP > 700 mg/L without fomepizole) Fomepizole/ethanol continued during dialysis (dose adjusted) Folinic acid/folic acid 50 mg IV 4–6 hourly (helps metabolise formate)

Describe the clinical features of LAST CNS: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation → seizures → coma CVS: hypertension/tachycardia early → bradycardia, wide QRS, VT/VF, asystole Bupivacaine is most cardiotoxic; cardiac arrest may occur without CNS warning Calculate her dose and give the maximum safe dose of bupivacaine 40 mL × 5 mg/mL = 200 mg Max bupivacaine ~2 mg/kg (2.5 mg/kg with adrenaline) – 200 mg is above the limit for a 70 kg patient without adrenaline (~150 mg) Outline the management of the cardiac arrest, including lipid emulsion dosing Stop injection, call for help, airway, 100% O2; control seizures with benzodiazepines 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg IV over 1 min, then infusion 15 mL/kg/h Repeat bolus up to twice at 5-min intervals; double infusion to 30 mL/kg/h; max 12 mL/kg total Modified ALS: small adrenaline doses (≤ 1 µg/kg); avoid vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, β-blockers and local anaesthetics (lidocaine) Prolonged CPR (may need > 1 h); consider ECMO
