Explain the proposed mechanisms of action of lipid emulsion Lipid sink: forms a lipid compartment in plasma that absorbs lipophilic drug away from tissues Lipid shuttle: carries drug to liver and muscle for storage/metabolism Direct cardiotonic effect: provides fatty acids to myocardium, improves calcium handling List the factors that increase the risk of LAST High dose, intravascular injection, highly vascular sites (intercostal > epidural > brachial plexus) Extremes of age, low muscle mass, pregnancy Cardiac disease, conduction block, low EF Hepatic/renal failure, acidosis, hypoxia (more free drug) Describe preventive measures Calculate and use the lowest effective dose; know maximum doses Ultrasound guidance; incremental injection with frequent aspiration Adrenaline test dose / adrenaline-containing solution as marker Monitoring during and 30 min after; lipid emulsion immediately available

Describe the clinical features of magnesium toxicity at different levels Therapeutic range ~2–4 mmol/L > 4–5 mmol/L: loss of deep tendon reflexes, nausea, flushing, somnolence > 6–7 mmol/L: respiratory depression, muscle paralysis > 7.5–12 mmol/L: heart block, cardiac arrest What is the first treatment? Give the dose Stop the magnesium infusion Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL (1 g) IV over 10 min – antagonises Mg at the neuromuscular junction and myocardium Support ventilation (bag–mask/intubation) if respiratory depression Why did toxicity develop and how should it be monitored Mg is excreted renally – oliguria/AKI in pre-eclampsia leads to accumulation Monitor hourly: reflexes, RR (> 12), SpO2, urine output (> 30 mL/h) Serum Mg levels if renal impairment or clinical concern Reduce or stop infusion if oliguric; furosemide/dialysis to enhance clearance in severe cases

List the indications for IV magnesium in the ICU, with doses Eclampsia prevention/treatment: 4 g IV over 5–15 min, then 1 g/h for 24 h Torsades de pointes: 2 g IV over 10 min Acute severe asthma: 1.2–2 g IV over 20 min Hypomagnesaemia, AF rate control adjunct, refractory hypokalaemia Describe the physiological actions of magnesium Calcium antagonist: blocks L-type calcium channels → smooth muscle relaxation, vasodilatation, bronchodilatation NMDA receptor antagonist (CNS), anticonvulsant in eclampsia Cofactor for Na/K-ATPase – needed to correct hypokalaemia Reduces acetylcholine release at NMJ → potentiates neuromuscular blockers What are the causes and consequences of hypomagnesaemia in the ICU Causes: diuretics, PPIs, alcohol, diarrhoea, refeeding, aminoglycosides/amphotericin, CRRT Consequences: arrhythmias (torsades), refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia Weakness, seizures, tetany Associated with worse outcome and longer ventilation

Define refractory septic shock and outline your stepwise approach Persistent hypotension despite high-dose vasopressors (e.g., noradrenaline > 0.5 µg/kg/min) and adequate fluid Check source control, adequacy of antibiotics, fluid status, cardiac function (echo), acidosis and calcium Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day Add adrenaline (especially if cardiac dysfunction) or angiotensin II Explain the mechanisms of vasodilatory shock Excess inducible NO synthase → NO → cGMP → vasodilatation Activation of KATP channels → hyperpolarisation of vascular smooth muscle Relative vasopressin deficiency Adrenergic receptor down-regulation and relative adrenal insufficiency What is the evidence for methylene blue and angiotensin II in septic shock Methylene blue: small RCTs show faster shock resolution and less vasopressor need; no definitive mortality benefit Angiotensin II (ATHOS-3, 2017): raised MAP in vasodilatory shock; no mortality difference; risk of thrombosis (VTE prophylaxis) Both are rescue therapies in refractory shock

Calculate the urinary anion gap and explain what it measures UAG = urine (Na + K) − Cl = (40 + 30) − 50 = +20 mmol/L UAG is an indirect measure of urinary ammonium (NH4+) excretion (NH4+ is excreted with Cl−) Negative UAG (−20 to −50) = high NH4+ excretion → kidneys responding normally → GI bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea) Positive UAG = low NH4+ → renal cause (distal RTA) Interpret her results and give the most likely diagnosis Positive UAG + urine pH > 5.5 despite acidosis + hypokalaemia Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis Causes: Sjögren, SLE, amphotericin, lithium, toluene; complications: nephrocalcinosis, stones What are the limitations of the urinary anion gap, and what is the urine osmolar gap Unreliable if other unmeasured anions in urine (ketones, hippurate from toluene, drugs like penicillins) Unreliable if urine Na < 20 (volume depletion) or polyuria Urine osmolar gap = measured urine osm − [2(Na + K) + urea + glucose]; NH4+ ≈ gap/2 Urine osmolar gap > 100–150 mOsm/kg = adequate NH4+ excretion

Compare the three main types of renal tubular acidosis Type 1 (distal): impaired H+ secretion; urine pH > 5.5; low K; stones/nephrocalcinosis; positive UAG Type 2 (proximal): impaired HCO3 reabsorption; urine pH < 5.5 when HCO3 low; low K; Fanconi syndrome (glycosuria, phosphaturia), myeloma, acetazolamide, tenofovir Type 4: hypoaldosteronism or resistance; high K; urine pH < 5.5; mild acidosis Type 4 causes: diabetic nephropathy (hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism), ACEI/ARB, spironolactone, heparin, trimethoprim What is the diagnosis in this patient and how would you treat it Type 4 RTA (hyperkalaemia, urine pH < 5.5, diabetes, ACEI) Reduce/stop K-sparing drugs; low K diet; loop or thiazide diuretic Fludrocortisone if not hypertensive/fluid overloaded; potassium binder List the causes of a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis GI HCO3 loss: diarrhoea, ileostomy, pancreatic fistula, ureterosigmoidostomy Renal: RTA, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors Iatrogenic: large-volume 0.9% saline Early CKD, recovery from DKA (ketones lost in urine)

Describe the three independent variables of the Stewart approach Strong ion difference (SID): fully dissociated cations minus anions (Na + K + Ca + Mg − Cl − lactate); normal ~40–42 Total weak acids (Atot): mainly albumin and phosphate PaCO2 H+ and HCO3− are dependent variables Calculate the apparent SID and explain why large-volume saline causes acidosis SIDa ≈ Na + K − Cl − lactate = 142 + 4 − 120 − 1 = 25 mEq/L (low; normal ~40) Low SID → more water dissociation → higher H+ → acidosis 0.9% saline has Na = Cl = 154 → SID 0; large volumes dilute plasma SID toward zero Balanced solutions have an effective SID ~27–29 → less acidosis How does his low albumin affect the acid–base picture Albumin is a weak acid; hypoalbuminaemia is a metabolic alkalosis It masks the acidosis and lowers the anion gap (correct AG: + 2.5 for every 10 g/L fall in albumin) Strong ion gap (SIG = SIDa − SIDe) identifies unmeasured anions

Using the traditional approach, calculate the albumin-corrected anion gap and the delta ratio AG = 138 − (90 + 24) = 24 mmol/L Corrected AG = 24 + 2.5 × (40 − 20)/10 = 24 + 5 = 29 mmol/L Delta: AG has risen by ~17 but HCO3 has not fallen at all (ΔAG/ΔHCO3 ≫ 2) → coexisting metabolic alkalosis Mixed disorder: high AG (lactic) acidosis + metabolic alkalosis (vomiting) with normal pH Interpret the same results using the Stewart approach SIDa = 138 − 90 − 6 = 42 (normal) despite lactate – because low chloride (vomiting) raises SID Hypoalbuminaemia (low Atot) adds alkalosis Lactate acidosis is hidden by hypochloraemic and hypoalbuminaemic alkalosis Compare the advantages and limitations of the bicarbonate, base excess and Stewart approaches Bicarbonate/AG: simple, bedside; misses mixed disorders if albumin not corrected Base excess: quantifies metabolic component; does not explain cause; partitioned BE helps Stewart: explains mechanisms (chloride, albumin, unmeasured anions); more complex, needs many measurements

What is the diagnosis and its mechanism Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (DDS) Rapid removal of urea from blood; urea leaves the brain more slowly (urea transporter down-regulation in uraemia) Osmotic gradient → water moves into brain cells → cerebral oedema Idiogenic osmoles and rapid correction of acidosis (CSF pH falls paradoxically) contribute List the risk factors First dialysis session with very high urea (> 60 mmol/L / BUN > 175 mg/dL) Severe metabolic acidosis; children and elderly Pre-existing neurological disease (TBI, stroke, seizures), raised ICP Aggressive (high blood flow, large dialyser, long) first session; hypernatraemia/hypoglycaemia How can it be prevented and treated First session short (2 h), low blood flow (150–250 mL/min), small dialyser – aim urea reduction ≤ 30–40% Daily short sessions or CRRT in high-risk patients (especially with brain injury) Treat: stop or slow dialysis; mannitol or hypertonic saline; seizure control Higher dialysate sodium

List the absolute indications for renal replacement therapy Refractory hyperkalaemia (> 6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes) Severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.15) Refractory fluid overload/pulmonary oedema Uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding); dialysable toxins Summarise the evidence on timing of RRT in AKI AKIKI (2016) and STARRT-AKI (2020): early RRT does not reduce mortality vs a delayed strategy; more adverse events with early AKIKI 2 (2021): waiting too long (beyond the delayed trigger) is harmful Strategy: start RRT for an absolute indication or prolonged severe oliguria/high urea Compare CRRT and intermittent HD in this patient and choose a modality CRRT: slow continuous removal, better haemodynamic tolerance, steady fluid balance, less ICP rise IHD: rapid clearance (better for hyperkalaemia, toxins), allows mobilisation, cheaper No mortality difference in trials; CRRT/SLED preferred in shock or brain injury Choose CRRT (on vasopressors) Dose 20–25 mL/kg/h effluent (RENAL, ATN trials: higher dose no benefit)

Explain how regional citrate anticoagulation works Citrate infused pre-filter chelates ionised calcium → prevents clotting in the circuit (target post-filter iCa 0.25–0.35 mmol/L) Most calcium–citrate complex is removed by the filter Remaining citrate is metabolised by liver (Krebs cycle) to bicarbonate; calcium is replaced post-filter to keep systemic iCa 1.0–1.2 Calculate the total-to-ionised calcium ratio and interpret it Ratio = 3.1 / 0.85 ≈ 3.6 Ratio > 2.5 indicates citrate accumulation Due to impaired citrate metabolism (liver failure, shock with poor perfusion) → bound calcium rises, ionised falls, metabolic acidosis with high AG How would you manage it Reduce or stop citrate (switch to heparin or no anticoagulation) Increase dialysate/replacement flow to remove more citrate–calcium complex Increase calcium replacement to correct ionised hypocalcaemia Treat acidosis; monitor every 4–6 h Note the opposite problem, citrate overload with good metabolism → metabolic alkalosis

What is the most likely cause and its mechanism Citrate-induced hypocalcaemia Stored blood products contain citrate, which chelates ionised calcium During rapid transfusion (or with liver dysfunction/hypothermia) citrate metabolism is overwhelmed Describe the consequences of hypocalcaemia in massive transfusion Myocardial depression, hypotension, prolonged QT, arrhythmias Impaired coagulation (calcium is factor IV) Part of the 'lethal diamond': hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy, hypocalcaemia Neuromuscular irritability (paraesthesia, tetany) How would you monitor and treat it Monitor ionised calcium frequently (every 30–60 min) during massive transfusion Keep iCa > 1.1 mmol/L Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL (or gluconate 30 mL) IV, repeated as needed Warm products and patient; correct acidosis Viscoelastic-guided product replacement

What is your immediate treatment? Give the dose and target 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL IV over 20 min (or 100 mL bolus; 2 mL/kg) Check Na after 20 min; repeat up to 2–3 times until symptoms stop Target rise 4–6 mmol/L in the first hours (enough to reduce cerebral oedema) Limit correction to ≤ 10 mmol/L in 24 h (8 if high risk of ODS) and ≤ 18 in 48 h Explain the pathophysiology of hyponatraemic encephalopathy Low plasma osmolality → water moves into brain cells → cerebral oedema Acute (< 48 h): no time for brain adaptation (loss of electrolytes and organic osmolytes) → high risk of herniation Exercise-associated: excess water intake + non-osmotic ADH release List the risk factors for osmotic demyelination syndrome Chronic hyponatraemia (> 48 h) with Na ≤ 105–110 mmol/L Alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease Hypokalaemia Rapid correction (> 8–10 mmol/L/24 h)

What has happened and why is it dangerous Overcorrection (11 mmol/L in 12 h) due to water diuresis once volume restored (ADH switched off) and K replaced High risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (chronic, alcoholic, hypokalaemic) ODS: dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, locked-in syndrome, days after correction How would you manage the overcorrection Stop hypertonic/isotonic saline Give desmopressin 1–2 µg IV/SC to stop the water diuresis (DDAVP clamp) Give 5% dextrose (e.g., 3 mL/kg/h) to lower Na back to the target Check Na every 1–2 h; aim to bring the rise back below 8 mmol/L/24 h Outline the diagnostic approach to hyponatraemia Measure plasma osmolality (exclude pseudohyponatraemia and hyperglycaemia) Urine osmolality: < 100 = excess water intake/beer potomania; > 100 = ADH present Urine Na: < 30 = low effective volume; > 30 = SIADH, diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, CSW Assess volume status; check TSH and cortisol

What is the most likely cause? Explain the pathophysiology Refeeding syndrome with severe hypophosphataemia Starvation depletes total body phosphate, K and Mg while serum levels may be normal Feeding (carbohydrate) → insulin release → intracellular shift of phosphate, K, Mg and glucose; phosphate used for ATP and 2,3-DPG Thiamine is consumed in carbohydrate metabolism → Wernicke's; sodium and water retention → fluid overload List the NICE criteria for high risk of refeeding One of: BMI < 16, unintentional weight loss > 15% in 3–6 months, little/no intake > 10 days, low K/PO4/Mg before feeding Or two of: BMI < 18.5, weight loss > 10%, little intake > 5 days, alcohol abuse or drugs (insulin, chemotherapy, antacids, diuretics) He is high risk (BMI 15, 10 days of no intake) Describe the clinical consequences of severe hypophosphataemia Respiratory muscle weakness, failure to wean Cardiac failure, arrhythmias Seizures, confusion, paraesthesia Rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, white cell and platelet dysfunction

Outline your plan for starting nutrition safely Thiamine 200–300 mg daily (Pabrinex) before feeding and for 10 days, plus vitamin B complex and multivitamin Start low: 5–10 kcal/kg/day (5 if BMI < 14), increase slowly over 4–7 days to target Correct K, PO4, Mg before and during feeding Monitor electrolytes daily (or twice daily) for the first week; ECG monitoring Describe the replacement of phosphate Severe (< 0.3–0.5 mmol/L) or symptomatic: IV phosphate 0.3–0.5 mmol/kg over 6–12 h Use potassium or sodium phosphate depending on K Risks: hypocalcaemia, metastatic calcification, hyperkalaemia; caution in renal failure What does the evidence say about caloric restriction in ICU refeeding Doig 2015 (Refeeding RCT): in ICU refeeding hypophosphataemia, restricting calories to 20 kcal/h for 2 days improved survival Gradual return to full feeding over the next days Hypophosphataemia after starting feeding in ICU should trigger caloric restriction

Which drugs should be given before endoscopy? Give doses and reasons Vasoactive drug as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected: terlipressin 2 mg IV 4-hourly (1 mg when bleeding controlled), or octreotide 50 µg bolus then 50 µg/h, for 2–5 days Antibiotic prophylaxis: ceftriaxone 1 g/day for up to 7 days – reduces infection, rebleeding and mortality IV erythromycin 250 mg 30–120 min before endoscopy – improves visualisation Avoid routine FFP/platelets to correct INR (no benefit, raises portal pressure); PPI may be given until endoscopy Describe your transfusion and resuscitation strategy Restrictive transfusion: transfuse at Hb < 7 g/dL, target 7–8 (Villanueva 2013: lower mortality and rebleeding) Avoid over-transfusion and excessive fluid (raises portal pressure → rebleeding) Airway protection (intubation) if massive haematemesis or encephalopathy before endoscopy When should endoscopy be performed, and what is done Within 12 h of presentation once resuscitated (Baveno VII) Endoscopic band ligation for oesophageal varices Cyanoacrylate glue injection for gastric (fundal) varices

What are the rescue options for refractory variceal bleeding Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken–Blakemore/Minnesota tube) as a bridge for up to 24 h (after intubation) Self-expanding oesophageal metal stent (fewer complications than balloon) Rescue TIPS Repeat endoscopy if feasible Define 'pre-emptive TIPS' and its indications TIPS placed within 72 h (ideally < 24 h) after initial successful endoscopic control in high-risk patients Indications: Child–Pugh C 10–13, or Child–Pugh B > 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy Reduces rebleeding and mortality (García-Pagán 2010) List the complications of balloon tamponade and of TIPS Balloon: oesophageal rupture/ulceration, aspiration, airway obstruction (balloon migration) Balloon: rebleeding after deflation in ~50% TIPS: hepatic encephalopathy, heart failure (raised preload), shunt dysfunction TIPS: liver failure, haemolysis, infection

State the King's College criteria for transplantation in paracetamol-induced ALF Arterial pH < 7.30 (or lactate > 3.0 mmol/L) after adequate fluid resuscitation OR all three within 24 h: INR > 6.5 (PT > 100 s), creatinine > 300 µmol/L (3.4 mg/dL), grade 3–4 encephalopathy Modified criteria: lactate > 3.5 mmol/L at 4 h, or > 3.0 after resuscitation, add sensitivity She meets criteria (pH 7.24; and INR, creatinine and grade 3 encephalopathy) State the King's College criteria for non-paracetamol ALF INR > 6.5 alone OR any 3 of: age < 10 or > 40, aetiology non-A non-B/drug reaction, jaundice to encephalopathy > 7 days, INR > 3.5, bilirubin > 300 µmol/L (17.5 mg/dL) Limitations: high specificity but lower sensitivity; MELD and lactate also used Outline her immediate management Continue N-acetylcysteine (benefit even late) Urgent referral to a transplant centre Intubate for grade 3–4 encephalopathy; protect against cerebral oedema Treat hypoglycaemia, infection screening, CRRT for AKI/hyperammonaemia

Explain why cerebral oedema occurs in ALF and its risk factors Ammonia is converted to glutamine in astrocytes → osmotic swelling (cytotoxic oedema) Loss of cerebral autoregulation, systemic inflammation increase cerebral blood flow Risk factors: ammonia > 150–200 µmol/L, hyperacute presentation, grade 3–4 encephalopathy, young age, AKI, vasopressor need Outline neuroprotective measures Head up 30°, sedation, normocapnia (PaCO2 35–40 mmHg), avoid hypoxia Induce hypernatraemia: Na 145–155 mmol/L with hypertonic saline Early CRRT to lower ammonia (high-dose, also controls temperature and acid–base) Mannitol for surges in ICP; avoid fever; consider ICP monitoring in selected patients What other organ support does he need Haemodynamic: noradrenaline for vasodilatory shock; hydrocortisone if refractory Glucose monitoring – hypoglycaemia common; give dextrose Infection surveillance; low threshold for antibiotics/antifungals Coagulopathy: no routine correction unless bleeding/procedures (INR is a prognostic marker)

boxes.t: Intra-abdominal hypertension and compartment syndrome — Q77
boxes.x: Describe how intra-abdominal pressure is measured Intravesical (bladder) pressure via urinary catheter, instilling ≤ 25 mL sterile saline Measured in mmHg at end-expiration, supine, transducer zeroed at the mid-axillary line at the iliac crest Abdominal muscles relaxed (no contractions) Define IAH grades and abdominal compartment syndrome, and calculate his abdominal perfusion pressure Normal IAP 5–7 mmHg; IAH = sustained IAP ≥ 12 mmHg Grades: I 12–15, II 16–20, III 21–25, IV > 25 mmHg ACS = sustained IAP > 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction APP = MAP − IAP = 70 − 24 = 46 mmHg (target ≥ 60) → he has ACS (grade III with oliguria and raised airway pressure) Explain the organ effects of raised IAP Renal: renal venous congestion and compression → oliguria/AKI Respiratory: raised diaphragm → reduced compliance, higher Pplat, hypoxaemia Cardiovascular: reduced venous return and CO; falsely high CVP Gut ischaemia (bacterial translocation), raised ICP

boxes.t: Intra-abdominal hypertension and compartment syndrome — Q78
boxes.x: Outline the medical management of intra-abdominal hypertension Evacuate intraluminal contents: NG and rectal decompression, prokinetics, enemas Evacuate space-occupying lesions: percutaneous drainage of ascites/collections Improve abdominal wall compliance: sedation, analgesia, neuromuscular blockade, avoid head-up > 20° Optimise fluids: avoid excess, diuretics or ultrafiltration once stable; aim APP ≥ 60 When is surgical decompression indicated, and what are its complications Refractory ACS (IAP > 20–25 with organ failure) despite medical measures Decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure (open abdomen, VAC) Complications: fluid/protein loss, fistula, infection, ventral hernia, reperfusion syndrome List the risk factors for intra-abdominal hypertension in ICU patients Large-volume fluid resuscitation (> 5 L/24 h), positive fluid balance Pancreatitis, abdominal surgery, trauma, ileus, ascites Obesity, prone positioning, high PEEP Sepsis, burns, massive transfusion

What is the diagnosis and its pathophysiology Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (NOMI) Splanchnic vasoconstriction due to low cardiac output, hypovolaemia and vasopressors (and digoxin) Mesenteric vasospasm leads to hypoperfusion and bowel infarction without vessel occlusion Describe the diagnostic findings CT angiography: narrowing of SMA branches, irregular ('string of sausages'), pruning, poor bowel wall enhancement Lactate is non-specific and rises late; normal lactate does not exclude ischaemia Signs of transmural infarction: pneumatosis, portal venous gas, free fluid Outline the management Treat the cause: optimise cardiac output and volume; reduce vasoconstrictors where possible Intra-arterial vasodilator (papaverine) via catheter in the SMA during angiography Laparotomy if peritonitis or signs of necrosis (resection, second-look surgery) Broad-spectrum antibiotics; bowel rest Prefer inodilators; avoid digoxin and high vasopressin doses

Describe the types of acute mesenteric ischaemia Arterial embolism (~50%): AF, post-MI; SMA just beyond the middle colic artery Arterial thrombosis (~25%): atherosclerosis, ostial; often prior chronic symptoms NOMI (~20%): low-flow states, vasopressors Mesenteric venous thrombosis (~5–10%): thrombophilia, portal hypertension, malignancy Which investigation is best and why CT angiography (triphasic) urgently – sensitivity/specificity > 90% Do not delay CT for a normal lactate or creatinine Outline the management of embolic AMI Immediate unfractionated heparin Urgent revascularisation: endovascular (aspiration, stent) or open embolectomy Laparotomy to assess viability and resect necrotic bowel; second-look at 24–48 h Fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics Long-term anticoagulation for AF

When should enteral nutrition start in ventilated patients? Explain why Within 24–48 h of ICU admission once haemodynamically stable (ESPEN 2023, ASPEN 2022) Maintains gut barrier integrity and immune function; reduces infection Early EN preferred over early PN and over delayed EN When should early enteral nutrition be delayed Uncontrolled shock (escalating vasopressors, rising lactate) Uncontrolled life-threatening hypoxaemia, hypercapnia or acidosis Active upper GI bleeding; overt bowel ischaemia; high-output fistula; abdominal compartment syndrome Gastric aspirate > 500 mL/6 h Describe the energy and protein targets in the first week Start hypocaloric/trophic: ≤ 70% of energy needs in the early phase (days 1–3), increasing to 80–100% after day 3 Use indirect calorimetry if available; otherwise 20–25 kcal/kg/day Protein 1.3 g/kg/day reached progressively (EFFORT Protein: high protein no benefit, possible harm in AKI) Avoid overfeeding (hyperglycaemia, increased CO2 production, liver dysfunction)

When would you start parenteral nutrition, and what is the evidence If EN is contraindicated or not tolerated: start PN within 3–7 days in well-nourished patients (ESPEN) Start PN early (asap) if severely malnourished or high nutritional risk EPaNIC (2011): early PN (day 2) vs late (day 8) – late PN had fewer infections and faster recovery CALORIES (2014): route (EN vs PN) did not affect mortality when calories similar How do you assess nutritional risk in the ICU NUTRIC score (age, APACHE II, SOFA, comorbidities, days in hospital before ICU, IL-6) – ≥ 5 high risk NRS-2002 ≥ 5 high risk; GLIM criteria for malnutrition Clinical: weight loss, low intake, muscle mass loss (ultrasound/CT) What is the role of gastric residual volume monitoring Routine GRV monitoring is not needed in most patients If used, delay EN only when GRV > 500 mL/6 h Manage intolerance with prokinetics (erythromycin, metoclopramide) and post-pyloric feeding

How is thyroid storm diagnosed Clinical diagnosis: thyrotoxicosis with organ decompensation (hyperthermia, CNS dysfunction, tachycardia/AF/heart failure, GI–hepatic dysfunction) Burch–Wartofsky score ≥ 45 highly suggestive (25–44 impending) Precipitant: surgery, infection, childbirth, iodine contrast, stopping antithyroid drugs Outline the management in order, with drugs and doses β-blocker: propranolol 60–80 mg orally 4–6-hourly (also blocks T4→T3) or esmolol infusion if heart failure concern Thionamide: PTU 500–1000 mg load then 250 mg 4-hourly (blocks synthesis and peripheral conversion) or methimazole 20 mg 4–6-hourly Iodine (Lugol's or potassium iodide) at least 1 h AFTER the thionamide – blocks release of stored hormone Hydrocortisone 100 mg 8-hourly (reduces T4→T3; treats relative adrenal insufficiency) Supportive: cooling, paracetamol (avoid aspirin – displaces T4 from binding proteins), fluids, treat precipitant; cholestyramine; plasmapheresis/thyroidectomy if refractory Why is iodine given 1 hour after the thionamide Iodine given first provides substrate for new hormone synthesis → can worsen thyrotoxicosis Thionamide first blocks thyroid peroxidase (organification), so the iodine cannot be used to make more hormone Iodine then inhibits release of preformed hormone (Wolff–Chaikoff effect)

Explain the mechanisms of thyrotoxic heart failure High-output state: increased metabolic demand, reduced SVR, increased blood volume Tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy (AF with rapid rate) → low-output failure Direct T3 effects on myocyte genes (α-myosin, SERCA) and arrhythmias How would you manage his rate and heart failure Short-acting β1 blocker (esmolol) titrated – rapid off if hypotension Avoid large doses of propranolol in decompensated heart failure; consider digoxin (higher doses needed) or amiodarone (caution: iodine load) Diuretics and ventilatory support as needed Anticoagulation for AF (high stroke risk in thyrotoxicosis) When are second-line therapies indicated Failure of medical therapy in 24–48 h or intolerance of thionamides (agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity) Therapeutic plasma exchange to remove circulating hormone Urgent thyroidectomy after preparation; ECMO for cardiogenic shock

What are the precipitants and clinical features of myxoedema coma Precipitants: infection, cold, surgery, stopping thyroxine, sedatives/opioids, stroke, amiodarone, lithium Features: decreased consciousness, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation Hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, pericardial effusion, ileus, non-pitting oedema What is the first drug treatment? Explain the order Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV 8-hourly FIRST (or together) until adrenal insufficiency excluded Thyroxine increases cortisol metabolism → may precipitate adrenal crisis IV levothyroxine 200–400 µg loading dose (lower in elderly/cardiac), then 1.6 µg/kg/day (75% IV) ± IV liothyronine (T3) 5–20 µg then 2.5–10 µg 8-hourly in selected patients (arrhythmia risk) Outline the supportive management Intubation/ventilation for hypoventilation and hypercapnia Passive rewarming (active rewarming can cause vasodilatation and collapse) Treat hyponatraemia (fluid restriction; hypertonic saline if severe/symptomatic) and hypoglycaemia Look for and treat infection; avoid sedatives

Explain how amiodarone affects thyroid function Contains 37% iodine by weight → large iodine load Hypothyroidism: Wolff–Chaikoff effect (failure to escape), especially with autoimmune thyroiditis Thyrotoxicosis: type 1 (iodine-induced synthesis) and type 2 (destructive thyroiditis) Why does hypothyroidism cause failure to wean Reduced hypoxic and hypercapnic ventilatory drive Respiratory muscle weakness (myopathy), diaphragm dysfunction Macroglossia, upper airway oedema, pleural effusions, obesity; sleep apnoea How would you treat his hypothyroidism safely Hydrocortisone cover until cortisol checked Cautious levothyroxine replacement (lower starting dose in elderly/cardiac disease) – risk of ischaemia and arrhythmia Review need for amiodarone (cardiology) Drain the effusion if causing tamponade; monitor ECG

State the diagnostic criteria for DKA Ketonaemia ≥ 3 mmol/L (or ketonuria ≥ 2+) Glucose > 11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) or known diabetes pH < 7.3 and/or HCO3 < 15 mmol/L She has severe DKA (pH < 7.1) What is the next step after starting IV fluids? Explain why Give IV potassium replacement and DELAY insulin until K ≥ 3.3–3.5 mmol/L Insulin drives K into cells → fatal hypokalaemia (arrhythmia, respiratory muscle weakness) Potassium 20–40 mmol/h (via central line if high concentration), with cardiac monitoring Once K ≥ 3.5: fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h; continue K in fluids (40 mmol/L when K 3.5–5.5) Describe the fluid regimen, targets and resolution criteria 0.9% saline or balanced crystalloid 1 L over 1 h, then 1 L over 2 h, 2 h, 4 h, 4 h (adjust to age/heart) Add 10% dextrose when glucose < 14 mmol/L, continuing insulin to clear ketones Targets: ketones fall ≥ 0.5 mmol/L/h, HCO3 rise ≥ 3 mmol/L/h, glucose fall 3 mmol/L/h Resolution: ketones < 0.6 mmol/L and pH > 7.3 (HCO3 > 15) Bicarbonate not recommended unless pH < 6.9–7.0

What is the diagnosis and why does it happen Euglycaemic DKA associated with SGLT2 inhibitors SGLT2 inhibitors cause glycosuria (lower glucose), reduce insulin and raise glucagon → ketogenesis Precipitated by surgery, fasting, acute illness, dose reduction of insulin How does management differ from classic DKA Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor Start dextrose (10%) early with the fixed-rate insulin because glucose is not high Diagnosis is missed if relying on glucose – check ketones in ill patients on SGLT2i Compare DKA and HHS HHS: glucose > 30 mmol/L (540 mg/dL), osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg, no significant ketosis (< 3 mmol/L), pH > 7.3 HHS: profound dehydration (100–220 mL/kg), older patients, higher mortality HHS: fluid first; insulin only when glucose stops falling with fluids (0.05 U/kg/h) HHS: aim slow correction (osmolality fall 3–8 mOsm/kg/h, Na fall ≤ 10 mmol/L/24 h); high VTE risk – prophylactic LMWH

Outline the treatment of candidaemia Echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) as initial therapy Step down to fluconazole after 5–7 days if isolate susceptible and patient clinically stable with negative repeat cultures Remove the central venous catheter as soon as possible Treat for 14 days after the first negative blood culture and resolution of symptoms What further investigations are needed Repeat blood cultures daily or every other day until negative Dilated fundoscopy (ophthalmology) within the first week to exclude endophthalmitis Echocardiography (TTE/TOE) if persistent candidaemia or suspicion of endocarditis List the risk factors for invasive candidiasis in the ICU Central venous catheters, total parenteral nutrition Broad-spectrum antibiotics, abdominal surgery (especially anastomotic leak), pancreatitis Candida colonisation at multiple sites, renal replacement therapy Immunosuppression, steroids, prolonged ICU stay

How would you decide whether to start empirical antifungal therapy Candida score (TPN 1, surgery 1, multifocal colonisation 1, severe sepsis 2) ≥ 3 → high risk Colonisation index ≥ 0.5 (number of sites colonised / sites cultured) Serum β-D-glucan (high negative predictive value) to support or rule out Empirical echinocandin reasonable in high-risk septic patients; stop if β-D-glucan negative and no improvement (EMPIRICUS: no benefit in unselected patients) What are the limitations of blood cultures and β-D-glucan Blood cultures positive in only ~50% of invasive candidiasis β-D-glucan false positives: haemodialysis cellulose membranes, albumin/IVIG, gauze, bacteraemia β-D-glucan not specific to Candida (also Aspergillus, Pneumocystis) Name the Candida species with resistance concerns C. glabrata (Nakaseomyces): reduced fluconazole susceptibility, emerging echinocandin resistance C. krusei (Pichia kudriavzevii): intrinsically fluconazole resistant C. auris: multidrug resistant, outbreaks, needs infection control

What is the diagnosis and the pathophysiology Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (menstrual) Exotoxin TSST-1 (or enterotoxins) acts as a superantigen Binds MHC class II and T-cell receptor outside the antigen site → massive T-cell activation and cytokine storm → shock and multi-organ failure Outline the antibiotic and adjunctive treatment, explaining the role of clindamycin Remove source (tampon), drain/debride any focus β-lactam with anti-staphylococcal activity (flucloxacillin/cefazolin; vancomycin if MRSA risk) PLUS clindamycin 600–900 mg IV 8-hourly Clindamycin inhibits protein synthesis (50S) → stops toxin production; effective regardless of inoculum size (no Eagle effect) IVIG (neutralising antibodies against superantigens) in severe/refractory cases, especially streptococcal TSS Compare staphylococcal and streptococcal TSS Strep TSS: usually from invasive soft-tissue infection (necrotising fasciitis), severe pain Strep: blood cultures positive in > 50%; staph: usually negative Strep TSS mortality higher (30–70%) Staph: desquamation of palms/soles 1–2 weeks later

What is the likely diagnosis and how would you confirm it Necrotising soft tissue infection (necrotising fasciitis), possibly with streptococcal toxic shock Clinical diagnosis: pain out of proportion, rapid spread, bullae, crepitus, systemic toxicity LRINEC score ≥ 6 suggestive (poor sensitivity); CT may show gas; do not delay surgery for imaging Describe the management Urgent surgical debridement (within hours) and repeated re-look surgery Broad-spectrum antibiotics: piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem + clindamycin (+ vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA) Resuscitation and organ support IVIG in streptococcal TSS (some evidence); hyperbaric O2 not routinely recommended Classify necrotising fasciitis by microbiology Type I: polymicrobial (anaerobes + Gram-negatives), diabetics, perineal (Fournier's) Type II: monomicrobial – group A Streptococcus (± S. aureus) Type III: Clostridium (gas gangrene) or Vibrio vulnificus

Explain what each ROTEM test measures EXTEM: extrinsic pathway (tissue factor) – CT reflects clotting factors; MCF reflects overall clot firmness (platelets + fibrinogen) FIBTEM: EXTEM + cytochalasin D (blocks platelets) → fibrinogen contribution to clot INTEM: intrinsic pathway (heparin effect if compared with HEPTEM) APTEM: aprotinin/TXA added – correction compared with EXTEM indicates hyperfibrinolysis Interpret his ROTEM results Low EXTEM MCF + very low FIBTEM MCF → main driver is severe hypofibrinogenaemia Platelet contribution = EXTEM MCF − FIBTEM MCF = 24 mm (also reduced → secondary platelet deficit) Normal CT → clotting factors adequate; APTEM same as EXTEM → no hyperfibrinolysis Outline the targeted treatment Fibrinogen replacement first: fibrinogen concentrate 3–4 g or cryoprecipitate (target FIBTEM MCF > 10–12 mm, fibrinogen > 1.5–2 g/L) Then platelets if EXTEM MCF still low despite normal FIBTEM (target > 50 ×10^9/L) Tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 h of injury then 1 g over 8 h (CRASH-2) Keep Ca2+ > 1.1, temperature > 35 °C, pH > 7.2 Repeat ROTEM after each intervention

Describe damage control resuscitation Permissive hypotension: SBP 80–90 mmHg until bleeding controlled (not in TBI: MAP ≥ 80) Early balanced blood products (RBC:FFP:platelets ~1:1:1, PROPPR); minimise crystalloid Early TXA (within 3 h) Rapid haemorrhage control: damage control surgery or angioembolisation (REBOA in selected) Define the 'lethal diamond' and how to prevent each component Hypothermia: warm fluids, forced-air warmers, warm theatre Acidosis: restore perfusion, limit saline Coagulopathy: early plasma, fibrinogen, viscoelastic guidance Hypocalcaemia: monitor ionised Ca, give calcium chloride Define massive transfusion ≥ 10 units RBC in 24 h, or replacement of one blood volume in 24 h Or ≥ 4 units in 1 h with ongoing need, or replacement of 50% blood volume in 3 h

Calculate his 4Ts score and interpret it Thrombocytopenia: > 50% fall, nadir ≥ 20 → 2 points Timing: day 5–10 → 2 points Thrombosis: new thrombosis → 2 points Other causes: none apparent → 2 points Total 8 (6–8 = high probability) What should be done now Stop all heparin, including flushes and LMWH (cross-reactivity) Start a non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban (hepatic clearance, preferred in renal failure), bivalirudin, fondaparinux or a DOAC Do not transfuse platelets (unless bleeding); do not start warfarin until platelets ≥ 150 (venous limb gangrene) Send immunoassay (anti-PF4) then functional assay (SRA/HIPA) to confirm Explain the pathophysiology of HIT IgG antibodies against heparin–platelet factor 4 (PF4) complexes Immune complexes bind platelet Fc receptors → platelet activation Thrombin generation → venous and arterial thrombosis (prothrombotic despite low platelets) Platelets consumed and cleared → thrombocytopenia

How would you anticoagulate her for bypass Check antibodies: if functional assay now negative (> 100 days or negative test) heparin may be used briefly for bypass only If antibodies still present (acute/subacute HIT): delay surgery if possible If urgent: bivalirudin for bypass, or plasma exchange before heparin, or heparin + antiplatelet (cangrelor/tirofiban) Avoid heparin entirely after surgery (flushes, LMWH) – use non-heparin anticoagulant Compare the non-heparin anticoagulants Argatroban: direct thrombin inhibitor, hepatic metabolism, monitored by aPTT, raises INR Bivalirudin: direct thrombin inhibitor, short half-life, partly renal Fondaparinux: factor Xa inhibitor, renal, long half-life DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban): used in stable patients without severe renal failure When should warfarin be started and how long should anticoagulation continue Start warfarin only when platelets ≥ 150 ×10^9/L, at low dose, overlapping ≥ 5 days with a parenteral agent until INR therapeutic Isolated HIT (no thrombosis): anticoagulate until platelets recover (often up to 4 weeks–3 months) HIT with thrombosis: 3 months

What is the reversal agent and dose Andexanet alfa – recombinant modified factor Xa decoy that binds factor Xa inhibitors Dose: high dose (800 mg bolus + 960 mg infusion) if rivaroxaban > 10 mg taken < 8 h ago; otherwise low dose (400 mg + 480 mg) ANNEXA-I (2024): better haemostatic efficacy than usual care in ICH, but more thrombotic events Alternative if andexanet unavailable: 4-factor PCC 50 U/kg (or 25–50 U/kg) Outline the other parts of his ICH management BP: lower SBP to target 140 mmHg (avoid < 130) within 1 h (INTERACT-3 care bundle) Activated charcoal if within 2–4 h of ingestion Neurosurgical review; glucose, temperature control; repeat CT for expansion How would you reverse dabigatran and warfarin Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV (monoclonal antibody fragment); haemodialysis removes dabigatran Warfarin: 4-factor PCC 25–50 U/kg (by INR) + vitamin K 5–10 mg IV Check drug-specific levels (anti-Xa calibrated, dilute thrombin time) when available

How would you manage her anticoagulation before surgery Assess urgency vs time since last dose (apixaban half-life ~12 h; longer in renal failure) Check anti-Xa level calibrated for apixaban if available (< 30–50 ng/mL usually safe for surgery) If surgery cannot wait and level is significant: 4F-PCC 25–50 U/kg (andexanet licensed for life-threatening bleeding, not surgery in many countries) Tranexamic acid during surgery if bleeding When can anticoagulation be restarted after surgery Prophylactic LMWH 6–12 h after surgery if haemostasis secure Therapeutic DOAC 24 h after low-bleeding-risk and 48–72 h after high-bleeding-risk surgery Balance thrombosis risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) against bleeding Compare the pharmacology of DOACs relevant to reversal Dabigatran: direct thrombin inhibitor, 80% renal excretion, dialysable Rivaroxaban/apixaban/edoxaban: factor Xa inhibitors, highly protein-bound, not dialysable Standard coagulation tests are unreliable (PT may be normal on apixaban) Specific reversal: idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet (Xa inhibitors)

What are the indications for thoracotomy in a trauma patient with haemothorax Initial drainage of > 1500 mL of blood on chest drain insertion Ongoing drainage > 200 mL/h for 2–4 h Persistent haemodynamic instability or ongoing need for transfusion despite resuscitation This patient meets the criteria → urgent thoracotomy What are the other life-threatening chest injuries to identify in the primary survey Tension pneumothorax Open pneumothorax Massive haemothorax Cardiac tamponade Flail chest with pulmonary contusion Airway obstruction/tracheobronchial injury Describe the immediate resuscitation Large-bore IV access, activate massive transfusion protocol, balanced products Permissive hypotension until surgical control (in penetrating trauma) TXA within 3 h; avoid hypothermia Consider autotransfusion from the chest drain

State the indications for resuscitative (ED) thoracotomy Penetrating thoracic trauma with traumatic cardiac arrest and signs of life within the last 15 min (best outcomes) Penetrating non-thoracic trauma with arrest < 5 min (lower survival) Blunt trauma with arrest < 10 min – very poor outcome; generally not recommended Requires skills and equipment available (within 10 min of arrest) What are the aims of resuscitative thoracotomy Release cardiac tamponade (pericardiotomy) Control cardiac or great vessel haemorrhage Cross-clamp the descending aorta to redirect blood to brain and heart Internal cardiac massage and defibrillation; treat air embolism How does traumatic cardiac arrest differ from medical cardiac arrest Treat reversible causes first (hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, hypoxia) – HOTT Chest compressions have lower priority than addressing causes Bilateral thoracostomies and rapid volume replacement with blood Adrenaline has a limited role in hypovolaemic arrest

boxes.t: Septic shock in severe CAP and vasopressors — June Q1
boxes.x: Outline your resuscitation and antimicrobial strategy in the first hours Balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg in the first 3 h, further fluid only if fluid-responsive (dynamic tests, CRT, lactate trend) Target MAP ≥ 65 mmHg; noradrenaline early, peripheral line acceptable until a central line is placed Cultures (blood × 2, sputum/ETA), urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigens, respiratory PCR – without delaying antibiotics Antibiotics within 1 h: β-lactam (e.g., ceftriaxone 2 g) + macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg); antipseudomonal/anti-MRSA cover only if risk factors Source/organ support: lung-protective ventilation if intubated, lactate re-measured within 2–4 h Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if noradrenaline ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h; in severe CAP early hydrocortisone reduces mortality (CAPE COD 2023) Compare the mechanism of action of noradrenaline and vasopressin Noradrenaline: potent α1 agonist (Gq → IP3 → intracellular Ca2+ → vasoconstriction) with modest β1 inotropy Vasopressin: V1a receptor on vascular smooth muscle (Gq → IP3/Ca2+), independent of adrenergic receptors Septic shock causes relative vasopressin deficiency; vasopressin also closes K-ATP channels and restores catecholamine sensitivity Vasopressin may spare the kidney (efferent > afferent constriction); can cause digital/mesenteric ischaemia Compare the mechanism of action of adrenaline and angiotensin II Adrenaline: α1, β1 and β2 agonist → vasoconstriction plus inotropy/chronotropy β2 stimulation of muscle glycolysis raises lactate (type B), tachyarrhythmias and hyperglycaemia Angiotensin II: AT1 receptor (Gq → IP3/DAG) → arteriolar constriction, aldosterone and vasopressin release Angiotensin II raised MAP in catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock (ATHOS-3); thrombosis risk, avoid in mesenteric ischaemia Describe your stepwise vasopressor escalation with supporting trial evidence Noradrenaline first line (SOAP II: dopamine more arrhythmias); MAP 65 is enough (SEPSISPAM; 65 trial in ≥ 65 years) Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min when noradrenaline 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min (VASST, VANISH: noradrenaline-sparing, no mortality difference) Echo to look for septic cardiomyopathy: add dobutamine or switch/add adrenaline if low cardiac output Refractory shock: angiotensin II (ATHOS-3) or methylene blue as rescue; re-check source, fluids, adrenal function Noradrenaline first; add vasopressin at 0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min; hydrocortisone if shock persists.

boxes.t: Upper GI bleeding on DAPT after STEMI — June Q2
boxes.x: Discuss resuscitation, transfusion targets and the evidence for haemostatic adjuncts (desmopressin, platelets, tranexamic acid) Airway protection if ongoing haematemesis or reduced consciousness; two large-bore IV lines, cross-match, activate massive haemorrhage protocol if needed Restrictive transfusion (Hb 7–8 g/dL) in GI bleeding generally; in recent ACS aim higher, around Hb 8–10 g/dL (MINT 2023 favoured liberal in MI) IV PPI bolus then infusion or high-dose intermittent; erythromycin 250 mg IV 30–120 min before endoscopy Platelet transfusion is not routinely recommended to reverse antiplatelet drugs in GI bleeding; ticagrelor's active drug also inhibits transfused platelets (PATCH showed harm in ICH, not GIB) Tranexamic acid not recommended: HALT-IT (12,009 pts) no mortality benefit and more venous thromboembolism Desmopressin has no good evidence in GI bleeding on antiplatelets; may be considered only as rescue Correct calcium and temperature; balanced product ratio if massive transfusion Discuss stent thrombosis risk and when to resume aspirin and the P2Y12 inhibitor Recent DES (< 30 days) with stopped DAPT has high stent thrombosis risk with high mortality (MI, death) Continue aspirin if possible; if stopped, resume as soon as haemostasis is secured, ideally within 24–72 h (stopping it raised death in Sung 2010) Hold ticagrelor only while bleeding is uncontrolled; resume within about 3–5 days of haemostasis, joint cardiology–GI decision Consider switching to clopidogrel (less potent) and keep long-term PPI co-therapy Outline medical, endoscopic, radiological and surgical management Endoscopy within 24 h, earlier (< 12 h) after resuscitation if haemodynamically unstable; Forrest classification guides therapy Combined endoscopic therapy: adrenaline injection plus a mechanical (clips) or thermal method; haemostatic powder or over-the-scope clip as rescue Re-bleeding: repeat endoscopy once; then transcatheter arterial embolisation (first salvage) Surgery (under-running of the ulcer) if embolisation fails or is unavailable; post-endoscopy high-dose PPI for 72 h, test and treat H. pylori No platelets, no TXA (HALT-IT), no good evidence for desmopressin; PATCH was in ICH, not GI bleeding. Restart aspirin early.

boxes.t: Refractory status epilepticus, PRIS, ketamine and pyridoxine — June Q3
boxes.x: Discuss the use, dosing and monitoring of midazolam, propofol and barbiturate infusions First line benzodiazepine (lorazepam 4 mg IV, midazolam 10 mg IM/IV, repeat once); second line levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg or valproate 40 mg/kg (ESETT: equal efficacy) Refractory SE: intubate, start continuous EEG; target seizure control or burst suppression for 24–48 h then wean Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg bolus then 0.05–2 mg/kg/h: haemodynamically stable but tachyphylaxis and accumulation in renal failure Propofol 1–2 mg/kg then 2–5 mg/kg/h: fast on/off; hypotension, hypertriglyceridaemia, avoid > 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 h (PRIS) Thiopental/pentobarbital: very effective but hypotension, myocardial depression, ileus, immunosuppression and prolonged half-life Monitor arterial pressure, vasopressor need, lactate, CK, triglycerides, and EEG for non-convulsive seizures Continue maintenance antiseizure drugs and search for the cause in parallel Describe the pathophysiology, features and management of propofol infusion syndrome Propofol impairs mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation and the respiratory chain → cellular energy failure in heart and muscle Risk: dose > 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 h, young age, catecholamines or steroids, low carbohydrate intake, critical illness Features: unexplained metabolic (lactic) acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, AKI, hepatomegaly, Brugada-like ECG, bradyarrhythmia and heart failure Stop propofol immediately; supportive care, glucose supply, RRT for acidosis/hyperkalaemia, pacing or ECMO for cardiac failure (lipid emulsion is NOT a treatment) Explain the rationale and indications for ketamine and pyridoxine Prolonged SE internalises GABA-A receptors and up-regulates NMDA receptors → benzodiazepine resistance Ketamine (NMDA antagonist) targets this mechanism; bolus 1–3 mg/kg then 1–10 mg/kg/h; supports blood pressure and allows lower vasopressor doses Pyridoxine (B6) is the cofactor for GAD, which makes GABA; isoniazid toxicity depletes it Give pyridoxine 1 g per g of isoniazid ingested (5 g IV if unknown); also in infant pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy PRIS: stop propofol and support; lipid emulsion is NOT a treatment. Ketamine targets NMDA up-regulation.

boxes.t: CRRT versus intermittent haemodialysis and anticoagulation — June Q4
boxes.x: Compare CRRT and intermittent haemodialysis in outcome, haemodynamics and solute clearance Mortality: no difference between CRRT and IHD in RCTs and meta-analyses (e.g., Hemodiafe 2006) CRRT gives slower fluid and solute removal → better haemodynamic tolerance in shock; preferred in haemodynamic instability (KDIGO) CRRT avoids rapid osmolar shifts and cerebral oedema → preferred in brain injury, acute liver failure (raised ICP) IHD clears small solutes faster: better for urgent hyperkalaemia and dialysable poisoning, needs fewer nursing resources and allows mobilisation Dose: delivered effluent 20–25 mL/kg/h is enough (RENAL, ATN trials); prescribe ~25–30 to allow for downtime Observational data suggest more dialysis dependence after IHD as first modality, but not proven in RCTs Timing: no benefit of very early start (STARRT-AKI, AKIKI); harm with very late start (AKIKI-2) Compare regional citrate, heparin and no-anticoagulation strategies for CRRT Regional citrate: chelates ionised calcium in the circuit (post-filter iCa 0.25–0.35 mmol/L), calcium is replaced systemically (iCa 1.0–1.2) KDIGO recommends citrate first line when not contraindicated: longer filter life, less bleeding than heparin Citrate accumulation in liver failure or shock (poor metabolism): total/ionised Ca ratio > 2.5, rising anion gap and acidosis Other citrate risks: metabolic alkalosis (citrate → bicarbonate), hypo-/hypercalcaemia, hypernatraemia Unfractionated heparin: cheap and reversible, aPTT 1.5× or anti-Xa monitoring; risks bleeding and HIT Monitoring: post-filter and systemic iCa every 6 h, adjust citrate and calcium infusions; daily total Ca, Na, bicarbonate No anticoagulation: when bleeding or severe coagulopathy; use predilution, high blood flow, minimise circuit interruptions Same mortality; CRRT for shock and raised ICP; citrate first line, watch total/ionised Ca > 2.5.

boxes.t: Weaning failure, diaphragm ultrasound, P0.1 and CROP — June Q5
boxes.x: List the causes of weaning failure by system Respiratory load: bronchospasm, secretions, high resistance (small ETT), low compliance (oedema, effusion, atelectasis), auto-PEEP Cardiac (weaning-induced pulmonary oedema): negative intrathoracic pressure raises venous return and LV afterload, plus catecholamine surge → ischaemia, raised LV filling pressure Neuromuscular: ICU-acquired weakness (CIP/CIM), diaphragm dysfunction (ventilator-induced, phrenic injury), residual sedation/NMB Metabolic: low phosphate, potassium, magnesium; hypothyroidism; anaemia; malnutrition; metabolic alkalosis reducing drive Fluid overload and positive balance: diurese before the next SBT Psychological and central: delirium, anxiety, sleep deprivation; excess or reduced respiratory drive Describe ultrasound assessment of the diaphragm Excursion: M-mode, low-frequency probe subcostally through the liver window; normal quiet breathing ≥ 1–1.5 cm Excursion < 1 cm suggests dysfunction and higher weaning failure risk; measure during spontaneous breathing (unsupported) Thickening fraction: high-frequency probe at the zone of apposition (8th–10th intercostal space), (end-inspiratory − end-expiratory thickness) / end-expiratory × 100 Thickening fraction < 20–30% predicts SBT failure; low thickness over time indicates ventilator-induced atrophy Explain P0.1 and the CROP index P0.1: airway pressure drop in the first 100 ms of an occluded inspiration; reflects central drive, independent of muscle strength Normal about 1–2 cmH2O; > 3.5–4 cmH2O suggests high drive/load and likely weaning failure; very low suggests over-assistance CROP = [dynamic compliance × maximal inspiratory pressure × (PaO2/PAO2)] / respiratory rate CROP ≥ 13 mL/breath/min predicts weaning success; combines mechanics, strength, gas exchange and rate (compare RSBI < 105) Diaphragm excursion < 1 cm or TF < 20–30% and P0.1 > 3.5–4 predict failure; CROP ≥ 13 predicts success.

boxes.t: Brain stem death and organ donation — June Q6
boxes.x: List the preconditions and exclusions before brain stem testing Known cause of irreversible structural brain damage; apnoeic coma on the ventilator Exclude depressant drugs (allow clearance or measure levels), neuromuscular blockade (train-of-four), hypothermia (core temperature > 34 °C) Correct metabolic and endocrine causes: Na 115–160 mmol/L, K > 2, glucose 3–20 mmol/L, Mg and PO4 within limits Stable circulation (MAP > 60 mmHg), normocapnia and normal pH before testing Describe the clinical brain stem tests and the apnoea test Absent pupillary light reflex, corneal reflex, oculovestibular (caloric) reflex No motor response in the cranial nerve distribution to central pain; absent gag and cough (tracheal suction) Apnoea test: pre-oxygenate with 100% O2; start PaCO2 ≥ 6.0 kPa (45 mmHg), pH < 7.40; disconnect with O2 insufflation via a catheter or CPAP No respiratory effort for 5 min with PaCO2 rising > 0.5 kPa (UK); US criteria PaCO2 ≥ 60 mmHg and ≥ 20 mmHg above baseline Two senior doctors (≥ 5 years registered, one consultant, not from the transplant team) perform two sets of tests; time of death is after the first set Ancillary tests (CT angiography, perfusion scan, EEG) only when the clinical tests cannot be completed How would you manage the conflict between the sons about organ donation Check for the patient's own wishes first: donor registry, advance directive or what he said; this has priority If unknown, ask both sons what their father would have wanted (substituted judgement), not what they want Hold a calm family meeting with the specialist donation nurse/team; separate the death conversation from the donation request; allow time Follow local law on consent and next of kin; in practice donation does not proceed against a firm objection of close family; document and offer support Patient's own wishes first; family conflict → do not proceed, support and document.

boxes.t: Post-ROSC care and temperature control — June Q7
boxes.x: Outline your immediate post-ROSC bundle Airway and ventilation: SpO2 94–98% (avoid hyperoxia), normocapnia PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, lung-protective volumes Circulation: MAP > 65 mmHg with fluids, noradrenaline ± dobutamine; urine output > 0.5 mL/kg/h, falling lactate; echo Coronary angiography: emergent if ST elevation or haemodynamic/electrical instability; otherwise not routine immediately (COACT, TOMAHAWK) Glucose control, treat seizures (EEG), sedation, search for the cause (CT head/chest if indicated) Compare the TTM1 and TTM2 trials and current guidance on temperature TTM1 (2013, n = 950): 33 °C vs 36 °C – no difference in mortality or neurological outcome TTM2 (2021, n = 1,900): 33 °C vs normothermia with fever treatment (≤ 37.5 °C) – no difference in 6-month mortality (50% vs 48%) or function; more arrhythmia with hypothermia ERC-ESICM: monitor core temperature and actively prevent fever (> 37.7 °C) for at least 72 h in comatose patients Hypothermia 32–36 °C is no longer routinely recommended; avoid prehospital cold fluids How would you manage shivering and hypotension during temperature control Assess shivering with the Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale (BSAS) Step-up: paracetamol, skin counter-warming, magnesium, buspirone → opioid (pethidine/fentanyl) or dexmedetomidine → propofol → neuromuscular blocker Hypotension: cold diuresis and vasodilation on rewarming → fluids guided by responsiveness, noradrenaline Myocardial stunning: echo, dobutamine; consider mechanical support in cardiogenic shock TTM2: no benefit of 33 °C; prevent fever > 37.7 °C for 72 h.

boxes.t: Neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest — June Q8
boxes.x: When and how should prognostication be done, and how do you avoid bias Not before 72 h after ROSC, in a patient with motor score ≤ 3, after excluding sedatives, NMB, hypothermia, hypotension, metabolic causes Use a multimodal approach – never a single predictor Self-fulfilling prophecy: withdrawal based on a poor prediction makes the prediction come true; use guideline-based criteria and repeat exams If uncertain, continue support and reassess; consider organ donation pathway if withdrawal is decided List the clinical and electrophysiological predictors of poor outcome Bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at ≥ 72 h (quantitative pupillometry helps) Status myoclonus within 72 h (generalised, persistent; EEG to separate from Lance-Adams) Bilaterally absent N20 SSEP waves at ≥ 24 h Highly malignant EEG after 24 h: suppressed background ± periodic discharges, or burst-suppression Describe the role of biomarkers and imaging, and the decision rule Neuron-specific enolase > 60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h (falsely high with haemolysis) Diffuse anoxic injury: CT loss of grey–white differentiation (GWR reduced), MRI diffusion restriction at 2–7 days Poor outcome is likely if ≥ 2 of the predictors are present (ERC-ESICM 2021) If criteria are not met, outcome is indeterminate: observe and re-evaluate ≥ 72 h, multimodal, ≥ 2 predictors; avoid self-fulfilling prophecy.

boxes.t: ICP monitoring and tiered management — June Q9
boxes.x: Discuss indications, monitoring methods and the ICP waveform Indications (BTF 4th edition): salvageable severe TBI (GCS 3–8) with abnormal CT; normal CT with ≥ 2 of age > 40, posturing, SBP < 90 mmHg External ventricular drain: gold standard, measures and drains CSF; risks infection and haemorrhage Intraparenchymal microsensor: easy, lower infection, cannot drain or be recalibrated (drift) Waveform P1 (percussion), P2 (tidal, compliance), P3 (dicrotic); P2 > P1 indicates poor compliance; Lundberg A (plateau) waves are pathological Non-invasive: optic nerve sheath diameter > 5.7–6 mm, TCD pulsatility index, CT signs – screening only Targets: ICP < 22 mmHg, CPP 60–70 mmHg Describe the tiered strategy to reduce ICP Tier 0: head up 30°, neck neutral, sedation/analgesia, normothermia, Na > 135, SpO2 > 94%, PaCO2 35–45, Hb > 7, treat seizures Tier 1: CPP 60–70, increase sedation, intermittent CSF drainage, mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline boluses Hypertonic saline vs mannitol: similar ICP effect; HTS for hypovolaemia/hypotension, mannitol causes diuresis; stop if osmolality > 320 or Na > 155–160 Tier 2: mild hypocapnia 32–35 mmHg, neuromuscular blockade trial, MAP challenge to test autoregulation Tier 3: barbiturate coma (if responsive to test dose), mild hypothermia 35–36 °C, secondary decompressive craniectomy RESCUEicp: craniectomy for refractory ICP lowered mortality but increased survival with severe disability DECRA: early bifrontal craniectomy for moderate ICP worsened outcome; Eurotherm: early hypothermia harmful Avoid in TBI: steroids (CRASH), prophylactic hyperventilation < 30 mmHg, routine hypothermia ICP < 22, CPP 60–70; tiered SIBICC; RESCUEicp = less death, more severe disability.

boxes.t: Fluid responsiveness versus fluid tolerance — June Q10
boxes.x: Define fluid responsiveness and fluid tolerance Responsiveness: stroke volume or cardiac output rises > 10–15% after fluid; the heart works on the steep part of the Frank–Starling curve Only about half of ICU patients are responsive; responsiveness does not mean the patient needs fluid Tolerance: ability to receive fluid without organ congestion Assess intolerance by venous congestion (VExUS score, hepatic/portal/renal Doppler) and lung ultrasound B-lines, rising EVLW Explain PPV and the end-expiratory occlusion test in ventilated patients PPV = (PPmax − PPmin)/PPmean; > 12–13% predicts responsiveness (grey zone 9–13%) PPV limits: needs controlled ventilation without effort, Vt ≥ 8 mL/kg, sinus rhythm, closed chest, normal IAP, HR/RR > 3.6, no RV failure EEOT: hold at end-expiration for 15 s raises venous return; CO rise > 5% predicts response EEOT works with low Vt and arrhythmia but needs real-time CO monitoring and no spontaneous effort during the hold Evaluate IVC variation and passive leg raising Ventilated: IVC distensibility > 12–18% suggests responsiveness; requires passive full ventilation Spontaneous breathing: collapsibility > 40–50% is unreliable (variable effort); unreliable with high IAP, RV failure, tamponade, high PEEP PLR: raises legs 45° from semi-recumbent, moves about 300 mL of venous blood; CO/SV rise > 10% predicts response PLR is valid in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmia; needs real-time CO measurement (not BP), unreliable with intra-abdominal hypertension Responsive ≠ needs fluid; check tolerance (VExUS, B-lines). PLR/EEOT need real-time CO.
